flashcards_qa.front: What is Least privilege? (Principle of Least Privilege)
flashcards_qa.back: Granting only the minimum permissions needed.

flashcards_qa.front: What is IAM Access Analyzer? (Principle of Least Privilege)
flashcards_qa.back: Tool generating least-privilege policies from activity.

flashcards_qa.front: Principle of Least Privilege: What is Least privilege?
flashcards_qa.back: Least privilege = grant only the permissions needed for a task.

flashcards_qa.front: During development a team grants a service broad permissions because they do not yet know exactly what it needs. Is that acceptable, and what must happen before production?
flashcards_qa.back: It is a reasonable development practice, since you often do not yet know which API calls are required. But before production the policy must be locked down to the specific services and operations the workload actually uses.

flashcards_qa.front: You must tighten an over-permissive role but do not know which actions the application actually calls. Which tool helps?
flashcards_qa.back: IAM Access Analyzer, which generates least-privilege policies from observed access activity so you can replace broad permissions with only what was actually used.

flashcards_qa.front: A role was granted s3:* during development and the application now runs in production unchanged. Is that acceptable under least privilege?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Broad development permissions must be locked down once requirements are known, so leaving s3:* in production violates least privilege.

flashcards_qa.front: An ETL job reads only from s3://logs/raw/. How should its IAM policy be scoped?
flashcards_qa.back: To the specific actions it needs, such as s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, on the specific bucket and prefix ARN, rather than s3:* on all resources.

flashcards_qa.front: How should permissions differ between the development and production stages of the same workload?
flashcards_qa.back: Development can start broad while the requirements are still unknown. Production must be locked down to the exact services and operations the workload requires.

flashcards_qa.front: Name two concrete steps for applying least privilege to an existing over-permissioned role.
flashcards_qa.back: Scope actions and resources tightly, naming specific APIs and specific bucket or prefix ARNs, and use IAM Access Analyzer to generate a policy from observed access activity.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Masking? (Data Masking, Anonymization & Salting)
flashcards_qa.back: Obfuscating part of a value (e.g., last 4 digits).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Anonymization? (Data Masking, Anonymization & Salting)
flashcards_qa.back: Replacing data so it's untraceable.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Salt? (Data Masking, Anonymization & Salting)
flashcards_qa.back: A random value added before hashing.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Rainbow table attack? (Data Masking, Anonymization & Salting)
flashcards_qa.back: Precomputed-hash lookup defeated by salting.

flashcards_qa.front: A reporting table must show only the last four digits of each account number. What technique is that, and which two AWS services provide it natively?
flashcards_qa.back: Data masking, which obfuscates part of a value. Glue DataBrew has built-in masking transforms, and Redshift supports CREATE MASKING POLICY for dynamic data masking.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the ways to anonymize data so individuals can no longer be traced?
flashcards_qa.back: Substitution, shuffling, encryption (deterministic or probabilistic), hashing, or simply deleting the field or not importing it at all.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Masking, Anonymization & Salting: What is Salting?
flashcards_qa.back: Salting = add a random salt before hashing to defeat rainbow tables and make identical inputs hash differently.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the requirements for salting hashes correctly?
flashcards_qa.back: Use strong random salts, a unique salt per user, rotate salts periodically, and apply the salt before hashing the value for storage.

flashcards_qa.front: You must encrypt a customer ID but still be able to join on it across tables. Deterministic or probabilistic encryption, and what is the trade-off?
flashcards_qa.back: Deterministic, because the same input always produces the same ciphertext so equality joins still work. Probabilistic encryption produces different output each time, which is more secure but breaks joins.

flashcards_qa.front: Is reusing a single salt for all users acceptable as long as the hash function is strong?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Each user needs a unique salt. Hashing alone is one-way but can collide, and one shared salt lets a single rainbow table attack every record.

flashcards_qa.front: Masked data can no longer be traced back to the individual. True?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Masking only hides part of a value, so the record often remains identifiable. Making an individual untraceable is anonymization.

flashcards_qa.front: Four techniques applied to a PII column: which hides part of it, which makes it untraceable, which is reversible with a key, and which is one-way?
flashcards_qa.back: Masking hides part of the value. Anonymization makes it untraceable. Encryption is reversible with the key. Hashing is one-way and should be salted.

flashcards_qa.front: Two design choices people commonly get wrong are encryption determinism and salt reuse. What is the right call on each?
flashcards_qa.back: Use deterministic encryption only when you need equality or joins, otherwise prefer probabilistic for stronger protection. Always use a unique random salt per user and never reuse one salt.

flashcards_qa.front: Analysts need to segment by ZIP code, must never see SSNs, and there is a legacy full-card-number column with no business use. What do you do with each?
flashcards_qa.back: Keep ZIP, generalizing or anonymizing if required. Mask or salted-hash the SSN so it cannot be read. Delete or simply do not import the card-number column, since deletion is the right technique when there is no business need.

flashcards_qa.front: State the salting best practices you would need on the exam.
flashcards_qa.back: A unique salt per user, strong random salt values, and periodic rotation, with the salt applied before hashing.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SCP? (Preventing Disallowed-Region Backups)
flashcards_qa.back: Service Control Policy (org-wide guardrail).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data residency? (Preventing Disallowed-Region Backups)
flashcards_qa.back: Requirement that data stay in certain regions.

flashcards_qa.front: Regulation requires all data to stay in eu-central-1 across an entire AWS Organization. How do you enforce it?
flashcards_qa.back: Use Organizations SCPs that deny actions outside the allowed Region, conditioned on the requested Region, plus IAM or S3 bucket policies with Region conditions at the account and resource level.

flashcards_qa.front: Which operations most often break data-residency rules without anyone noticing?
flashcards_qa.back: Backups and replication. RDS, Aurora, and Redshift snapshot copies or cross-Region replication can move data out of the permitted Region, so policies must focus on where actions happen.

flashcards_qa.front: How would you detect that someone accidentally copied a snapshot into a disallowed Region?
flashcards_qa.back: CloudTrail records the API call, and CloudWatch (with alarms or EventBridge rules) alerts on it, so the pair catches accidental cross-Region data movement.

flashcards_qa.front: Your S3 bucket policy restricts uploads to one Region. Is data residency now guaranteed?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Cross-Region backups, snapshot copies, and replication can still move data out, so those actions need Region conditions too.

flashcards_qa.front: Can an account administrator override a Region restriction imposed by an Organizations SCP?
flashcards_qa.back: No. SCPs are org-wide guardrails that account admins cannot override. IAM and bucket policies, which live inside the account, can be changed by them.

flashcards_qa.front: You need a Region restriction that even an account administrator cannot remove. Which mechanism?
flashcards_qa.back: An Organizations SCP, because it is an org-wide guardrail. IAM and bucket policies live inside the account and can be changed by its administrators.

flashcards_qa.front: Sketch both the enforcement and the detection design for a data-residency Region restriction on backups.
flashcards_qa.back: Enforce with policies that deny backup and replication actions using a Region condition, applied org-wide via SCPs and reinforced with IAM and bucket policies. Detect with CloudTrail feeding CloudWatch or EventBridge to catch anything that slips through.

flashcards_qa.front: What is IAM user? (IAM Users, Groups & Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: An identity for one person.

flashcards_qa.front: What is IAM group? (IAM Users, Groups & Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: A collection of users (no nested groups).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Inline policy? (IAM Users, Groups & Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: A policy attached to a single user.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Policy statement? (IAM Users, Groups & Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: Effect/Principal/Action/Resource(/Condition).

flashcards_qa.front: Do you need to create separate IAM users in each Region you operate in?
flashcards_qa.back: No. IAM is a global service, so users, groups, roles, and policies are not Region-scoped. After initial setup you should work as IAM users rather than as root.

flashcards_qa.front: Can an IAM group contain another IAM group?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Groups contain only users. A user can belong to multiple groups or to none at all.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you give the same permissions to 20 users, and how do you then grant one of them an exception?
flashcards_qa.back: Attach a JSON policy to a group containing the 20 users, since a group policy applies to all its members. For the one-off, attach an inline policy directly to that single user.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the elements of an IAM policy statement.
flashcards_qa.back: Effect (Allow or Deny), Principal, Action, Resource, and an optional Condition.

flashcards_qa.front: An architect proposes nesting an admins group inside an engineering group. Is that possible?
flashcards_qa.back: No. IAM groups cannot be nested because they contain only users. Add the users to both groups instead.

flashcards_qa.front: Should day-to-day administration be performed with the root account?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Root is for initial account setup only. After that, create IAM users or roles with appropriate permissions for everyday work.

flashcards_qa.front: In an IAM policy statement, which element says what can be done and which says to what?
flashcards_qa.back: Action says what, listing the API operations. Resource says to what, listing the ARNs. Effect allows or denies, Principal is who, and Condition adds optional constraints.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the difference in blast radius between a group policy and an inline policy?
flashcards_qa.back: A group policy applies to every member of that group. An inline policy is attached to a single identity and applies only to it.

flashcards_qa.front: Does the Action element of a policy specify which resources the policy applies to?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Action lists the API operations, while Resource lists the ARNs the operations may be performed on.

flashcards_qa.front: A user belongs to two groups, one allowing s3:GetObject and one denying it, and also has an inline allow. What is the effective outcome?
flashcards_qa.back: Denied. Permissions accumulate across all group, managed, and inline policies, but an explicit Deny anywhere always wins.

flashcards_qa.front: Which two IAM facts about groups and the root account are most often tested?
flashcards_qa.back: Groups contain only users and cannot be nested, and the root account is for setup only, after which you work through IAM users and roles.

flashcards_qa.front: What is MFA? (IAM MFA)
flashcards_qa.back: Multi-Factor Authentication (password + device).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Virtual MFA? (IAM MFA)
flashcards_qa.back: App-based token (Google Authenticator/Authy).

flashcards_qa.front: What is U2F key? (IAM MFA)
flashcards_qa.back: Physical security key (e.g., YubiKey).

flashcards_qa.front: Which IAM feature defends against brute-force password guessing, and what can it enforce?
flashcards_qa.back: An IAM password policy, which can require a minimum length and specific character types, force expiration, and prevent password reuse.

flashcards_qa.front: IAM MFA: What is MFA?
flashcards_qa.back: MFA = password (know) + device (own); recommended for root and all IAM users.

flashcards_qa.front: Which MFA device types does AWS support?
flashcards_qa.back: Virtual MFA apps such as Google Authenticator and Authy, U2F security keys such as YubiKey, hardware key fobs from Gemalto, and SurePassID fobs for GovCloud.

flashcards_qa.front: What two factors does MFA combine?
flashcards_qa.back: Something you know, your password, plus something you own, the MFA device that produces the code.

flashcards_qa.front: A user needs MFA tokens for several AWS accounts on one phone. Which virtual MFA app suits this?
flashcards_qa.back: Authy, because it supports multiple tokens on a single device. Google Authenticator is oriented around one phone with a single token per setup.

flashcards_qa.front: Can one YubiKey (U2F security key) be used by multiple AWS users?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. A single U2F security key supports multiple users.

flashcards_qa.front: Which control mitigates brute-force password attacks, and which mitigates a password that has already been stolen?
flashcards_qa.back: A password policy, with length, complexity, expiry, and reuse rules, mitigates brute force. MFA mitigates a stolen password by requiring a second factor you physically own.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a virtual MFA app and a U2F security key both serve multiple AWS accounts or users?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes, with a caveat. Authy holds multiple tokens on one device and one U2F key supports multiple users, whereas Google Authenticator is oriented around a single device and token per setup.

flashcards_qa.front: State what MFA is and list the AWS device options.
flashcards_qa.back: MFA combines something you know, the password, with something you own, the device. Options are virtual apps (Google Authenticator, Authy), U2F keys (YubiKey), hardware key fobs (Gemalto), and SurePassID for GovCloud.

flashcards_qa.front: What is IAM role? (IAM Roles)
flashcards_qa.back: An identity assumed by services to gain permissions.

flashcards_qa.front: An application running on EC2 needs to read from DynamoDB. What do you attach, and why not credentials?
flashcards_qa.back: An IAM role attached to the instance. Roles grant permissions to AWS services and instances and are assumed rather than owned by a person, so no long-lived keys are stored on the instance.

flashcards_qa.front: Give a concrete example of an IAM role in use.
flashcards_qa.back: An EC2 instance role: the role is attached to the instance, and the application retrieves temporary credentials from instance metadata to access AWS resources.

flashcards_qa.front: Which IAM roles come up most commonly?
flashcards_qa.back: EC2 instance roles, Lambda execution roles, and CloudFormation service roles.

flashcards_qa.front: Is storing an IAM user's access keys in an EC2 application's config file an acceptable way to grant it S3 access?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Attach an IAM role to the instance instead. Roles supply temporary credentials automatically, so long-lived user keys never need to be embedded.

flashcards_qa.front: Who or what assumes an IAM role?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS services and resources, such as EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and CloudFormation, assume roles. Human identities are normally IAM users or federated identities.

flashcards_qa.front: Choose between an IAM role and an IAM user for a data engineer who logs in, and for a Glue job that reads S3.
flashcards_qa.back: The engineer gets an IAM user or a federated identity, because that is a person. The Glue job gets an IAM role, because services and instances assume roles.

flashcards_qa.front: Why are IAM roles the secure alternative to embedding credentials?
flashcards_qa.back: Because the role is assumed by the service and supplies short-lived, automatically rotated credentials, so there are no long-lived access keys to leak in code or configuration.

flashcards_qa.front: What is In-flight encryption? (Encryption 101)
flashcards_qa.back: TLS/SSL protecting data over the network.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Encryption at rest? (Encryption 101)
flashcards_qa.back: Encrypting stored data (server-side).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Client-side encryption? (Encryption 101)
flashcards_qa.back: Client encrypts before upload; server can't read it.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Envelope encryption? (Encryption 101)
flashcards_qa.back: Encrypting a data key with another key.

flashcards_qa.front: Encryption 101: What is Encryption in flight?
flashcards_qa.back: Encryption in flight = TLS/SSL (HTTPS), preventing man-in-the-middle.

flashcards_qa.front: In server-side encryption at rest, who performs the encryption and with what?
flashcards_qa.back: The server, meaning the AWS service, encrypts the data as it stores it using a data key. The client sends plaintext and the service handles encryption.

flashcards_qa.front: Requirement: AWS must never be able to read the plaintext. Which approach, and what technique underpins it?
flashcards_qa.back: Client-side encryption, where you encrypt and decrypt on the client so the server only ever stores ciphertext. It typically uses envelope encryption, with a data key protected by a master key.

flashcards_qa.front: Encryption 101: What distinction is easy to mix up here — network?
flashcards_qa.back: In flight (network) vs at rest (storage) vs client-side (end-to-end).

flashcards_qa.front: Encryption 101: What distinction is easy to mix up here — encryption?
flashcards_qa.back: In flight vs at rest vs client-side encryption.

flashcards_qa.front: With client-side encryption, can the AWS service decrypt your objects?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The service never holds the plaintext or the keys required, so it cannot decrypt the data, which is precisely the point of client-side encryption.

flashcards_qa.front: Does server-side encryption at rest prevent AWS from reading your plaintext?
flashcards_qa.back: No. With server-side encryption the service holds the data key and performs the encryption, so it can decrypt. Only client-side encryption keeps plaintext away from AWS.

flashcards_qa.front: What is KMS key? (AWS KMS)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed encryption key (symmetric/asymmetric).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Customer managed key? (AWS KMS)
flashcards_qa.back: Your own KMS key ($1/mo; supports custom policies).

flashcards_qa.front: What is KMS key policy? (AWS KMS)
flashcards_qa.back: Resource policy controlling key access.

flashcards_qa.front: What is CloudTrail? (AWS KMS)
flashcards_qa.back: Audits every KMS key-use API call.

flashcards_qa.front: You must prove who used an encryption key and when. Which service, and where is the audit trail?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS KMS manages the keys and integrates with IAM, and every key-use API call is recorded in CloudTrail, which provides the audit trail.

flashcards_qa.front: If a KMS key has no key policy, can an account administrator still use it?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Without a key policy nobody has access. The key policy controls access, and custom key policies are what enable cross-account use.

flashcards_qa.front: Which KMS key type do AWS services use, and when do you need the other type?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS services use symmetric keys, and the key material is never exposed to you. Asymmetric keys, with a public/private pair, are for encryption or signing outside AWS where callers only hold the public key.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the three KMS key ownership types, their cost, and which one lets you import your own key material.
flashcards_qa.back: AWS owned keys are free and invisible to you. AWS managed keys are free and named aws/<service>. Customer managed keys cost about $1 per month and are the type where you can import key material and control policy and rotation.

flashcards_qa.front: AWS KMS: What is Rotation: AWS managed?
flashcards_qa.back: Rotation: AWS managed = auto yearly; customer managed = auto (set period)/on-demand; imported = manual.

flashcards_qa.front: AWS KMS: What's the answer/service for — Keys are per-region; cross-region copy needs snapshot?
flashcards_qa.back: Keys are per-region; cross-region copy needs snapshot → re-encrypt with a different key → restore.

flashcards_qa.front: You copy an encrypted EBS snapshot to another Region. Why can the original KMS key not be used there?
flashcards_qa.back: Because KMS keys are Region-scoped. The snapshot must be re-encrypted with a key in the destination Region as part of the copy.

flashcards_qa.front: A user with full IAM administrator rights gets AccessDenied when using a KMS key. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: Because KMS access is governed by the key policy. If the key policy does not grant access, IAM permissions alone are not enough.

flashcards_qa.front: You must share an encrypted RDS snapshot with another AWS account. Which key type is required?
flashcards_qa.back: A customer managed key, about $1 per month. AWS managed keys cannot be shared cross-account, so cross-account snapshot sharing needs a CMK whose key policy grants the other account.

flashcards_qa.front: Can you extract the key material of a KMS symmetric key to use inside your own application?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Symmetric KMS keys never leave KMS in plaintext. If external parties must encrypt without calling KMS, use an asymmetric key and distribute the public key.

flashcards_qa.front: Can an AWS managed KMS key be shared with another AWS account?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Cross-account sharing requires a customer managed key, at about $1 per month, whose key policy grants the other account. AWS owned and AWS managed keys cannot be shared.

flashcards_qa.front: How does key rotation differ across the KMS key types?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS owned and AWS managed keys are rotated automatically by AWS on a fixed schedule. Customer managed keys can use automatic rotation or be rotated manually, and imported key material must be rotated manually.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the steps to move a KMS-encrypted snapshot to another Region?
flashcards_qa.back: Copy the snapshot and re-encrypt it with a KMS key in the destination Region, since keys are Region-scoped, then restore from the copy. For cross-account sharing the source key policy must grant the other account, which requires a customer managed key.

flashcards_qa.front: Two KMS details worth memorizing: rotation behavior by key type, and when to choose asymmetric keys.
flashcards_qa.back: Rotation is automatic for AWS owned and AWS managed keys, optional automatic or manual for customer managed keys, and manual for imported material. Asymmetric keys are for encryption or signing outside AWS, while AWS services themselves use symmetric keys.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Amazon Macie? (Amazon Macie)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed PII-discovery service for S3.

flashcards_qa.front: You must find out whether any of your S3 buckets contain PII. Which service, and how does it work?
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon Macie, which uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and help protect sensitive data such as PII in Amazon S3.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon Macie: What's the answer/service for — Findings are delivered via EventBridge (?
flashcards_qa.back: Findings are delivered via EventBridge (→ SNS/Lambda).

flashcards_qa.front: How much setup does Amazon Macie require?
flashcards_qa.back: Very little. It is essentially one-click to enable, after which you specify which S3 buckets to scan, and findings can be routed through EventBridge.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each need to a service: find PII in S3, validate data quality rules, manage encryption keys.
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon Macie finds PII in S3. Glue Data Quality validates data quality rules. AWS KMS manages encryption keys.

flashcards_qa.front: A question asks how to discover sensitive data sitting in S3. Is Amazon Macie the expected answer?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. Discovering sensitive data or PII in S3 is the exam cue for Amazon Macie.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe Macie's role and how you get notified of its findings.
flashcards_qa.back: It is the PII-discovery service for S3, using machine learning and pattern matching. Findings are published to EventBridge, so they can be routed into alerting or remediation workflows.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Secrets Manager? (AWS Secrets Manager)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed secret storage with rotation.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Multi-region secret? (AWS Secrets Manager)
flashcards_qa.back: Replicated secret with synced read replicas.

flashcards_qa.front: Database credentials must be rotated automatically every 30 days. Which service, and how does the rotation happen?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Secrets Manager, which can force rotation every X days and uses a Lambda function to generate and apply the new secret.

flashcards_qa.front: Which databases does Secrets Manager integrate with natively for credential rotation?
flashcards_qa.back: RDS and Aurora for MySQL and PostgreSQL, where rotation of the database credentials is handled for you.

flashcards_qa.front: Are secrets stored in Secrets Manager encrypted?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. Secrets can be encrypted with AWS KMS.

flashcards_qa.front: A multi-Region application and its DR plan need the same secret available in both Regions. Which feature?
flashcards_qa.back: Multi-Region secrets, where Secrets Manager replicates the secret and keeps read replicas in sync across Regions.

flashcards_qa.front: AWS Secrets Manager: What's the answer/service for — secrets/RDS-Aurora credentials?
flashcards_qa.back: Exam cue: secrets/RDS-Aurora credentials → Secrets Manager.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to store an application's feature-flag configuration, and separately to rotate RDS credentials. Which service for each?
flashcards_qa.back: SSM Parameter Store for the configuration, since it is cheaper and needs no rotation. Secrets Manager for the RDS credentials, because it supports forced rotation and native RDS integration.

flashcards_qa.front: Does SSM Parameter Store force automatic rotation of the values it stores?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Parameter Store has no forced rotation. Secrets Manager is the service that enforces rotation every X days.

flashcards_qa.front: A question describes automatically rotating Aurora database credentials. Is Secrets Manager the expected answer?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. RDS and Aurora credential rotation is the cue for AWS Secrets Manager.

flashcards_qa.front: Which two capabilities separate Secrets Manager from SSM Parameter Store?
flashcards_qa.back: Forced automatic rotation, implemented with Lambda, and native RDS/Aurora credential integration. Parameter Store is aimed at configuration and offers neither, though it is cheaper.

flashcards_qa.front: When would you use multi-Region secret replication?
flashcards_qa.back: For disaster recovery and multi-Region applications, so that each Region reads a synchronized local replica of the secret.

flashcards_qa.front: What is WAF? (AWS WAF)
flashcards_qa.back: Layer-7 web application firewall.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Web ACL? (AWS WAF)
flashcards_qa.back: Set of WAF rules protecting a resource.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Rate-based rule? (AWS WAF)
flashcards_qa.back: Counts requests per IP (DDoS protection).

flashcards_qa.front: You must block SQL injection attempts against an application. Which service, and which targets can it attach to?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS WAF, which protects at Layer 7 over HTTP. It deploys on ALB, API Gateway, CloudFront, AppSync, and Cognito User Pools, but not on an NLB, which operates at Layer 4.

flashcards_qa.front: Which rule types can a WAF Web ACL contain?
flashcards_qa.back: IP set matches of up to 10,000 addresses each, string and regex matching on headers, body, and URI for SQL injection and XSS, size constraints, geo-match rules, and rate-based rules for Layer-7 DDoS.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the scope of a Web ACL, and how do you reuse rules across them?
flashcards_qa.back: Web ACLs are regional, except when associated with CloudFront, where they are global. Rule groups let you package reusable rules and share them across Web ACLs.

flashcards_qa.front: A client requires a fixed IP address to allowlist, and you also need Layer-7 protection. How do you architect it?
flashcards_qa.back: Put AWS Global Accelerator in front of the ALB to provide static IPs, and attach WAF to the ALB. WAF cannot attach to an NLB, so Global Accelerator supplies the fixed IPs instead.

flashcards_qa.front: Can you attach a WAF Web ACL to a Network Load Balancer?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The NLB operates at Layer 4. WAF supports ALB, API Gateway, CloudFront, AppSync, and Cognito User Pools.

flashcards_qa.front: Which load balancer works with AWS WAF, and which does not?
flashcards_qa.back: The ALB works, because it is Layer 7. The NLB does not, being Layer 4. If you need static IPs together with WAF, front the ALB with Global Accelerator.

flashcards_qa.front: Requirement: static IP addresses for allowlisting plus WAF inspection. What is the pattern?
flashcards_qa.back: Global Accelerator in front of an ALB that has WAF attached, which gives fixed anycast IPs while keeping Layer-7 inspection.

flashcards_qa.front: Which WAF rule type helps against a Layer-7 flood coming from a small number of clients?
flashcards_qa.back: Rate-based rules, which count requests per IP over a time window and block sources that exceed the threshold.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each attack to a service: a volumetric SYN flood, and a SQL injection attempt.
flashcards_qa.back: The SYN flood is Layer 3/4, so AWS Shield. The SQL injection is Layer 7, so AWS WAF.

flashcards_qa.front: State WAF's supported targets and the workaround when you also need a fixed IP.
flashcards_qa.back: Supported targets are ALB, API Gateway, CloudFront, AppSync, and Cognito User Pools, but not NLB. For a fixed IP, place Global Accelerator in front of the WAF-protected ALB.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the WAF rule types you would use for injection attacks, country blocking, and flood control.
flashcards_qa.back: String and regex match rules on URI, headers, and body for SQL injection and XSS, geo-match rules to block by country, and rate-based rules for Layer-7 flood control.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Shield Standard? (AWS Shield)
flashcards_qa.back: Free automatic L3/4 DDoS protection.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Shield Advanced? (AWS Shield)
flashcards_qa.back: Paid advanced DDoS protection + response team.

flashcards_qa.front: What is DDoS? (AWS Shield)
flashcards_qa.back: Distributed Denial of Service attack.

flashcards_qa.front: Which AWS service is dedicated to DDoS protection, and in what tiers?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Shield, available as Shield Standard, which is free and automatic, and Shield Advanced, which is paid.

flashcards_qa.front: What DDoS protection do you get for free without enabling anything, and what does it cover?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Shield Standard, automatically enabled for all customers, protecting against Layer 3/4 attacks such as SYN floods, UDP floods, and reflection attacks.

flashcards_qa.front: A company wants 24/7 expert help during attacks and protection from DDoS-driven scaling bills. Which offering, at what cost, and covering what?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Shield Advanced, at roughly $3,000 per month, covering EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, and Route 53, and adding a 24/7 DDoS Response Team plus cost protection against attack-driven scaling charges.

flashcards_qa.front: How does Shield Advanced handle Layer-7 attacks?
flashcards_qa.back: It automatically creates and deploys WAF rules to mitigate Layer-7 DDoS, on top of its Layer 3/4 protection.

flashcards_qa.front: Split the responsibility between AWS Shield and AWS WAF.
flashcards_qa.back: Shield handles DDoS attacks, primarily at Layer 3/4, with Advanced extending into Layer 7. WAF handles web exploits at Layer 7, including SQL injection, XSS, bad bots, and geo and rate rules.

flashcards_qa.front: Is AWS WAF the right service to stop a Layer 3/4 volumetric flood?
flashcards_qa.back: No. That is AWS Shield's role. WAF operates at Layer 7 against web exploits.

flashcards_qa.front: Does Shield Advanced create WAF rules on your behalf?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. It automatically generates and deploys WAF rules for Layer-7 DDoS mitigation.

flashcards_qa.front: Does Shield Standard have to be enabled and paid for?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Shield Standard is free and automatically enabled for all customers, covering Layer 3 and 4 attacks. Shield Advanced is the paid tier, at roughly $3,000 per month.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish Shield from WAF, and Shield Standard from Shield Advanced.
flashcards_qa.back: Shield addresses DDoS while WAF addresses Layer-7 web exploits. Shield Standard is free and automatic for Layer 3/4, whereas Shield Advanced is paid and adds Layer-7 mitigation through auto-generated WAF rules, a 24/7 response team, and cost protection.

flashcards_qa.front: What is EMRFS encryption? (AWS Services Security Deep Dive)
flashcards_qa.back: S3-side encryption for EMR (SSE-S3/KMS/client-side).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Kerberos/Apache Ranger? (AWS Services Security Deep Dive)
flashcards_qa.back: EMR authentication (AD) / authorization (RBAC).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Glue resource policy? (AWS Services Security Deep Dive)
flashcards_qa.back: Protects the Data Catalog.

flashcards_qa.front: What is TDE? (AWS Services Security Deep Dive)
flashcards_qa.back: Transparent Data Encryption (SQL Server/Oracle).

flashcards_qa.front: A KCL consumer application cannot start reading a Kinesis stream. Which non-Kinesis permission is most likely missing?
flashcards_qa.back: DynamoDB read and write permissions. The KCL stores its checkpoints and lease table in DynamoDB, so the consumer's role needs DynamoDB access as well.

flashcards_qa.front: Can EMRFS read S3 objects that were encrypted with SSE-C?
flashcards_qa.back: No. EMRFS supports SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, and client-side encryption, but not SSE-C.

flashcards_qa.front: You must encrypt the root volume of EMR cluster nodes. Which mechanism works, and which does not?
flashcards_qa.back: EBS encryption with KMS covers the root volume. LUKS does not encrypt the root volume, so it cannot satisfy that requirement on its own.

flashcards_qa.front: What are Redshift's at-rest encryption options, and how does it authenticate COPY and UNLOAD to S3?
flashcards_qa.back: At rest it can use AWS KMS or an external HSM device. For COPY and UNLOAD it uses an attached IAM role, or less preferably inline credentials.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you protect the Glue Data Catalog, and how do you secure Glue's database connections?
flashcards_qa.back: Encrypt the catalog with KMS and restrict access using resource policies. For connections, configure Glue to require JDBC over SSL.

flashcards_qa.front: You enable IAM database authentication on RDS PostgreSQL. Does that also control what the user can do inside the database?
flashcards_qa.back: No. IAM authentication, supported for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB, covers authentication only. In-database permissions such as table grants are still managed inside the database.

flashcards_qa.front: Which S3 encryption modes does EMRFS support?
flashcards_qa.back: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, and client-side encryption. SSE-C is not supported.

flashcards_qa.front: Does LUKS encryption cover the root volume of an EMR node?
flashcards_qa.back: No. LUKS does not cover the root volume, so use EBS encryption with KMS for it.

flashcards_qa.front: Two easily-missed security facts: what extra permission does a KCL application need, and what are Redshift's at-rest options?
flashcards_qa.back: A KCL application needs DynamoDB read and write permissions for checkpointing. Redshift can encrypt at rest using either AWS KMS or an external HSM.

flashcards_qa.front: EMR has two distinct encryption surfaces. Name them and the options available for each.
flashcards_qa.back: EMRFS data in S3 can use SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, or client-side encryption, but not SSE-C. Local disks on the nodes use HDFS or NVMe encryption and LUKS for attached volumes, with EBS-KMS being the option that covers the root volume.

flashcards_qa.front: Is AWS KMS the only option for encrypting a Redshift cluster at rest?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Redshift can also encrypt at rest using an external HSM device, which is the choice when key material must stay in your own hardware security module.

flashcards_qa.front: Draw the line between what RDS IAM authentication controls and what it does not.
flashcards_qa.back: IAM authentication controls who may connect, using a token instead of a password, for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB. What that user may then read or write is governed by grants inside the database itself.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the two EMR encryption gotchas worth memorizing?
flashcards_qa.back: EMRFS does not support SSE-C, supporting only SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, and client-side encryption. LUKS does not cover the root volume, which needs EBS encryption with KMS.

flashcards_qa.front: Name three service-specific security facts from the security deep-dive worth memorizing.
flashcards_qa.back: KCL consumers need DynamoDB permissions for checkpointing, Redshift encrypts at rest with either KMS or an HSM, and the Glue Data Catalog is protected with KMS encryption plus resource policies.

flashcards_qa.front: What is VPC? (VPC, Subnets & Gateways)
flashcards_qa.back: Virtual Private Cloud (regional private network).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Subnet? (VPC, Subnets & Gateways)
flashcards_qa.back: AZ-scoped partition of a VPC (public/private).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Internet Gateway? (VPC, Subnets & Gateways)
flashcards_qa.back: Provides internet access to public subnets.

flashcards_qa.front: What is NAT Gateway? (VPC, Subnets & Gateways)
flashcards_qa.back: Outbound internet for private subnets.

flashcards_qa.front: You must design a network that spans three Availability Zones in one Region. Do you need three separate VPCs?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A VPC is Region-wide, so you create one VPC and one subnet per AZ inside it. Subnets are AZ-scoped; VPCs are not.

flashcards_qa.front: Two subnets sit in the same VPC. An EC2 instance in subnet A can reach the internet; an identically configured instance in subnet B cannot. What is the most likely difference?
flashcards_qa.back: Subnet A's route table has a route to the Internet Gateway, which is what makes a subnet public. Subnet B has no IGW route, so it is private. Public vs private is defined by the route table, not by a subnet setting.

flashcards_qa.front: EC2 instances in a private subnet must download OS patches from the internet, but nothing on the internet may initiate a connection to them. What do you add?
flashcards_qa.back: A NAT Gateway (AWS-managed) or NAT Instance (self-managed) in a public subnet. It gives private subnets outbound-only internet access while leaving them unreachable from inbound connections.

flashcards_qa.front: Should the NAT Gateway be launched into the private subnet whose instances need outbound access?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The NAT Gateway goes in a public subnet. The private subnet's route table points to the NAT, and the NAT routes onward through the Internet Gateway.

flashcards_qa.front: An architect adds an Internet Gateway route to a private subnet's route table so its instances can reach the internet. Why does this fail the requirement?
flashcards_qa.back: An IGW route makes the subnet public, which also permits inbound connections from the internet. Outbound-only access requires routing the private subnet to a NAT Gateway or NAT Instance instead.

flashcards_qa.front: A team needs outbound internet access for private subnets but wants no servers to size, patch, or make highly available themselves. Which option?
flashcards_qa.back: NAT Gateway, because it is AWS-managed and highly available. A NAT Instance is an EC2 instance you must size, patch, and make HA yourself.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a single subnet span two Availability Zones to make it highly available?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A subnet lives in exactly one AZ. Because the VPC itself is Region-wide, high availability comes from creating a subnet in each AZ within that VPC.

flashcards_qa.front: You are told a subnet is private. What can you conclude about its route table?
flashcards_qa.back: That it has no route to an Internet Gateway. A public subnet is one whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW; a private subnet does not.

flashcards_qa.front: Which VPC component gives a subnet two-way internet reachability, and which gives outbound-only access?
flashcards_qa.back: Internet Gateway gives two-way reachability and is what defines a public subnet. NAT Gateway gives outbound-only access for private subnets, and the NAT itself sits in a public subnet.

flashcards_qa.front: Trace the path a package-update request takes from an EC2 instance in a private subnet out to the internet.
flashcards_qa.back: Private-subnet instance to its route table, to the NAT Gateway in a public subnet, to the Internet Gateway, then out to the internet. Return traffic for that connection is allowed; new inbound connections are not.

flashcards_qa.front: What is NACL? (NACLs, Security Groups & Flow Logs)
flashcards_qa.back: Subnet-level stateless firewall (allow+deny).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Security Group? (NACLs, Security Groups & Flow Logs)
flashcards_qa.back: Instance-level stateful firewall (allow only).

flashcards_qa.front: What is VPC Flow Logs? (NACLs, Security Groups & Flow Logs)
flashcards_qa.back: Logs of IP traffic for troubleshooting.

flashcards_qa.front: NACLs, Security Groups & Flow Logs: What is NACL?
flashcards_qa.back: NACL = subnet-level, stateless, allow AND deny (IP only); default allows all.

flashcards_qa.front: NACLs, Security Groups & Flow Logs: What is Security Group?
flashcards_qa.back: Security Group = instance/ENI-level, stateful, allow only, can reference other SGs.

flashcards_qa.front: A packet arrives destined for an EC2 instance in a subnet. In what order are the NACL and the security group evaluated?
flashcards_qa.back: The NACL first, at the subnet boundary, then the security group at the instance/ENI. A NACL deny drops the packet before the security group is ever consulted.

flashcards_qa.front: Connectivity between two instances fails intermittently and you need to see which IP traffic is being allowed and which is denied. Which feature, and where can the output go?
flashcards_qa.back: VPC Flow Logs, which capture accepted and rejected IP traffic at VPC, subnet, or ENI level. They can be delivered to Amazon S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Kinesis Data Firehose.

flashcards_qa.front: You must block one specific malicious IP address from reaching an entire subnet. Which control do you use, and why can the other one not do it?
flashcards_qa.back: A NACL, because it is stateless, applies at the subnet level, and supports explicit DENY rules. Security groups are stateful, instance-level, and allow-only, so they cannot express a deny.

flashcards_qa.front: Can VPC Flow Logs only be delivered to CloudWatch Logs?
flashcards_qa.back: No. They can go to Amazon S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Kinesis Data Firehose.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a security group need an explicit rule to allow return traffic?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Security groups are stateful, so return traffic is automatically allowed. NACLs are stateless, which is why they need a rule in each direction.

flashcards_qa.front: An application in a private subnet cannot reach an external API and you suspect a network control is dropping the traffic. How do you confirm it, and where would you send the data to query it with SQL?
flashcards_qa.back: Enable VPC Flow Logs and look for REJECT records to pinpoint the offending NACL or security group. Send them to S3 and query with Athena; CloudWatch Logs or Firehose are the alternatives for streaming/alerting.

flashcards_qa.front: What is VPC Peering? (VPC Connectivity)
flashcards_qa.back: Private connection between two VPCs (non-transitive).

flashcards_qa.front: What is VPC Endpoint? (VPC Connectivity)
flashcards_qa.back: Private access to AWS services (gateway/interface).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Site-to-Site VPN? (VPC Connectivity)
flashcards_qa.back: Encrypted on-prem↔VPC link over the internet.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Direct Connect? (VPC Connectivity)
flashcards_qa.back: Private physical connection to AWS.

flashcards_qa.front: VPC A is peered with VPC B, and VPC B is peered with VPC C. Can instances in A reach instances in C over those peerings?
flashcards_qa.back: No. VPC Peering is not transitive, so A needs its own direct peering connection with C. Peered VPCs also must have non-overlapping CIDR ranges.

flashcards_qa.front: EC2 instances in a private subnet must read from S3 and DynamoDB without traversing the internet or a NAT Gateway. What do you create, and which type?
flashcards_qa.back: VPC Endpoints. Gateway endpoints serve S3 and DynamoDB (route-table based); every other AWS service uses an Interface endpoint, which is an ENI with a private IP in your subnet.

flashcards_qa.front: You need on-premises to VPC connectivity working within the week and can accept traffic riding the public internet. Which option?
flashcards_qa.back: Site-to-Site VPN, an encrypted tunnel over the public internet that can be stood up in hours. Direct Connect is private but takes roughly a month to provision.

flashcards_qa.front: A company needs consistent, high-bandwidth transfer from its data center to AWS that never touches the public internet, and can wait for provisioning. Which option?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Direct Connect, a dedicated private physical link. It is secure and fast but takes about a month to establish.

flashcards_qa.front: Two VPCs both use the CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. Can you peer them?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Peered VPCs must have non-overlapping CIDR blocks. Peering is also non-transitive, so each pair needs its own connection.

flashcards_qa.front: Can you use a Gateway VPC endpoint to reach Kinesis Data Streams privately?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Gateway endpoints support only S3 and DynamoDB. Kinesis and all other services require an Interface endpoint.

flashcards_qa.front: Rank Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect on setup time and on whether traffic crosses the public internet.
flashcards_qa.back: Site-to-Site VPN: set up in minutes to hours, encrypted but carried over the public internet. Direct Connect: about a month to provision, but a dedicated private line that bypasses the internet.

flashcards_qa.front: You need private access from one private subnet to both Amazon S3 and Amazon SNS. Which endpoint type for each?
flashcards_qa.back: S3 gets a Gateway endpoint. SNS needs an Interface endpoint, because Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

flashcards_qa.front: An auditor asks whether traffic on your on-premises link crosses the public internet. How does the answer differ between Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect?
flashcards_qa.back: Site-to-Site VPN does cross the public internet, though it is encrypted in transit. Direct Connect does not, because it is a private physical connection.

flashcards_qa.front: You are asked to connect four VPCs with peering so that all of them can communicate. How many peering connections are required, and what IP constraint applies?
flashcards_qa.back: Six connections, one for every pair, because peering is not transitive. All four VPCs must also have non-overlapping CIDR ranges.

flashcards_qa.front: Design task: give a private subnet private access to S3, and connect on-premises to the VPC by tomorrow. What do you choose?
flashcards_qa.back: A Gateway VPC endpoint for S3 (Interface endpoints would be needed for other services), and a Site-to-Site VPN for the on-premises link because it is fast to set up. Direct Connect would be the choice if you had about a month.

flashcards_qa.front: What is PrivateLink? (AWS PrivateLink)
flashcards_qa.back: Privately expose a service to other VPCs via an NLB/ENI.

flashcards_qa.front: You must expose one internal service to 50 customer VPCs without peering, internet gateways, NAT, or route-table changes in their accounts. What do you use?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS PrivateLink. It privately exposes a single service across VPCs with no peering, IGW, NAT, or route table changes, and the traffic stays on the AWS private network.

flashcards_qa.front: What must the service provider and the service consumer each put in place for PrivateLink to work?
flashcards_qa.back: Provider: front the service with a Network Load Balancer. Consumer: an interface endpoint (ENI) in their VPC. PrivateLink connects the two.

flashcards_qa.front: Does PrivateLink traffic leave the AWS network?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It stays entirely on the private AWS network and never touches the public internet.

flashcards_qa.front: A SaaS provider currently peers its VPC with each of 100 customer VPCs and finds it unmanageable. What scales better?
flashcards_qa.back: PrivateLink: one NLB-fronted service that many VPCs consume through endpoints. Peering is network-to-network, non-transitive, and does not scale to many consumers.

flashcards_qa.front: When is VPC Peering the wrong choice compared with PrivateLink?
flashcards_qa.back: When you only want to expose a single service, especially to many VPCs. Peering opens whole-network connectivity, is non-transitive, and scales poorly; PrivateLink exposes one service and scales to many consumers.

flashcards_qa.front: Does PrivateLink give the consumer VPC full network access to the provider's VPC?
flashcards_qa.back: No. PrivateLink exposes only the specific service behind the provider's NLB. Full network-to-network reachability is what VPC Peering provides.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a provider expose a service through PrivateLink using an Application Load Balancer?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The provider side requires a Network Load Balancer; the consumer side gets an interface endpoint (ENI).

flashcards_qa.front: Justify PrivateLink over VPC Peering for a single service consumed by many VPCs, and sketch the architecture.
flashcards_qa.back: PrivateLink scales to many consumers without CIDR or route-table coordination and exposes only the one service. Architecture: provider service behind an NLB, through PrivateLink, to an interface endpoint (ENI) in each consumer VPC, entirely over the private AWS network.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Route 53? (DNS & Amazon Route 53)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed authoritative DNS and registrar.

flashcards_qa.front: What is A / AAAA record? (DNS & Amazon Route 53)
flashcards_qa.back: Hostname → IPv4 / IPv6.

flashcards_qa.front: What is CNAME? (DNS & Amazon Route 53)
flashcards_qa.back: Hostname → another hostname (not at zone apex).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Hosted zone? (DNS & Amazon Route 53)
flashcards_qa.back: Container of DNS records (public/private).

flashcards_qa.front: DNS & Amazon Route 53: What is Route 53?
flashcards_qa.back: Route 53 = managed, authoritative DNS; only AWS service with a 100% availability SLA; also a domain registrar.

flashcards_qa.front: DNS & Amazon Route 53: What's the answer/service for — Records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (hostname?
flashcards_qa.back: Records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (hostname→hostname; not at zone apex), NS (name servers).

flashcards_qa.front: Internal hostnames must resolve only for resources inside your VPC and must not be visible on the internet. Which Route 53 construct?
flashcards_qa.back: A private hosted zone associated with that VPC. Public hosted zones answer queries from the internet.

flashcards_qa.front: You try to point example.com at an ALB's DNS name with a CNAME record and Route 53 rejects it. Why, and what works instead?
flashcards_qa.back: CNAME records are not allowed at the zone apex (example.com). Use a CNAME on a subdomain such as www.example.com, or a Route 53 Alias record at the apex.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each need to a DNS record type: map a hostname to an IPv4 address; to an IPv6 address; to another hostname; delegate a zone.
flashcards_qa.back: A for IPv4, AAAA for IPv6, CNAME for hostname-to-hostname, and NS to specify the name servers for a hosted zone (delegation).

flashcards_qa.front: Can you create a CNAME record for example.com, the zone apex?
flashcards_qa.back: No. CNAMEs are not permitted at the top node of a zone. They work on subdomains such as www.example.com; at the apex use an Alias record.

flashcards_qa.front: The same domain name must resolve to a public address for internet users and to a private address for callers inside the VPC. How does Route 53 handle this?
flashcards_qa.back: With both a public hosted zone for internet queries and a private hosted zone associated with the VPC for internal queries, which is split-view DNS.

flashcards_qa.front: An application is being made reachable over IPv6. Is an A record sufficient?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A records hold IPv4 addresses, so IPv6 requires an AAAA record. CNAME points a hostname at another hostname rather than at an address.

flashcards_qa.front: You must publish an IPv6 address for a subdomain, point the zone apex at a load balancer, and keep one internal name resolvable only inside the VPC. What do you use?
flashcards_qa.back: AAAA for the IPv6 subdomain; an Alias record at the apex, because CNAME is barred there; and a private hosted zone for the internal-only name.

flashcards_qa.front: What is CloudFront? (Amazon CloudFront)
flashcards_qa.back: Global CDN caching at edge locations.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Origin? (Amazon CloudFront)
flashcards_qa.back: Backend CloudFront caches (S3/VPC/custom).

flashcards_qa.front: What is OAC? (Amazon CloudFront)
flashcards_qa.back: Origin Access Control securing S3 origins.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Invalidation? (Amazon CloudFront)
flashcards_qa.back: Forcing a cache refresh by path.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon CloudFront: What is CloudFront?
flashcards_qa.back: CloudFront = CDN caching content at 200+ edge locations for low-latency global reads + DDoS protection.

flashcards_qa.front: Which origin types can CloudFront use, and how do you stop an S3 origin from being reached directly?
flashcards_qa.back: Origins can be S3 buckets, VPC origins (private ALB, NLB, or EC2), or custom HTTP origins. Lock down an S3 origin with Origin Access Control plus a bucket policy that allows only that distribution.

flashcards_qa.front: The first user in a region requests a file through CloudFront and it is slow; every user after that gets it quickly. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: The first request was a cache miss, so the edge location fetched the object from the origin and cached it. Later requests are served from the edge until the TTL expires.

flashcards_qa.front: One workload serves static assets to a worldwide audience; another needs a low-latency copy of a changing dataset in two specific Regions. Which service for each?
flashcards_qa.back: CloudFront for the global static content, since it caches at edge locations with a TTL. S3 Cross-Region Replication for the per-Region copy, since it is near-real-time and suits dynamic data.

flashcards_qa.front: You pushed corrected images to the origin but CloudFront is still serving the old ones, and the TTL is 24 hours. What do you do?
flashcards_qa.back: Create a CloudFront invalidation for the affected path, such as /images/* or * for everything, which forces a refresh before the TTL expires.

flashcards_qa.front: Is CloudFront the right choice for keeping a full copy of an S3 bucket in another Region?
flashcards_qa.back: No. CloudFront is a global edge cache, not a replica. S3 Cross-Region Replication is what creates a per-Region copy of the data.

flashcards_qa.front: Requirement: content is reachable only through CloudFront and never through the bucket's own S3 URL. How do you enforce it?
flashcards_qa.back: Enable Origin Access Control on the distribution and set an S3 bucket policy that grants access only to that distribution, which blocks direct bucket access.

flashcards_qa.front: Must you wait for the TTL to expire before CloudFront will serve an updated object?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A cache invalidation by path forces an immediate refresh from the origin.

flashcards_qa.front: In one sentence each: what does CloudFront cache, and what does S3 Cross-Region Replication do?
flashcards_qa.back: CloudFront caches copies of content at edge locations for low-latency global reads. S3 CRR asynchronously replicates objects into a bucket in another Region.

flashcards_qa.front: You want CloudFront in front of an ALB that has no public IP and must remain private. Which origin configuration?
flashcards_qa.back: A VPC origin, which lets CloudFront reach a private ALB, NLB, or EC2 inside the VPC. A public custom origin would require making the backend internet-facing.

flashcards_qa.front: What drives the choice between CloudFront and S3 Cross-Region Replication, and how do you pick a CloudFront origin?
flashcards_qa.back: Choose CloudFront when the goal is global low-latency caching of mostly static content, and CRR when the goal is an actual data copy in another Region. For origins: S3 plus OAC for buckets, a VPC origin for private ALB/NLB/EC2, and a custom HTTP origin for anything else.

flashcards_qa.front: A bad deployment shipped a broken CSS file that is now cached at edge locations worldwide with a long TTL. What is the fastest fix?
flashcards_qa.back: Issue a CloudFront invalidation for that path, for example /css/*, which purges the edge caches immediately instead of waiting for the TTL to expire.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Metric? (CloudWatch Metrics)
flashcards_qa.back: A monitored variable (e.g., CPUUtilization).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Namespace? (CloudWatch Metrics)
flashcards_qa.back: Container for a service's metrics.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Dimension? (CloudWatch Metrics)
flashcards_qa.back: An attribute of a metric (up to 30).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Custom Metric? (CloudWatch Metrics)
flashcards_qa.back: A user-defined metric (e.g., memory usage).

flashcards_qa.front: How are CloudWatch metrics organized, and what else does a metric carry?
flashcards_qa.back: Metrics live in namespaces, generally one per AWS service, and each metric has dimensions, up to 30 of them, which are attributes such as instance ID, plus a timestamp for each data point.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to alarm on EC2 memory utilization. Is that available out of the box?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Memory is not a default EC2 metric, so you must publish it as a Custom Metric, typically using the CloudWatch Unified Agent.

flashcards_qa.front: You must deliver CloudWatch metrics into your data lake in near real time. Which feature, and through what?
flashcards_qa.back: CloudWatch Metric Streams, which deliver metrics near real time through Kinesis Data Firehose to destinations such as S3 for Athena, Redshift, or OpenSearch, or to third-party providers.

flashcards_qa.front: CloudWatch Metrics: What is Default EC2 monitoring?
flashcards_qa.back: Default EC2 monitoring = 5 min; detailed monitoring = 1 min.

flashcards_qa.front: An alarm on EC2 memory usage cannot find the metric. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: Because memory usage is not one of the default EC2 metrics. It has to be published as a Custom Metric, which the CloudWatch Unified Agent can do.

flashcards_qa.front: Which service carries the data when you enable CloudWatch Metric Streams?
flashcards_qa.back: Kinesis Data Firehose, which delivers the streamed metrics near real time to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, or third-party destinations.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the metric interval for EC2 default monitoring versus detailed monitoring?
flashcards_qa.back: Default monitoring publishes at 5-minute intervals. Detailed monitoring publishes at 1-minute intervals, for an extra charge.

flashcards_qa.front: Which EC2 metrics come by default, and which require you to publish them yourself?
flashcards_qa.back: CPU, network, and disk I/O metrics come by default. Memory and swap usage are not default and must be published as Custom Metrics via the agent.

flashcards_qa.front: You need metrics continuously exported for analysis rather than just viewed. Which feature, and how does it compare with dashboards?
flashcards_qa.back: Metric Streams, which continuously deliver metrics near real time through Firehose into analytics destinations. Dashboards only visualize metrics inside CloudWatch and are not an export mechanism.

flashcards_qa.front: Two CloudWatch metrics facts worth memorizing: EC2 memory, and how Metric Streams deliver data?
flashcards_qa.back: EC2 memory is not a default metric and needs a Custom Metric published by the Unified Agent. Metric Streams deliver metrics near real time via Kinesis Data Firehose.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Log group? (CloudWatch Logs)
flashcards_qa.back: Container of log streams (per app).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Logs Insights? (CloudWatch Logs)
flashcards_qa.back: Query engine for historical logs.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Subscription Filter? (CloudWatch Logs)
flashcards_qa.back: Real-time log streaming to a destination.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Destination? (CloudWatch Logs)
flashcards_qa.back: Virtual representation of a Kinesis stream for cross-account subscriptions.

flashcards_qa.front: How are CloudWatch Logs organized, what retention is possible, and are they encrypted?
flashcards_qa.back: Log groups, usually one per application, contain log streams, usually one per instance or source. Retention can be set from 1 day to 10 years, or never expire, and logs are encrypted by default.

flashcards_qa.front: Which sources can send data into CloudWatch Logs?
flashcards_qa.back: The SDK, the CloudWatch agents, Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, Lambda, VPC Flow Logs, API Gateway, CloudTrail, and Route 53.

flashcards_qa.front: CloudWatch Logs: What is Logs Insights?
flashcards_qa.back: Logs Insights = query engine on HISTORICAL data (not real-time).

flashcards_qa.front: You need log data in S3 for occasional analysis, and separately streamed to Lambda in real time. Which two mechanisms?
flashcards_qa.back: A batch export to S3 using CreateExportTask, which can take up to 12 hours to appear, for the occasional analysis. Subscription Filters for real-time streaming to Kinesis, Firehose, or Lambda.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you aggregate CloudWatch Logs from many accounts into one central account?
flashcards_qa.back: With a subscription Destination in the central account, a destination access policy allowing the sending accounts, and an IAM role the service can assume to deliver the data.

flashcards_qa.front: Can CloudWatch Logs Insights be used to alert on log events as they arrive?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Logs Insights queries historical log data. For real-time reaction use metric filters with alarms, or Subscription Filters streaming to Lambda or Kinesis.

flashcards_qa.front: Is a CloudWatch Logs export to S3 a suitable way to react to log events in near real time?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The batch export via CreateExportTask can take up to 12 hours. Real-time reaction needs a Subscription Filter streaming to Kinesis, Firehose, or Lambda.

flashcards_qa.front: Which CloudWatch Logs feature enables cross-account log aggregation?
flashcards_qa.back: Subscription Destinations, combined with a destination access policy and an assumable IAM role, which let log events from other accounts flow into a central account.

flashcards_qa.front: You need log events delivered within seconds. Batch S3 export or Subscription Filters?
flashcards_qa.back: Subscription Filters, which stream in real time. Batch S3 export is slow and can take up to 12 hours.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish CloudWatch Logs Insights from real-time log streaming.
flashcards_qa.back: Logs Insights is an interactive query tool over historical log data. Real-time streaming, via Subscription Filters to Kinesis, Firehose, or Lambda, is what you use to react to events as they arrive.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe the two ways to get log data out of CloudWatch Logs, and how cross-account aggregation is configured.
flashcards_qa.back: Batch export to S3 with CreateExportTask, which is slow, or Subscription Filters for real-time streaming to Kinesis, Firehose, or Lambda. Cross-account aggregation uses a subscription Destination in the central account plus a destination access policy and an assumable IAM role.

flashcards_qa.front: Is CloudWatch Logs Insights a real-time monitoring tool?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It queries historical log data. Real-time needs metric filters with alarms or Subscription Filters.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Unified Agent? (CloudWatch Unified Agent)
flashcards_qa.back: CloudWatch agent for logs + granular metrics.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SSM Parameter Store? (CloudWatch Unified Agent)
flashcards_qa.back: Central config store for the Unified Agent.

flashcards_qa.front: An EC2 instance shows no application logs in CloudWatch. What is missing?
flashcards_qa.back: The CloudWatch agent, which is not installed by default, along with an IAM role granting it permission to publish. The same agent also works on on-premises servers.

flashcards_qa.front: Does the older CloudWatch Logs Agent collect memory and disk metrics?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The Logs Agent collects logs only. The newer Unified Agent collects both logs and system metrics such as RAM, disk, and swap.

flashcards_qa.front: How can you manage CloudWatch Unified Agent configuration across a fleet centrally?
flashcards_qa.back: Store the agent configuration in SSM Parameter Store, from which the Unified Agent can be centrally configured and updated.

flashcards_qa.front: Which EC2 system metrics are missing from the defaults, and how do you get them?
flashcards_qa.back: Memory and swap usage are not in the default EC2 metrics. Install the CloudWatch Unified Agent to collect them as custom metrics.

flashcards_qa.front: Do default EC2 CloudWatch metrics include memory and swap utilization?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Those are guest-level metrics the hypervisor cannot see, so you need the CloudWatch Unified Agent to publish them.

flashcards_qa.front: Which agent should you install if you need both logs and detailed system metrics, centrally configured?
flashcards_qa.back: The CloudWatch Unified Agent, which collects logs and metrics such as RAM, processes, disk, and swap, and can be configured centrally through SSM Parameter Store. The older Logs Agent handles logs only.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the functional difference between the Unified Agent and the Logs Agent?
flashcards_qa.back: The Unified Agent collects metrics as well as logs. The Logs Agent, which it replaces, collects logs only.

flashcards_qa.front: Where do the default EC2 metrics come from, and where do memory and swap metrics come from?
flashcards_qa.back: Default metrics such as CPU and network are published by the hypervisor without any agent. Memory and swap are guest-level and only appear if the CloudWatch Unified Agent collects and publishes them.

flashcards_qa.front: Which metrics require the CloudWatch Unified Agent, and where can its configuration be stored centrally?
flashcards_qa.back: It is required for memory and swap metrics, which are not EC2 defaults, and its configuration can be centrally managed through SSM Parameter Store.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Alarm state? (CloudWatch Alarms)
flashcards_qa.back: OK / INSUFFICIENT_DATA / ALARM.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Composite Alarm? (CloudWatch Alarms)
flashcards_qa.back: Combines alarms with AND/OR.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Metric filter? (CloudWatch Alarms)
flashcards_qa.back: Turns log matches into a metric for alarms.

flashcards_qa.front: What states can a CloudWatch alarm be in, and what does the period control?
flashcards_qa.back: The states are OK, INSUFFICIENT_DATA, and ALARM. The period is the length of time over which the metric is evaluated, and it can go down to 10 or 30 seconds for high-resolution metrics.

flashcards_qa.front: CloudWatch Alarms: What's the answer/service for — Targets: EC2 actions, Auto Scaling actions, SNS (?
flashcards_qa.back: Targets: EC2 actions, Auto Scaling actions, SNS (→ Lambda).

flashcards_qa.front: You get paged constantly because several individual alarms fire together. What feature reduces the noise?
flashcards_qa.back: Composite Alarms, which combine multiple alarms with AND/OR logic so you are notified once on the meaningful condition rather than by each underlying alarm.

flashcards_qa.front: An EC2 instance fails its system status check. What can an alarm do about it, and what is preserved?
flashcards_qa.back: An alarm on the status check can trigger EC2 instance recovery, which brings the instance back with the same private and public IPs, the same metadata, and the same placement group.

flashcards_qa.front: You need an alarm that fires when a specific string appears in your application logs. How, and how do you test it?
flashcards_qa.back: Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter for the pattern and build an alarm on the resulting metric. Test the alarm using the set-alarm-state CLI call to force it into ALARM.

flashcards_qa.front: What can a Composite Alarm express that a single alarm cannot?
flashcards_qa.back: A condition across multiple alarms combined with AND/OR logic. A single alarm evaluates only one metric.

flashcards_qa.front: After a CloudWatch-triggered EC2 recovery, do you need to update DNS or reconfigure clients?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Recovery preserves the same IP addresses, metadata, and placement group, so clients and DNS entries remain valid.

flashcards_qa.front: Can log content drive a CloudWatch alarm?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. A metric filter over CloudWatch Logs turns matching log events into a metric, and you can alarm on that metric.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a single CloudWatch alarm combine two metrics with AND logic?
flashcards_qa.back: No. One alarm evaluates one metric. Combining alarms with AND or OR requires a Composite Alarm, which is also how you reduce alert noise.

flashcards_qa.front: Name three kinds of action a CloudWatch alarm can take and when each applies.
flashcards_qa.back: EC2 actions such as stop, terminate, reboot, or recover, for instance-level problems. Auto Scaling actions to add or remove capacity in response to load. SNS notifications to alert people or trigger downstream automation.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you reduce alarm noise, and how do you alarm on something that only appears in logs?
flashcards_qa.back: Use Composite Alarms combining several alarms with AND/OR so only the meaningful combination notifies you. For log-only conditions, create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter and alarm on the metric it produces.

flashcards_qa.front: What does EC2 instance recovery preserve, and how do you verify an alarm's action without waiting for a real event?
flashcards_qa.back: Recovery keeps the same IP addresses, metadata, and placement group. To verify the action, force the state with the set-alarm-state CLI call.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Management event? (Amazon CloudTrail)
flashcards_qa.back: Resource operation (default-logged).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data event? (Amazon CloudTrail)
flashcards_qa.back: High-volume operation (S3 object/Lambda invoke; off by default).

flashcards_qa.front: What is CloudTrail Insights? (Amazon CloudTrail)
flashcards_qa.back: Anomaly detection over management events.

flashcards_qa.front: Is CloudTrail something you must enable, and what does it record?
flashcards_qa.back: It is enabled by default. It records API calls and events across your account, whether they came from the console, the SDK, the CLI, or from AWS services themselves.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the CloudTrail event categories and say which are logged by default.
flashcards_qa.back: Management events, logged by default and split into read and write. Data events, such as S3 object-level operations and Lambda invocations, which are high volume and not logged by default. And Insights events, for anomaly detection.

flashcards_qa.front: Which CloudTrail feature spots unusual activity, and how does it decide what is unusual?
flashcards_qa.back: CloudTrail Insights, which baselines your normal write-event activity and flags deviations from that baseline as unusual.

flashcards_qa.front: How long does CloudTrail keep events by default, and what do you do if you need longer?
flashcards_qa.back: Ninety days by default in Event History. For longer retention, deliver the trail to S3 and query it with Athena, or use CloudTrail Lake.

flashcards_qa.front: You need a record of every S3 GetObject call but see nothing in CloudTrail. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: Because those are data events, which are high volume and not logged by default. You must explicitly enable S3 object-level data events on the trail.

flashcards_qa.front: An audit requires two years of API history. How do you satisfy that with CloudTrail?
flashcards_qa.back: Deliver the trail to an S3 bucket, which has no 90-day limit, and query it with Athena. CloudTrail Lake is the alternative, with retention up to seven years.

flashcards_qa.front: Can CloudTrail tell you why an application was slow?
flashcards_qa.back: No. CloudTrail records who did what and when, as an audit log of API activity. Performance metrics come from CloudWatch.

flashcards_qa.front: Which CloudTrail event type is on by default, and which must you turn on and why?
flashcards_qa.back: Management events are on by default. Data events, such as S3 object-level actions and Lambda invocations, must be enabled explicitly because their volume, and therefore cost, is very high.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each question to a service: who deleted this bucket, and why is CPU at 95 percent?
flashcards_qa.back: Who deleted the bucket comes from CloudTrail, the API audit log. CPU utilization comes from CloudWatch metrics.

flashcards_qa.front: Are S3 object-level access events logged by CloudTrail by default?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Those are data events, which are off by default because of their volume. Management events are logged by default.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you keep CloudTrail history beyond 90 days, and how do you get anomaly detection?
flashcards_qa.back: Send the trail to S3 and query it with Athena, or use CloudTrail Lake for retention up to seven years. For anomaly detection, enable CloudTrail Insights, which baselines normal write activity.

flashcards_qa.front: What is CloudTrail Lake? (AWS CloudTrail Lake)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed data lake for CloudTrail events (SQL-queryable).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Advanced event selector? (AWS CloudTrail Lake)
flashcards_qa.back: Fine-grained event-collection control.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Channel? (AWS CloudTrail Lake)
flashcards_qa.back: Integration for non-AWS event sources.

flashcards_qa.front: How does CloudTrail Lake store events, how do you query it, and how long can it retain data?
flashcards_qa.back: It stores events in ORC, a columnar format, which you query with SQL. Default retention can be up to seven years.

flashcards_qa.front: AWS CloudTrail Lake: When or why would you use this?
flashcards_qa.back: Choose management/data events; KMS events add up fast (excluded by default).

flashcards_qa.front: CloudTrail Lake ingestion is costing too much. Which feature limits what gets stored?
flashcards_qa.back: Advanced event selectors, which give fine-grained control over which events are ingested and stored, so you can exclude high-volume noise.

flashcards_qa.front: Can CloudTrail Lake hold audit events from non-AWS systems?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. Channels let you integrate events from outside AWS, such as Okta or LaunchDarkly, alongside your AWS events.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the cost best practice when querying CloudTrail Lake?
flashcards_qa.back: Constrain queries by event time, which limits how much data is scanned and therefore both execution time and cost.

flashcards_qa.front: A CloudTrail Lake query is slow and expensive. What is the first thing to change?
flashcards_qa.back: Add an event-time constraint to the query so it scans a narrow time range rather than the full retention period.

flashcards_qa.front: Which event type is notorious for inflating CloudTrail Lake costs, and what is its default?
flashcards_qa.back: KMS management events, which are extremely high volume because every decrypt call is logged. They are off by default, and enabling them can blow up ingestion cost.

flashcards_qa.front: Why are CloudTrail Lake queries efficient?
flashcards_qa.back: Because events are stored in ORC, a columnar format, so a query only reads the columns and time ranges it needs.

flashcards_qa.front: Does plain CloudTrail let you run SQL over years of event history?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Its Event History covers 90 days. For SQL over long history use CloudTrail Lake, which stores events in ORC for up to seven years, or deliver to S3 and query with Athena.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the levers for controlling CloudTrail Lake cost, and the pitfall to avoid.
flashcards_qa.back: Constrain queries by event time so less data is scanned, and use advanced event selectors to limit what is ingested. The pitfall is enabling KMS management events, whose volume can dramatically increase cost.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Config rule? (AWS Config)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed/custom compliance check.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Remediation? (AWS Config)
flashcards_qa.back: Fixing non-compliance via SSM automation.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Config item? (AWS Config)
flashcards_qa.back: A recorded configuration snapshot (billed).

flashcards_qa.front: Which service records how your resources were configured over time and checks them against rules?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Config, which records configuration changes and evaluates compliance against rules. It is per-Region, and findings can be aggregated across Regions and accounts.

flashcards_qa.front: How is AWS Config priced, and why does that matter?
flashcards_qa.back: You pay per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation, which means a large, frequently changing estate can make Config expensive.

flashcards_qa.front: What kinds of AWS Config rules exist, and when do they run?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS managed rules, of which there are 75 or more, and custom rules backed by Lambda. They can be triggered on configuration change or evaluated at periodic intervals.

flashcards_qa.front: Can AWS Config block a non-compliant action from happening?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Config is evaluation and compliance reporting only. Preventing actions requires IAM policies or Organizations SCPs.
