flashcards_qa.front: Can a single AWS budget send notifications for an unlimited number of thresholds?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A budget supports up to five notifications.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the four AWS Budgets types, and say when you would reach for Budgets instead of Cost Explorer.
flashcards_qa.back: Usage, cost, reservation (RI utilization for EC2, ElastiCache, RDS, Redshift), and Savings Plans budgets. Use Budgets when you need to set a threshold and be alerted; use Cost Explorer to visualize and forecast after the fact.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Cost Explorer? (AWS Cost Explorer)
flashcards_qa.back: Cost/usage visualization and forecasting tool.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Savings Plan? (AWS Cost Explorer)
flashcards_qa.back: Discount commitment (alternative to RIs).

flashcards_qa.front: You need to see cost and usage trends over the past year, drilling from account level down to an individual resource. Which service?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Cost Explorer, which visualizes and analyzes cost and usage over time, from high level down to resource level, at monthly or hourly granularity.

flashcards_qa.front: Management asks for a commitment-based way to reduce compute spend. What does Cost Explorer offer?
flashcards_qa.back: Recommendations for optimal Savings Plans, an alternative to Reserved Instances, based on your historical usage.

flashcards_qa.front: Can Cost Explorer forecast usage as far as 18 months ahead?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. It forecasts usage up to 18 months out, projected from your past usage.

flashcards_qa.front: Which billing and cost service is most likely to appear on the DEA-C01 exam?
flashcards_qa.back: Cost Explorer, which the course flags as likely the only billing service tested, with AWS Budgets as its alerting counterpart.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to chart last quarter's spend by service, and separately to prevent a billing surprise next month. Which tool for each?
flashcards_qa.back: Cost Explorer to chart, analyze, and forecast the historical spend. AWS Budgets to set a threshold and be alerted before overspending.

flashcards_qa.front: Is Cost Explorer the service that alerts you when a budget threshold is breached?
flashcards_qa.back: No. That is AWS Budgets. Cost Explorer analyzes and forecasts but does not raise alarms.

flashcards_qa.front: How far ahead can Cost Explorer project usage, and on what basis?
flashcards_qa.back: Up to 18 months ahead, projected from your past usage.

flashcards_qa.front: Can AWS Cost Explorer alert you when spend crosses a threshold?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Thresholds and alarms come from AWS Budgets. Cost Explorer visualizes and analyzes spend and forecasts up to 18 months, and recommends Savings Plans.

flashcards_qa.front: What is API Gateway? (Amazon API Gateway)
flashcards_qa.back: Serverless API front door for clients.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Edge-Optimized? (Amazon API Gateway)
flashcards_qa.back: Global endpoint via CloudFront (default).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Private API? (Amazon API Gateway)
flashcards_qa.back: VPC-only endpoint via interface VPC endpoints.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Custom authorizer? (Amazon API Gateway)
flashcards_qa.back: Lambda-based API auth.

flashcards_qa.front: You need a fully managed REST front door for Lambda functions and some HTTP backends, with no servers to run. Which service?
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon API Gateway. It is serverless and integrates with Lambda, HTTP backends, and any AWS service.

flashcards_qa.front: Which API-management capabilities does API Gateway provide out of the box?
flashcards_qa.back: Authentication, usage plans and API keys, stages and versioning, throttling, WebSocket support, Swagger/OpenAPI import, request and response transformation and validation, SDK generation, and caching.

flashcards_qa.front: Mobile clients must send records into Kinesis Data Streams but must never hold AWS credentials. How do you design this?
flashcards_qa.back: Put API Gateway in front. It can integrate directly with AWS services such as Kinesis, SQS, and Step Functions, so clients call the API and never receive AWS credentials.

flashcards_qa.front: Three APIs need different reach: one globally distributed, one for a single Region, one reachable only inside a VPC. Which endpoint type for each?
flashcards_qa.back: Edge-Optimized for global reach through CloudFront, Regional for same-Region clients, and Private for VPC-only access through interface endpoints plus a resource policy.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the options for authenticating callers of an API Gateway API, and what is needed for HTTPS on a custom domain?
flashcards_qa.back: IAM roles for internal AWS callers, Amazon Cognito for external users, or a Lambda custom authorizer. For HTTPS you need an ACM certificate, in us-east-1 for edge-optimized endpoints, plus a Route 53 record.

flashcards_qa.front: Your API's entire client base sits inside your VPC. Which endpoint type, and how does it differ from Regional?
flashcards_qa.back: Private, which is reachable only through interface VPC endpoints and gated by a resource policy. Regional is publicly reachable within one Region, and Edge-Optimized fronts it globally through CloudFront.

flashcards_qa.front: You are deploying an edge-optimized API with a custom domain and your ACM certificate lives in eu-west-1. Will it work?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Edge-optimized endpoints require the ACM certificate in us-east-1, because they are fronted by CloudFront.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each case to an API Gateway auth option: internal service-to-service calls; a public mobile app's users; bespoke token validation logic.
flashcards_qa.back: IAM roles for internal calls, Amazon Cognito for external app users, and a Lambda custom authorizer for bespoke token logic.

flashcards_qa.front: Is a Regional API Gateway endpoint reachable only from inside your VPC?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Regional endpoints are publicly reachable within one Region. VPC-only access requires a Private endpoint with interface endpoints and a resource policy.

flashcards_qa.front: Is creating IAM users the right way to authenticate external consumer-app users to an API Gateway API?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Use Amazon Cognito for external users. IAM suits internal AWS callers, and a Lambda custom authorizer covers anything bespoke.

flashcards_qa.front: Why would you choose API Gateway over simply putting an Application Load Balancer in front of the backend?
flashcards_qa.back: API Gateway adds API-specific features an ALB lacks: authentication via IAM, Cognito, or a custom authorizer, throttling, usage plans and API keys, stages and versioning, caching, request validation, and SDK generation. A plain ALB only routes HTTP traffic.

flashcards_qa.front: Pick the endpoint type for a globally distributed audience, and state the certificate constraint that comes with it.
flashcards_qa.back: Edge-Optimized, which routes through CloudFront. Its ACM certificate must be in us-east-1, whereas Regional and Private endpoints use a certificate in their own Region.

flashcards_qa.front: You must expose Kinesis, SQS, and Step Functions to untrusted external clients securely. What do you build?
flashcards_qa.back: API Gateway with service integrations in front of them, so clients never hold AWS credentials. Authenticate external users with Cognito, internal callers with IAM, or use a Lambda authorizer, and add throttling and usage plans.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Structured data? (Types of Data)
flashcards_qa.back: Data organized in a defined schema (rows/columns, fixed types), easily queried with SQL.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Unstructured data? (Types of Data)
flashcards_qa.back: Data with no predefined schema that must be pre-processed to extract meaning before querying.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Semi-structured data? (Types of Data)
flashcards_qa.back: Data with partial/flexible structure via tags, hierarchies, or key-value pairs; schema may be inconsistent.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Schema? (Types of Data)
flashcards_qa.back: The defined organization (columns, types, relationships) of a dataset.

flashcards_qa.front: Types of Data: What is Structured?
flashcards_qa.back: Structured = schema known up front, easily queryable with SQL, consistent columns/types. Examples: RDBMS tables, clean CSV, Excel.

flashcards_qa.front: Types of Data: What is Unstructured?
flashcards_qa.back: Unstructured = no schema; must extract structure/metadata first (index it) before querying. Examples: text corpora, media files, emails.

flashcards_qa.front: Types of Data: What is Semi-structured?
flashcards_qa.back: Semi-structured = partial/flexible structure via tags or key-value pairs; schema exists but may vary row to row. Examples: JSON, XML, log files, email headers.

flashcards_qa.front: Is a CSV file automatically structured data?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It is structured only if the columns are consistent across every row. A CSV with ragged rows or arbitrary content is not structured data.

flashcards_qa.front: Which everyday data source is the canonical example of semi-structured data, and why?
flashcards_qa.back: Log files. They contain recognizable fields such as timestamp, level, and message, so structure exists, but the layout varies line to line and fields may be missing, so they must be parsed.

flashcards_qa.front: Is a log file unstructured data?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It is semi-structured, because it contains recognizable fields such as timestamp and level even though the layout varies. Unstructured means no tags or structure at all, like a raw image.

flashcards_qa.front: Someone argues a file is structured because it is an Excel spreadsheet. Is that reasoning valid?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The file format alone does not determine the data type. An Excel file or CSV holding arbitrary junk is unstructured, because it is the organization of the content that decides.

flashcards_qa.front: Both structured and semi-structured data are queryable. What actually separates them?
flashcards_qa.back: Rigidity of schema. Structured data has a fixed, consistent schema across every record. Semi-structured data, such as JSON, allows records to have differing fields.

flashcards_qa.front: Classify each as semi-structured or unstructured: JSON, XML, a plain text note, and a photograph.
flashcards_qa.back: JSON and XML are semi-structured because they are tagged. The plain text note and the photograph are unstructured, having no tags or field markers.

flashcards_qa.front: Why are log files classed as semi-structured rather than unstructured?
flashcards_qa.back: Because they contain field-like tokens such as timestamp, level, and message, so structure genuinely exists, but the layout is inconsistent from line to line, which means the structure has to be parsed out rather than simply read.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the real basis for the structured, semi-structured, and unstructured distinction?
flashcards_qa.back: The presence and consistency of a schema, not the file format. The same format can fall into different categories depending on how consistently its content is organized.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Volume? (Properties of Data (3 Vs))
flashcards_qa.back: The amount/size of data being handled.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Velocity? (Properties of Data (3 Vs))
flashcards_qa.back: The speed at which data is generated, collected, and processed.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Variety? (Properties of Data (3 Vs))
flashcards_qa.back: The range of data types, formats, and sources involved.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Batch processing? (Properties of Data (3 Vs))
flashcards_qa.back: Processing data in scheduled groups rather than continuously.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Stream processing? (Properties of Data (3 Vs))
flashcards_qa.back: Processing data continuously as it arrives in real time.

flashcards_qa.front: How does data volume influence the ingestion method you choose?
flashcards_qa.back: Small volumes can go over the internet through the console or an API upload. Massive volumes may need physical transfer with the AWS Snow Family, because the network would take too long.

flashcards_qa.front: What does the velocity of data determine in an architecture, and which distinction does the exam like to test?
flashcards_qa.back: It determines batch versus streaming processing. The exam commonly tests real-time versus near-real-time, which maps to Kinesis Data Streams versus Firehose.

flashcards_qa.front: What does variety refer to, and what does high variety imply for your design?
flashcards_qa.back: The range of formats and sources, which maps back to structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data. High variety usually means blending multiple sources and formats, and often multiple specialized stores.

flashcards_qa.front: Are IoT specifics heavily tested on the exam?
flashcards_qa.back: No, the exam de-emphasizes IoT specifics, although IoT sensor streams remain the classic example of high-velocity data.

flashcards_qa.front: A requirement says records must be available for processing immediately versus within a few minutes. Which service for each?
flashcards_qa.back: Immediately points to Kinesis Data Streams, which is real time with custom consumers and replay. Within a few minutes points to Kinesis Data Firehose, which is near real time with managed delivery.

flashcards_qa.front: A dataset is only a few gigabytes but arrives in twelve different formats from nine systems. Which of the three Vs is high here?
flashcards_qa.back: Variety is high, because it concerns formats and sources. Volume is low, since a small dataset can still be highly varied.

flashcards_qa.front: A dataset arrives slowly but is enormous. Is that high velocity?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Size is volume; velocity is how fast data arrives and must be processed. A huge dataset arriving slowly is high volume and low velocity.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a consumer replay data from Kinesis Data Firehose?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Firehose does not store data, so there is no replay. Kinesis Data Streams retains data for 1 to 365 days and supports replay.

flashcards_qa.front: A scenario says analytics must reflect events within seconds; another says the data warehouse should be updated within minutes. Which service each, and what is the tell?
flashcards_qa.back: Seconds means Kinesis Data Streams; minutes means Firehose. The tell is the latency wording, with words like immediately or real time pointing to Streams and within minutes or near real time pointing to Firehose.

flashcards_qa.front: An organization must analyze relational records, JSON documents, and images together. What does high variety imply architecturally?
flashcards_qa.back: That no single database will serve everything. You typically land data in multiple specialized stores and put a unified query and catalog layer over the top, for example S3 plus the Glue Data Catalog with Athena.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data warehouse? (Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse)
flashcards_qa.back: Centralized structured repository optimized for complex read-heavy analytics (schema-on-write, ETL).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data lake? (Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse)
flashcards_qa.back: Repository of raw data in native format with no predefined schema (schema-on-read, ELT).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data lakehouse? (Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse)
flashcards_qa.back: Hybrid combining warehouse performance/reliability with lake flexibility/low cost.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Schema-on-write? (Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse)
flashcards_qa.back: Structure is applied before data is stored (warehouse).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Schema-on-read? (Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse)
flashcards_qa.back: Structure is applied when data is read/queried (lake).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data mart? (Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse)
flashcards_qa.back: A subset/view of warehouse data tailored to a specific team or use case.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ACID? (Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse)
flashcards_qa.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — transactional guarantees (added to lakes by Delta Lake).

flashcards_qa.front: Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse: What is Warehouse?
flashcards_qa.back: Warehouse = schema-on-write + ETL (Extract, Transform, Load). Lake = schema-on-read + ELT (Extract, Load, Transform).

flashcards_qa.front: What is the fundamental difference in what a data warehouse and a data lake store?
flashcards_qa.back: A warehouse stores structured, already-transformed data ready for analysis. A lake stores raw data in its original form, in any format.

flashcards_qa.front: Is changing the schema of a data warehouse cheap and quick?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Warehouses are less agile, and a schema change means a costly migration. Lakes are flexible because structure is applied at read time.

flashcards_qa.front: Must an organization choose between a data warehouse and a data lake?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Using both is a valid architecture, with the same data held in each for different purposes, for example raw in the lake and curated in the warehouse.

flashcards_qa.front: Warehouses vs Lakes vs Lakehouse: What is AWS lakehouse?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS lakehouse = Lake Formation + S3 + Redshift Spectrum. Delta Lake brings ACID transactions to big data (Databricks origin).

flashcards_qa.front: In which of ETL and ELT does the transform happen before loading, and which pattern belongs to a lake?
flashcards_qa.back: ETL transforms before load, which suits a warehouse. ELT loads raw data first and transforms later or on read, which suits a lake.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the only difference between ETL and ELT, and which store does each pair with?
flashcards_qa.back: The order of the transform and load steps. Warehouses use ETL, transforming before load. Lakes use ELT, loading raw and transforming afterwards.

flashcards_qa.front: Which store enforces schema-on-write and which uses schema-on-read?
flashcards_qa.back: A warehouse enforces schema-on-write, so data must conform as it is loaded. A lake uses schema-on-read, so the structure is applied when the data is queried.

flashcards_qa.front: Someone claims Redshift and Redshift Spectrum are the same thing. What is the distinction?
flashcards_qa.back: Redshift is the data warehouse engine holding data in its own managed storage. Redshift Spectrum queries data left in S3, which is the lakehouse pattern, so they are not the same.

flashcards_qa.front: Contrast a data warehouse with a data lake across content, format, and schema handling.
flashcards_qa.back: A warehouse holds structured, transformed data in a fixed format with schema-on-write. A lake holds raw data in any format with schema-on-read.

flashcards_qa.front: When would you use Redshift Spectrum rather than loading data into Redshift?
flashcards_qa.back: When the data should stay in S3, for example infrequently queried or very large history, and you still want to query it with Redshift SQL and join it to warehouse tables. Loading into Redshift suits hot, frequently queried data.

flashcards_qa.front: Why does schema-on-write and ETL suit a warehouse while schema-on-read and ELT suit a lake?
flashcards_qa.back: A warehouse's value is fast, reliable queries over conformed data, so the schema is enforced and transformation happens before load. A lake's value is keeping everything cheaply and deciding later how to interpret it, so raw data is loaded first and the schema is applied at read time.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe the lakehouse pattern and name the AWS services that implement it.
flashcards_qa.back: A warehouse-style SQL query engine operating directly over raw lake storage. On AWS that is Redshift Spectrum, or Athena, querying data in S3, with governance and fine-grained permissions provided by Lake Formation.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data mesh? (Data Mesh)
flashcards_qa.back: Decentralized socio-technical approach where domains own their data and expose it as products under federated governance.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data domain? (Data Mesh)
flashcards_qa.back: A team/area responsible for a specific set of data products.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data product? (Data Mesh)
flashcards_qa.back: Curated, governed data a domain exposes for others to consume.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Federated governance? (Data Mesh)
flashcards_qa.back: Central standards/policies applied by autonomous domains.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Mesh: What is Data mesh?
flashcards_qa.back: Data mesh = decentralized, domain-oriented data OWNERSHIP with federated governance and central standards.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the four principles of a data mesh.
flashcards_qa.back: Domain ownership of data, data treated as a product, self-service data infrastructure, and federated computational governance.

flashcards_qa.front: Does adopting a data mesh mean adopting a particular set of AWS services?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A data mesh does not prescribe any specific technology or architecture. AWS services are one possible implementation of the idea.

flashcards_qa.front: What does a data mesh contrast with?
flashcards_qa.back: Centralized approaches, where a single warehouse or lake team owns all of the organization's data, rather than each domain owning and publishing its own.

flashcards_qa.front: A colleague says they are building a data mesh by deploying a data lake. What is wrong with that statement?
flashcards_qa.back: A data mesh is an organizational and governance model about who owns and publishes data. A data lake is a storage technology. A mesh may use lakes, but deploying one does not create a mesh.

flashcards_qa.front: What does federated governance mean in a data mesh?
flashcards_qa.back: Central standards with distributed ownership. It is neither a single central team owning everything nor an absence of governance.

flashcards_qa.front: Can you buy or deploy a data mesh?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A data mesh is an organizational and governance model about who owns and publishes data as products. Lakes and warehouses are the technologies it may be built on.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare federated and centralized data governance.
flashcards_qa.back: Federated means individual domains own their data while central standards and policies apply across them. Centralized means one team owns and controls all the data.

flashcards_qa.front: Why is a data mesh described as primarily organizational?
flashcards_qa.back: Because its substance is who owns, publishes, and governs data, treating datasets as products owned by domain teams under shared standards. It is not a product you deploy, and no specific technology is required.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Mesh: What's a hard concept to master in this lesson?
flashcards_qa.back: The balance of decentralized ownership with centralized standards (federated governance).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Extract? (Managing & Orchestrating ETL)
flashcards_qa.back: Retrieving raw data from source systems (DBs, CRMs, files, APIs).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Transform? (Managing & Orchestrating ETL)
flashcards_qa.back: Cleansing, enriching, reformatting, aggregating, and fixing data.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Load? (Managing & Orchestrating ETL)
flashcards_qa.back: Writing transformed data into the target store.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Orchestration? (Managing & Orchestrating ETL)
flashcards_qa.back: Automating the order, scheduling, and reliability of pipeline steps.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Imputation? (Managing & Orchestrating ETL)
flashcards_qa.back: Filling missing values with placeholders/estimates.

flashcards_qa.front: Restate the difference between ETL and ELT and which architecture each belongs to.
flashcards_qa.back: ETL transforms data before loading it, which is the warehouse pattern. ELT loads raw data first and transforms it later, which is the lake pattern. The letters are the same, only the order changes.

flashcards_qa.front: At which stages of a pipeline must you protect data integrity, and what can go wrong?
flashcards_qa.back: At both extract and load. Extraction can fail through failed or partial API calls, and loading can fail through failed disk or target writes, so both ends need validation and retry.

flashcards_qa.front: What kinds of work fall under the transform step of a pipeline?
flashcards_qa.back: Cleansing bad values, enriching records with additional data, converting formats, aggregating, encoding and decoding, and handling missing data.

flashcards_qa.front: Which AWS services can orchestrate an ETL pipeline?
flashcards_qa.back: Glue Workflows, EventBridge, Amazon MWAA running Airflow, AWS Step Functions, and Lambda.

flashcards_qa.front: Which of ETL and ELT is the data lake pattern, and why?
flashcards_qa.back: ELT. A lake stores raw data cheaply and applies structure and transformation later at read time, so load comes before transform.

flashcards_qa.front: Spell out the order of operations in ETL versus ELT.
flashcards_qa.back: ETL is extract, transform, then load, so only conformed data reaches the target. ELT is extract, load, then transform, so raw data lands first and transformation happens in place afterwards.

flashcards_qa.front: You must choose an orchestrator for a pipeline. What distinguishes Step Functions, Glue Workflows, and MWAA?
flashcards_qa.back: Step Functions is state-machine orchestration across many AWS services, defined declaratively. Glue Workflows is Glue-native and only coordinates Glue jobs, crawlers, and triggers. MWAA runs Airflow Python DAGs, which suits complex, code-based, portable pipelines.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the difference between orchestrating an ETL pipeline and executing the ETL itself?
flashcards_qa.back: Execution is the service that actually transforms data, such as a Glue job or an EMR step. Orchestration is the layer that decides what runs when and handles dependencies, retries, and branching, which is what Step Functions, MWAA, EventBridge, and Glue Workflows do.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each scenario to an orchestrator: a nightly Glue-only pipeline, a complex Python-defined workflow, a cross-service workflow with retries and branching, and a simple scheduled trigger.
flashcards_qa.back: Glue Workflows for the Glue-only pipeline, MWAA for the Python DAG, Step Functions for the cross-service workflow with error handling, and EventBridge for the simple schedule or event trigger.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the different operations that the word transform can cover in a pipeline, and when each applies.
flashcards_qa.back: Cleansing to remove or fix bad values, enrichment to add data from another source, reformatting to change file or field formats, aggregation to summarize, encoding and decoding for representation changes, and imputation to fill missing values when they cannot simply be dropped.

flashcards_qa.front: What is JDBC? (Data Sources & Formats)
flashcards_qa.back: Java Database Connectivity — Java-based DB interface; platform-independent, language-dependent.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ODBC? (Data Sources & Formats)
flashcards_qa.back: Open Database Connectivity — driver-based DB interface; platform-dependent, language-independent.

flashcards_qa.front: What is CSV? (Data Sources & Formats)
flashcards_qa.back: Comma/delimiter-separated, human-readable tabular text format.

flashcards_qa.front: What is JSON? (Data Sources & Formats)
flashcards_qa.back: Human-readable, semi-structured key-value interchange format.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Avro? (Data Sources & Formats)
flashcards_qa.back: Binary, row-based format that stores data plus its schema.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Parquet? (Data Sources & Formats)
flashcards_qa.back: Binary, columnar storage format optimized for analytics and compression.

flashcards_qa.front: Is JDBC usable from a Python application?
flashcards_qa.back: No, not directly, since JDBC is a Java API. It is platform-independent but language-dependent. ODBC is the language-independent option, though it depends on platform drivers.

flashcards_qa.front: What is CSV good for, and must its delimiter be a comma?
flashcards_qa.back: It is human-readable, tabular, well suited to small and medium datasets, and is the universal interchange format. The delimiter need not be a comma, as tab-separated TSV shows.

flashcards_qa.front: What are JSON's characteristics and typical uses?
flashcards_qa.back: It is human-readable, semi-structured key-value data with a flexible and nestable schema, which makes it common for web APIs and NoSQL databases.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe Avro and say when it is the right choice.
flashcards_qa.back: Avro is a binary, row-based format that embeds the schema alongside the data. That makes it ideal where the schema changes over time and for efficient serialization and transport, such as streaming and write-heavy workloads.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe Parquet and say when it is the right choice.
flashcards_qa.back: Parquet is a binary columnar format, which makes it ideal for analytics that read a subset of columns from a wide table. It compresses extremely well and is used by Spark, Hive, Impala, and Redshift Spectrum.

flashcards_qa.front: You have a write-heavy streaming pipeline with an evolving schema, and separately an analytics table queried by column. Which format for each?
flashcards_qa.back: Avro for the streaming pipeline, since it is row-based and carries its schema with the data, which handles schema change well. Parquet for the analytics table, since it is columnar and read-optimized.

flashcards_qa.front: Which of JDBC and ODBC is language-independent, and which is platform-independent?
flashcards_qa.back: ODBC is language-independent, though it depends on platform-specific drivers. JDBC is platform-independent, but it is tied to Java.

flashcards_qa.front: You need database connectivity from a non-Java application. JDBC or ODBC?
flashcards_qa.back: ODBC, because it is language-independent and works through drivers. JDBC is a Java-only API.

flashcards_qa.front: Which of CSV, JSON, Avro, and Parquet are human-readable text, and which are binary?
flashcards_qa.back: CSV and JSON are human-readable text. Avro and Parquet are binary formats.

flashcards_qa.front: State the Avro versus Parquet distinction, which the exam tests often.
flashcards_qa.back: Avro is row-based and stores the schema with the data, so it suits writes, transport, and evolving schemas. Parquet is columnar, so it suits read-heavy analytics that touch a subset of columns and compresses better.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a CSV file hold records with different fields from one another?
flashcards_qa.back: No, not meaningfully, since CSV is rigid and tabular with consistent columns. JSON is the flexible, nestable format where records may carry different fields.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you decide between Avro and Parquet for a given dataset?
flashcards_qa.back: Choose Avro when the schema evolves and the workload is write- or transport-heavy, such as streaming ingestion, because it is row-based and self-describing. Choose Parquet when the workload is read-heavy analytics over a subset of columns, because columnar storage scans less and compresses better.

flashcards_qa.front: State precisely which axis of independence belongs to JDBC and which to ODBC.
flashcards_qa.back: JDBC is platform-independent but language-dependent, being Java-based. ODBC is language-independent but platform-dependent, needing drivers for the platform.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Fact table? (Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution)
flashcards_qa.back: Central table of measures and foreign keys in a star schema.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Dimension table? (Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution)
flashcards_qa.back: Descriptive-attribute table linked to the fact table.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Star schema? (Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution)
flashcards_qa.back: Fact table surrounded by dimension tables joined by keys.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ERD? (Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution)
flashcards_qa.back: Entity Relationship Diagram showing tables and their key relationships.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data lineage? (Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution)
flashcards_qa.back: A traceable record of data's flow and transformations across its lifecycle.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Schema evolution? (Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution)
flashcards_qa.back: Changing a schema over time without breaking existing processes.

flashcards_qa.front: Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution: What is Star schema?
flashcards_qa.back: Star schema = central fact table + surrounding dimension tables joined by primary/foreign keys.

flashcards_qa.front: In a star schema, what does the fact table hold and what do the dimension tables hold?
flashcards_qa.back: The fact table holds the numeric measures plus foreign keys to the dimensions. Dimension tables hold the descriptive attributes used to slice those measures.

flashcards_qa.front: How are relationships between tables diagrammed?
flashcards_qa.back: With an Entity Relationship Diagram, or ERD, showing the entities and the relationships and cardinality between them.

flashcards_qa.front: What does data lineage trace, and what is it used for?
flashcards_qa.back: It traces the flow and transformations data undergoes from source to destination. It is used for debugging pipelines, for regulatory compliance, and for documentation.

flashcards_qa.front: Modeling, Lineage, Schema Evolution: What is Schema evolution?
flashcards_qa.back: Schema evolution = change schema over time without breaking systems; Glue Schema Registry handles versioning/compatibility.

flashcards_qa.front: The exam sometimes draws on AWS blog architectures. Give an example related to lineage.
flashcards_qa.back: Capturing Spark lineage in AWS Glue with the Spline agent and storing the resulting lineage graph in Amazon Neptune, which is a documented AWS blog pattern.

flashcards_qa.front: Given an unfamiliar schema, how do you tell a fact table from a dimension table?
flashcards_qa.back: The fact table contains the numeric measures and the foreign keys, and is usually much larger. Dimension tables contain descriptive attributes and a primary key, and are comparatively small.

flashcards_qa.front: Does data lineage tell you how a schema changed over time?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Lineage traces where data came from and what transformed it. Managing structural change safely is schema evolution, a separate concern.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a snowflake schema have fewer tables than a star schema?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Snowflake normalizes dimensions into sub-dimension tables, so it has more tables and more joins. A star schema keeps dimensions flat and denormalized.

flashcards_qa.front: Which concept answers where the data went, and which answers how the schema changed?
flashcards_qa.back: Lineage answers where the data went and what transformed it. Schema evolution answers how the schema changed and how to do so safely.

flashcards_qa.front: You are shown an ERD of a star schema. How do you identify the fact table?
flashcards_qa.back: Look for the central table holding numeric measures and multiple foreign keys pointing out to the surrounding tables. The surrounding tables, holding descriptive attributes, are the dimensions.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish data lineage from schema evolution in terms of what each gives you.
flashcards_qa.back: Lineage gives an audit of data movement and transformations, which supports debugging and compliance. Schema evolution gives a strategy for changing structure safely, for example adding fields without breaking existing consumers.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Index? (DB Performance Optimization)
flashcards_qa.back: A structure enabling fast row lookups, avoiding full table scans.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Partitioning? (DB Performance Optimization)
flashcards_qa.back: Splitting data into segments (e.g., by date) to scan less and parallelize.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Compression? (DB Performance Optimization)
flashcards_qa.back: Encoding data more compactly to cut storage and I/O.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Full table scan? (DB Performance Optimization)
flashcards_qa.back: Reading every row — a sign a needed index is missing.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the three main levers for optimizing database performance.
flashcards_qa.back: Indexing, partitioning, and compression.

flashcards_qa.front: What does indexing achieve beyond speed?
flashcards_qa.back: It avoids full table scans when locating rows, and it can also enforce uniqueness and referential integrity through unique and primary key indexes.

flashcards_qa.front: What does partitioning give you, and what do you usually partition by?
flashcards_qa.back: It reduces how much data a query has to scan, makes lifecycle management easier such as dropping old partitions, and enables parallel processing. It is most often done by a query dimension such as date.

flashcards_qa.front: What does compression buy you, and which codecs does Redshift support?
flashcards_qa.back: It reduces storage and disk I/O. Redshift supports GZIP, LZOP, BZIP2, and Zstandard.

flashcards_qa.front: Can compression ever make a workload slower?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. Over-aggressive compression can shift a workload from I/O-bound to CPU-bound, because the time saved reading data is lost decompressing it.

flashcards_qa.front: Why does columnar storage compress better than row storage?
flashcards_qa.back: Because a column holds values of the same type and often similar values, which compresses far more effectively than a row mixing many different data types together.

flashcards_qa.front: You enable the highest compression level and the job gets slower. What is happening?
flashcards_qa.back: The workload has flipped from I/O-bound to CPU-bound. Compression cut the bytes read but decompression now dominates the runtime, so a lighter codec is the right balance.

flashcards_qa.front: You partition a large table but query times do not improve. Why might that be?
flashcards_qa.back: Because the partition key does not match how the data is queried, so every query still scans all partitions. Partitioning only helps when partitions align with the access pattern, and a poorly chosen key can also create skew.

flashcards_qa.front: Does adding an index reduce how much data a query scans in the first place?
flashcards_qa.back: No, not in the partitioning sense. Indexing speeds up finding rows within the data being scanned. Partitioning is what prunes whole chunks of data from the scan.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish an I/O-bound workload from a CPU-bound one, and what can move a job between them.
flashcards_qa.back: An I/O-bound job is limited by reading data from storage, while a CPU-bound job is limited by computation. Heavy compression reduces I/O but adds decompression work, which can flip a job from I/O-bound to CPU-bound.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you choose a compression codec for a large analytics table?
flashcards_qa.back: Pick one that reduces I/O enough to speed up scans without making decompression the bottleneck. A lighter codec such as LZO or Zstandard often beats maximum-ratio options like BZIP2 when CPU is the constraint.

flashcards_qa.front: Explain why columnar compression outperforms row-based compression.
flashcards_qa.back: Within a column, values share a data type and often repeat or fall in a narrow range, so encodings like run-length and dictionary compression work very well. A row interleaves many different types, which gives compressors far less redundancy to exploit.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Random sampling? (Data Sampling Techniques)
flashcards_qa.back: Each item has equal probability of selection.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Stratified sampling? (Data Sampling Techniques)
flashcards_qa.back: Dividing into subgroups (strata) and sampling each to ensure representation.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Systematic sampling? (Data Sampling Techniques)
flashcards_qa.back: Selecting every k-th item by a fixed rule.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Stratum? (Data Sampling Techniques)
flashcards_qa.back: A homogeneous subgroup within the population.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Sampling Techniques: What is Random sampling?
flashcards_qa.back: Random sampling = equal selection probability; good for homogeneous data.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Sampling Techniques: What is Stratified sampling?
flashcards_qa.back: Stratified sampling = split into strata, sample each, ensuring representation of every subgroup.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Sampling Techniques: What is Systematic sampling?
flashcards_qa.back: Systematic sampling = pick every k-th item using a fixed interval/rule.

flashcards_qa.front: Does stratified sampling preserve the true proportions of each category?
flashcards_qa.back: Not necessarily. Its purpose is to ensure every category is represented in the sample, which may mean deliberately over-representing rare categories.

flashcards_qa.front: You are sampling a dataset in which one important category makes up 0.5 percent of rows. Random or stratified sampling?
flashcards_qa.back: Stratified, because random sampling could miss the rare category entirely. Stratified sampling guarantees each subgroup appears in the sample.

flashcards_qa.front: In systematic sampling, is each record selected at random?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Systematic sampling picks at a fixed interval, such as every hundredth record. Random sampling has no pattern and gives each record an equal independent chance.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish stratified from systematic sampling.
flashcards_qa.back: Stratified sampling divides the data into categories and samples within each one, guaranteeing coverage. Systematic sampling picks records at a fixed interval regardless of which category they fall into.

flashcards_qa.front: When is stratified sampling required, and when will random sampling do?
flashcards_qa.back: Stratified is required when the data is imbalanced or when certain categories matter and must be represented. Random sampling is sufficient when the data is relatively homogeneous.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Data skew? (Data Skew Mechanisms)
flashcards_qa.back: Unequal distribution of data/traffic across partitions or nodes.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Celebrity problem? (Data Skew Mechanisms)
flashcards_qa.back: A hot key receiving disproportionate traffic, overloading its partition.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Temporal skew? (Data Skew Mechanisms)
flashcards_qa.back: Recent time-based partitions growing much larger than older ones.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Salting? (Data Skew Mechanisms)
flashcards_qa.back: Adding a random prefix to a key to distribute hot keys more evenly.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Adaptive partitioning? (Data Skew Mechanisms)
flashcards_qa.back: Dynamically adjusting partitions based on observed distribution.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Skew Mechanisms: What is Data skew?
flashcards_qa.back: Data skew = imbalanced data/traffic across partitions or nodes.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Skew Mechanisms: What is 'Celebrity problem'?
flashcards_qa.back: 'Celebrity problem' = a hot key overloads its partition due to uneven access.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Skew Mechanisms: What is Temporal skew?
flashcards_qa.back: Temporal skew = newer time-based partitions become disproportionately large.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you detect data skew before it becomes an outage?
flashcards_qa.back: Monitor the distribution of data and traffic across partitions or shards, and set CloudWatch alarms so you are alerted when the distribution becomes uneven.

flashcards_qa.front: How does salting mitigate a hot partition key?
flashcards_qa.back: By prefixing or appending a random value to the key before partitioning, so what was one hot key is spread across multiple partitions.

flashcards_qa.front: Your partition keys hash evenly, yet one partition is overwhelmed. How is that possible?
flashcards_qa.back: Because even hashing only balances the number of keys, not the traffic to them. If one key is enormously popular, which is the celebrity problem, its partition is hot regardless of hashing.

flashcards_qa.front: Is temporal skew just another name for data skew in general?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Temporal skew is specifically the growth of time-based partitions, where the current time partition absorbs all the writes. General skew is any uneven distribution.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish data skew from data sampling.
flashcards_qa.back: Skew is a problem: data or traffic is unevenly distributed across partitions. Sampling is a technique for selecting a subset of data, and it is sometimes used to detect skew.

flashcards_qa.front: Is salting a more disruptive fix for skew than repartitioning?
flashcards_qa.back: No, it is the less disruptive one. Salting adds randomness to keys and can be applied incrementally. Repartitioning reshuffles all the data under a new scheme.

flashcards_qa.front: Why does uniform hashing fail to solve skew when traffic is uneven?
flashcards_qa.back: Because hashing distributes keys, not requests. One extremely popular key, the celebrity problem, still maps to a single partition, so that partition receives disproportionate traffic no matter how well the hash spreads keys.

flashcards_qa.front: Writes to your time-partitioned table all land on one partition. What is this called, and how do you fix it?
flashcards_qa.back: Temporal skew, caused by partitioning on time so the current partition absorbs all writes. Mitigate it by salting the key to spread writes across multiple partitions, or by using adaptive partitioning.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Completeness? (Data Validation & Profiling)
flashcards_qa.back: Whether all expected data is present (no critical missing values).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Consistency? (Data Validation & Profiling)
flashcards_qa.back: Uniform representation of data across sources/tables.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Accuracy? (Data Validation & Profiling)
flashcards_qa.back: Whether data correctly reflects reality/ground truth.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Integrity? (Data Validation & Profiling)
flashcards_qa.back: Whether relationships between data remain valid over time.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Cross-field validation? (Data Validation & Profiling)
flashcards_qa.back: Comparing related fields/sources to detect inconsistencies.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the four dimensions of data quality.
flashcards_qa.back: Completeness, consistency, accuracy, and integrity.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you measure completeness?
flashcards_qa.back: By counting nulls and calculating null percentages per field and comparing them against what the requirements allow.

flashcards_qa.front: How is consistency checked, and what does a failure look like?
flashcards_qa.back: Through cross-field and cross-source validation. A typical failure is the same measure represented differently in two sources, for example mismatched value ranges, units, or scales.

flashcards_qa.front: How is data integrity typically verified?
flashcards_qa.back: With foreign-key checks confirming that relationships between tables remain valid over time, so no child rows reference missing parents.

flashcards_qa.front: You find missing values in an incoming dataset. What are your options?
flashcards_qa.back: Handle them deliberately: drop the affected records, impute a value, or report and reject the data. Silently ignoring them is not one of the options.

flashcards_qa.front: A field is formatted identically everywhere but holds the wrong values. Which quality dimension has failed?
flashcards_qa.back: Accuracy, which is correctness against reality. Consistency, meaning uniform representation across sources, is satisfied here.

flashcards_qa.front: Two systems both store a value in a consistent format, but the value is wrong. Is that a consistency failure?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Consistent representation is satisfied, so this is an accuracy failure, meaning the value does not match reality. Consistency failures look like one system using Celsius and another Fahrenheit.

flashcards_qa.front: Data Validation & Profiling: What distinction is easy to mix up here?
flashcards_qa.back: A '5' on a 1–5 scale is top rating but looks poor when merged into a 1–10 scale — a consistency failure.

flashcards_qa.front: Is a foreign key pointing at a missing row a completeness problem?
flashcards_qa.back: No. That is an integrity problem, meaning a broken relationship. Completeness concerns missing values such as nulls where data is required.

flashcards_qa.front: Map each symptom to a quality dimension: null fields, mismatched units between sources, values that do not reflect reality, and orphaned foreign keys.
flashcards_qa.back: Null fields are completeness. Mismatched units are consistency. Values not reflecting reality are accuracy. Orphaned foreign keys are integrity.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you choose between dropping, imputing, and rejecting records with missing data?
flashcards_qa.back: By what the requirements can tolerate. Drop when the records are few and non-essential, impute when a reasonable estimate preserves more value than deleting, and report or reject when the missing data means the record cannot be trusted at all.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Aggregation? (SQL Aggregations & Grouping)
flashcards_qa.back: Computing a summary value over rows (COUNT/SUM/AVG/MAX/MIN).

flashcards_qa.front: What is GROUP BY? (SQL Aggregations & Grouping)
flashcards_qa.back: Splitting rows into groups by column value(s).

flashcards_qa.front: What is ORDER BY? (SQL Aggregations & Grouping)
flashcards_qa.back: Sorting result rows ascending or descending.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Pivot? (SQL Aggregations & Grouping)
flashcards_qa.back: Transforming row-level data into columnar form.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Conditional aggregation? (SQL Aggregations & Grouping)
flashcards_qa.back: Using CASE inside an aggregate to compute multiple filtered results.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the SQL aggregate functions and how you name the resulting column.
flashcards_qa.back: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, and MIN. Use AS to alias the result column.

flashcards_qa.front: You need three differently filtered counts in one result row. Why will WHERE not do, and what will?
flashcards_qa.back: WHERE applies a single filter to the whole query, so it cannot produce differently filtered aggregates side by side. Use CASE expressions inside the aggregate functions to compute several conditional aggregates in one SELECT.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Aggregations & Grouping: What's the answer/service for — GROUP BY produces one row per unique group; multiple columns?
flashcards_qa.back: GROUP BY produces one row per unique group; multiple columns → one row per combination (nested grouping).

flashcards_qa.front: What does ORDER BY do, and what is its default direction?
flashcards_qa.back: It sorts the output rows. The default is ascending, and you add DESC for descending.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Aggregations & Grouping: What's the answer/service for — Pivoting = rows?
flashcards_qa.back: Pivoting = rows→columns; conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE WHEN...)) is a portable pivot method.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a WHERE clause produce two differently filtered counts in the same result row?
flashcards_qa.back: No. WHERE applies one filter to the whole query. Use CASE inside the aggregate functions to compute several differently conditioned aggregates at once.

flashcards_qa.front: Do you need to memorize exact PIVOT syntax for the exam?
flashcards_qa.back: No. PIVOT syntax varies between database engines. What matters is the concept of turning rows into columns.

flashcards_qa.front: You need counts of orders by status as separate columns in one row. WHERE or CASE?
flashcards_qa.back: CASE, using expressions such as COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN 1 END) per status. WHERE would restrict the whole query to a single status.

flashcards_qa.front: Does GROUP BY sort the result rows?
flashcards_qa.back: No. GROUP BY collapses rows into groups so aggregates are computed per group. Sorting is ORDER BY's job.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you produce several filtered counts in one query instead of running several queries with different WHERE clauses?
flashcards_qa.back: With COUNT(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 END) once per condition in the SELECT list, which yields one row containing all the filtered counts.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you read the output of a query with GROUP BY on two columns plus an ORDER BY?
flashcards_qa.back: There is one row per distinct combination of the grouped columns, with the aggregates computed for that combination, and those rows are then sorted according to the ORDER BY.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Inner join? (SQL JOIN Types)
flashcards_qa.back: Returns only rows with matches in both tables (intersection).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Left outer join? (SQL JOIN Types)
flashcards_qa.back: All rows from the left table plus matches (nulls where unmatched).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Right outer join? (SQL JOIN Types)
flashcards_qa.back: All rows from the right table plus matches (nulls where unmatched).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Full outer join? (SQL JOIN Types)
flashcards_qa.back: All rows from both tables, nulls where no match.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Cross join? (SQL JOIN Types)
flashcards_qa.back: Cartesian product — every combination of rows from both tables.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL JOIN Types: What is Plain JOIN?
flashcards_qa.back: Plain JOIN = INNER JOIN = intersection (matches only).

flashcards_qa.front: SQL JOIN Types: What is LEFT JOIN?
flashcards_qa.back: LEFT JOIN = all left rows + matched right (nulls when unmatched); RIGHT JOIN = all right rows.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL JOIN Types: What is FULL OUTER JOIN?
flashcards_qa.back: FULL OUTER JOIN = all rows from both, nulls where unmatched — good for spotting mismatched keys.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL JOIN Types: What is CROSS JOIN?
flashcards_qa.back: CROSS JOIN = Cartesian product (every combination); grows very fast; rarely useful.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a LEFT JOIN keep unmatched rows from the right table?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It keeps every row from the left table and fills right-side columns with nulls where there is no match. Keeping all right rows is a RIGHT JOIN.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare a FULL OUTER JOIN with an INNER JOIN.
flashcards_qa.back: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that match on both sides. A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, using nulls where there is no match.

flashcards_qa.front: Two tables of 1,000 and 500 rows are joined with CROSS JOIN. What do you get?
flashcards_qa.back: Five hundred thousand rows, the Cartesian product of N times M. That is rarely intended, so a CROSS JOIN should be deliberate.

flashcards_qa.front: How do left and right outer joins relate to each other?
flashcards_qa.back: They are mirror images. The only difference is which side is preserved in full, so a LEFT JOIN can always be rewritten as a RIGHT JOIN by swapping the table order.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a FULL OUTER JOIN return every combination of rows from both tables?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It returns matched rows plus unmatched rows from each side padded with nulls. Every possible combination is a CROSS JOIN.

flashcards_qa.front: Given two tables with partially overlapping keys, which rows and nulls does each outer join produce?
flashcards_qa.back: LEFT keeps all left rows, with nulls for right columns where there is no match. RIGHT keeps all right rows, with nulls on the left. FULL OUTER keeps everything from both sides, with nulls on whichever side is missing. INNER keeps only matching rows with no nulls from the join.

flashcards_qa.front: You suspect keys are missing on both sides of a relationship. Which join helps you find them?
flashcards_qa.back: A FULL OUTER JOIN, because it surfaces unmatched rows from both tables at once. Rows with nulls on one side identify keys that exist only in the other table.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Regular expression? (SQL Regular Expressions)
flashcards_qa.back: A pattern-matching language for searching strings.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ~ / ~*? (SQL Regular Expressions)
flashcards_qa.back: Case-sensitive / case-insensitive regex match operators.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ^ and $? (SQL Regular Expressions)
flashcards_qa.back: Anchors for start-of-string and end-of-string.

flashcards_qa.front: What is | (pipe)? (SQL Regular Expressions)
flashcards_qa.back: Alternation (OR) between patterns.

flashcards_qa.front: What is \d \w \s \t? (SQL Regular Expressions)
flashcards_qa.back: Shortcuts: digit, word char, whitespace, tab.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What is ~?
flashcards_qa.back: ~ = case-sensitive regex match; ~* = case-insensitive; ! negates (!~*).

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What is ^?
flashcards_qa.back: ^ = start of string; $ = end of string.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What is |?
flashcards_qa.back: | = OR; [a-z] = range; {n} = repeat count; \d/\w/\s/\t shortcuts.

flashcards_qa.front: Why use a regular expression instead of the LIKE operator?
flashcards_qa.back: Because regex is a far stronger pattern-matching tool, supporting anchors, alternation, character classes, and quantifiers, whereas LIKE offers only simple wildcards.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What distinction is easy to mix up here — inside?
flashcards_qa.back: ^ inside a pattern means 'start of string' (outside a character class); inside [] it can mean negation — exam focuses on the anchor use.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What distinction is easy to mix up here — matches?
flashcards_qa.back: 'boo$' matches 'boo' but not 'book'; '^boo' matches both 'boo' and 'book'.

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What distinction is easy to mix up here — case-sensitive?
flashcards_qa.back: ~ (case-sensitive) vs ~* (case-insensitive).

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What distinction is easy to mix up here — starts?
flashcards_qa.back: ^boo (starts with) vs boo$ (ends with).

flashcards_qa.front: SQL Regular Expressions: What distinction is easy to mix up here — case?
flashcards_qa.back: ~ vs ~* — case sensitivity.

flashcards_qa.front: What does the condition column ~* '^(fire|ice)' match?
flashcards_qa.back: Any value that starts with either fire or ice, matched case-insensitively. The caret anchors to the start of the string, the parentheses with the pipe give the alternation, and ~* is the case-insensitive match operator.

flashcards_qa.front: In SQL regular expressions, what do the caret and dollar signs anchor, and how do ~ and ~* differ?
flashcards_qa.back: The caret anchors the match to the start of the string and the dollar sign to the end. The tilde is a case-sensitive match, while tilde-asterisk is case-insensitive.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Repository? (Git Review)
flashcards_qa.back: A Git-tracked project (local or remote).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Branch? (Git Review)
flashcards_qa.back: An independent line of development.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Staging area? (Git Review)
flashcards_qa.back: Where changes are placed (git add) before commit.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Commit? (Git Review)
flashcards_qa.back: A recorded snapshot of staged changes.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Merge? (Git Review)
flashcards_qa.back: Combining changes from one branch into another.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Rebase? (Git Review)
flashcards_qa.back: Reapplying commits from one branch onto another base.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to discard all local changes back to the last commit, and separately to undo a commit that is already pushed. Which git commands?
flashcards_qa.back: git reset --hard resets both the staging area and the working directory to the last commit, discarding local changes. git revert creates a new commit that undoes the earlier one, which is the safe choice for already-shared history.

flashcards_qa.front: Does git clone merge remote changes into your current branch?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Clone downloads an entire repository for the first time. Fetching and merging remote changes into your branch is git pull.

flashcards_qa.front: Which git command retrieves remote changes without merging them?
flashcards_qa.back: git fetch. It updates your remote-tracking branches only, whereas git pull fetches and then merges.

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: Recall a key exam fact. — merge
flashcards_qa.back: git merge integrates another branch; git rebase reapplies commits onto another base.

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: Recall a key exam fact. — stash
flashcards_qa.back: git stash temporarily shelves changes; git stash pop restores them.

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: Recall a key exam fact. — checkout
flashcards_qa.back: git checkout -b creates a new branch and switches to it at once.

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: What distinction is easy to mix up here — preserves?
flashcards_qa.back: git merge vs git rebase — merge preserves history/creates merge commit; rebase reapplies commits onto a new base.

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: What distinction is easy to mix up here — moves?
flashcards_qa.back: git reset (moves branch/staging, can lose work with --hard) vs git revert (safe, adds a new inverse commit).

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: What distinction is easy to mix up here — fetch?
flashcards_qa.back: git pull (fetch + merge) vs git fetch (fetch only, no merge).

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: What distinction is easy to mix up here — rewrite?
flashcards_qa.back: reset vs revert — rewrite/move vs safe inverse commit.

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: What distinction is easy to mix up here — replayed?
flashcards_qa.back: merge vs rebase — merge commit vs replayed commits.

flashcards_qa.front: Git Review: What distinction is easy to mix up here — with-merge?
flashcards_qa.back: pull vs fetch — with-merge vs without-merge.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish git pull from git fetch, and git reset from git revert.
flashcards_qa.back: git fetch downloads remote changes without touching your branch, while git pull fetches and merges them in. git reset --hard moves your branch and discards local changes, while git revert adds a new commit that undoes a previous one, leaving history intact.

flashcards_qa.front: When would you merge a branch rather than rebase it?
flashcards_qa.back: Merge when the branch is shared or already pushed, since it preserves history and creates a merge commit without rewriting anyone's commits. Rebase when the branch is local and you want a clean linear history, because it rewrites commits onto the new base.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Bucket? (Amazon S3 Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: Top-level S3 container; globally unique name, region-scoped.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Object? (Amazon S3 Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: A file stored in S3 (value/body plus metadata).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Key? (Amazon S3 Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: The full path of an object (prefix + object name).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Prefix? (Amazon S3 Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: The path portion of a key before the object name.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Multipart upload? (Amazon S3 Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: Uploading a large file in parallel parts (required > 5 GB).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Pre-signed URL? (Amazon S3 Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: A time-limited URL embedding the requester's signature/credentials.

flashcards_qa.front: Two teams in different Regions both try to create a bucket called sales-data. What happens, and what does that tell you about bucket scope?
flashcards_qa.back: The second attempt fails, because bucket names are the only globally unique namespace in AWS. The bucket itself is still created in and scoped to a specific Region.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon S3 Fundamentals: What is Object key?
flashcards_qa.back: Object key = prefix + object name (full path); S3 has no true directories.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon S3 Fundamentals: What is Max object size?
flashcards_qa.back: Max object size = 5 TB; multipart upload is required for files > 5 GB (recommended > 100 MB).

flashcards_qa.front: What are the rules for a valid S3 bucket name?
flashcards_qa.back: Three to 63 characters, all lowercase, no underscores, not formatted as an IP address, and it must start with a lowercase letter or a number.

flashcards_qa.front: A user opens the plain object URL for a private S3 object and gets Access Denied, but a pre-signed URL for the same object works. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: The pre-signed URL embeds the generating principal's credentials and a signature, so S3 authorizes it as that principal. The plain URL carries no credentials, so it fails unless the object is public.

flashcards_qa.front: What can be attached to an individual S3 object?
flashcards_qa.back: Metadata, up to 10 tags, and a version ID if versioning is enabled on the bucket.

flashcards_qa.front: Someone says an S3 bucket is global, someone else says it is regional. Who is right?
flashcards_qa.back: Both, in different senses. The bucket name must be globally unique across all of AWS, but the bucket itself lives in one Region.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to give an external party temporary access to one private object. Plain object URL or pre-signed URL?
flashcards_qa.back: A pre-signed URL, which carries a credential-based signature and expires. The plain object URL returns Access Denied unless the object is made public, which you do not want.

flashcards_qa.front: Does creating a folder in the S3 console create a real directory?
flashcards_qa.back: No. S3 keys are flat strings and a folder is just a key prefix. The console displays prefixes as folders as a convenience.

flashcards_qa.front: Which S3 number is 5 GB and which is 5 TB?
flashcards_qa.back: Five GB is the point above which multipart upload is required for a single PUT. Five TB is the maximum size of a single S3 object.

flashcards_qa.front: Explain precisely why a pre-signed URL succeeds where the public object URL fails.
flashcards_qa.back: Because the pre-signed URL includes a signature derived from the credentials of the principal that generated it, so S3 evaluates the request as that authorized principal. The plain URL is an anonymous request, which is denied unless the object is publicly readable.

flashcards_qa.front: How does S3 actually organize keys, and what are folders?
flashcards_qa.back: Keys are flat strings within a bucket, with no real hierarchy. Folders are a user-interface convenience layered over common key prefixes.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Bucket policy? (S3 Security & Bucket Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: Resource-based JSON policy attached to an S3 bucket.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Principal? (S3 Security & Bucket Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: The account/user a policy statement applies to.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Effect? (S3 Security & Bucket Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: Allow or Deny in a policy statement.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ACL? (S3 Security & Bucket Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: Access Control List (object/bucket level); finer-grained, can be disabled.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Block Public Access? (S3 Security & Bucket Policies)
flashcards_qa.back: Setting that prevents a bucket from becoming public.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Security & Bucket Policies: What is Bucket policy JSON?
flashcards_qa.back: Bucket policy JSON = Resource, Effect (Allow/Deny), Action, Principal.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Security & Bucket Policies: What is Principal '*' + Allow GetObject?
flashcards_qa.back: Principal '*' + Allow GetObject = public read.

flashcards_qa.front: State the rule S3 uses to decide whether a request is allowed.
flashcards_qa.back: Access is granted if either the identity's IAM policy allows it or the resource policy allows it, and no explicit Deny applies anywhere.

flashcards_qa.front: An IAM role in account B needs to read a bucket in account A. What must account A add?
flashcards_qa.back: A bucket policy on the bucket granting access to the principal in account B. Cross-account access to a bucket requires the resource policy; the other account's IAM policy alone is not enough.

flashcards_qa.front: An application on EC2 needs S3 access. IAM user credentials or an IAM role?
flashcards_qa.back: An IAM role attached to the instance, which supplies temporary rotating credentials. Embedding IAM user keys on the instance is the thing to avoid.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you guarantee that no bucket in an account can be made public, even by a careless bucket policy?
flashcards_qa.back: Enable S3 Block Public Access, which overrides policies and can be enforced account-wide to prevent accidental exposure.

flashcards_qa.front: A bucket policy allows a principal and their IAM policy also allows it, but an SCP explicitly denies it. What is the result?
flashcards_qa.back: Denied. An explicit Deny anywhere in the evaluation always wins over any Allow.

flashcards_qa.front: Is an IAM policy on the calling role sufficient for cross-account access to an S3 bucket?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Cross-account access requires a bucket policy, the resource-based policy on the bucket, granting the external principal. The caller's IAM policy alone is not enough.

flashcards_qa.front: A bucket policy grants public read, but objects still return Access Denied. What is the likely cause?
flashcards_qa.back: S3 Block Public Access is enabled, which overrides the public bucket policy and keeps the bucket private.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the essential difference between an IAM policy and a bucket policy?
flashcards_qa.back: What they are attached to. IAM policies attach to identities such as users, groups, and roles. Bucket policies attach to the resource, namely the bucket itself.

flashcards_qa.front: How do Allow and explicit Deny interact in S3 access evaluation?
flashcards_qa.back: An explicit Deny always overrides any Allow, no matter where the Allow comes from.

flashcards_qa.front: Write out the combined S3 access evaluation rule.
flashcards_qa.back: A request succeeds if the IAM identity policy allows it or the resource policy allows it, and there is no explicit Deny in any applicable policy.

flashcards_qa.front: Why can Block Public Access keep a bucket private even when its bucket policy grants everyone read access?
flashcards_qa.back: Because Block Public Access is evaluated as an override at the account or bucket level and blocks public grants outright, regardless of what the bucket policy says. It exists specifically to prevent accidental data leaks.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Versioning? (S3 Versioning)
flashcards_qa.back: Bucket-level feature keeping multiple versions of each object.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Delete marker? (S3 Versioning)
flashcards_qa.back: A placeholder that hides an object on delete while keeping versions.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Version ID? (S3 Versioning)
flashcards_qa.back: Identifier of a specific object version ('null' for pre-versioning objects).

flashcards_qa.front: At what level is S3 versioning enabled?
flashcards_qa.back: At the bucket level, so it applies to all objects in the bucket rather than being set per object.

flashcards_qa.front: You delete an object in a versioned bucket. Is it gone?
flashcards_qa.back: No. S3 adds a delete marker, which hides the object but leaves the versions intact, so the delete is recoverable by removing the marker.

flashcards_qa.front: What version ID do objects that existed before versioning was enabled have?
flashcards_qa.back: The literal version ID null.

flashcards_qa.front: You suspend versioning on a bucket. What happens to the versions already stored?
flashcards_qa.back: They are kept. Suspending versioning stops new versions being created but does not delete existing ones, so it is a safe operation.

flashcards_qa.front: Is deleting an object from a versioned bucket permanent?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It adds a delete marker, which hides the object but leaves the versions intact, so it is recoverable. Deleting a specific version ID is what is permanent.

flashcards_qa.front: An object shows version ID null in a versioned bucket. What does that mean?
flashcards_qa.back: It was uploaded before versioning was enabled on the bucket, so it carries the null version ID.

flashcards_qa.front: Which S3 delete operation is permanent, and which is recoverable?
flashcards_qa.back: Deleting the object without specifying a version adds a delete marker and is recoverable. Deleting a specific version ID is permanent.

flashcards_qa.front: A user accidentally deleted an important object in a versioned bucket. How do you restore it?
flashcards_qa.back: Delete the delete marker that was created. Removing the marker makes the latest version current again, because the original delete never removed any data.

flashcards_qa.front: Why do some objects in a versioned bucket have a version ID of null?
flashcards_qa.back: Because they were created before versioning was turned on. Versioning does not retroactively assign IDs, so those pre-existing objects are labelled null.

flashcards_qa.front: What is CRR? (S3 Replication)
flashcards_qa.back: Cross-Region Replication between buckets in different regions.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SRR? (S3 Replication)
flashcards_qa.back: Same-Region Replication between buckets in one region.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Batch Replication? (S3 Replication)
flashcards_qa.back: Feature to replicate existing/failed objects.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Delete marker replication? (S3 Replication)
flashcards_qa.back: Optional replication of delete markers.

flashcards_qa.front: What is RTC? (S3 Replication)
flashcards_qa.back: Replication Time Control — 15-minute replication SLA.

flashcards_qa.front: What must be true of both buckets before S3 replication can be configured?
flashcards_qa.back: Versioning must be enabled on both the source and the destination bucket.

flashcards_qa.front: Is S3 replication synchronous, and can it cross accounts?
flashcards_qa.back: It is asynchronous, so the destination lags slightly behind the source. It can replicate across accounts as well as across Regions.

flashcards_qa.front: You enable replication on a bucket that already holds a million objects. What gets replicated?
flashcards_qa.back: Only new objects written after replication is enabled. Existing objects, and any that previously failed, require S3 Batch Replication to backfill.

flashcards_qa.front: How are deletes handled by S3 replication?
flashcards_qa.back: Delete markers can optionally be replicated if you enable that setting. Deletions that target a specific version ID are never replicated.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Replication: What's the answer/service for — No chaining of replication (A?
flashcards_qa.back: No chaining of replication (A→B and B→C does not put A's objects in C).

flashcards_qa.front: Give the typical use cases for Cross-Region Replication and for Same-Region Replication.
flashcards_qa.back: CRR is used for compliance and data residency, lower-latency access in another Region, and cross-account copies. SRR is used for log aggregation and for syncing production data into a test environment.

flashcards_qa.front: You need a contractual guarantee on how quickly objects replicate. Which feature?
flashcards_qa.back: S3 Replication Time Control, which gives a 15-minute replication SLA together with replication monitoring metrics.

flashcards_qa.front: Does Same-Region Replication copy objects into another Region?
flashcards_qa.back: No, by definition it copies into another bucket in the same Region. Copying to a different Region is Cross-Region Replication.

flashcards_qa.front: Replication is configured and working for new uploads, but old objects are still missing at the destination. Why, and what fixes it?
flashcards_qa.back: Replication only applies to objects written after it was enabled. Run S3 Batch Replication to copy the existing objects and retry any that failed.

flashcards_qa.front: Bucket A replicates to bucket B, and bucket B replicates to bucket C. Do A's objects reach C?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Replication does not chain, so objects replicated into B are not further replicated on to C.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the single difference between CRR and SRR?
flashcards_qa.back: Whether the destination bucket is in a different Region, which is CRR, or the same Region, which is SRR.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare how a delete marker and a version-ID delete behave under replication.
flashcards_qa.back: Delete markers can be replicated, but only if you explicitly enable that option. Deletes that specify a version ID are never replicated, so a permanent version delete stays local to the source.

flashcards_qa.front: You just enabled replication on an existing bucket. What extra step do you need for full coverage?
flashcards_qa.back: Run S3 Batch Replication, since ordinary replication only handles newly written objects and Batch Replication is what backfills existing objects and retries failures.

flashcards_qa.front: Summarize the replication behaviors around deletes and chaining.
flashcards_qa.back: Delete markers replicate only if you opt in, deletes of a specific version ID never replicate, and replication does not chain, so a destination bucket does not forward objects on to a third bucket.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Durability? (S3 Storage Classes)
flashcards_qa.back: Probability an object is not lost (11 nines for all classes).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Availability? (S3 Storage Classes)
flashcards_qa.back: How readily data can be accessed (varies by class).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Intelligent-Tiering? (S3 Storage Classes)
flashcards_qa.back: Automatic movement between access tiers by usage.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Glacier? (S3 Storage Classes)
flashcards_qa.back: Low-cost archival storage classes.

flashcards_qa.front: Is durability the same across S3 storage classes, and what varies?
flashcards_qa.back: Durability is eleven nines in every class. What varies is availability and how many Availability Zones the data is stored across.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the risk that comes with S3 One Zone-IA?
flashcards_qa.back: It stores data in a single Availability Zone, so if that AZ is destroyed the data is lost. Durability within the AZ is still eleven nines, but AZ-level resilience is absent.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Storage Classes: What is Glacier Instant?
flashcards_qa.back: Glacier Instant = ms; Flexible = expedited 1–5 min / standard 3–5 hr / bulk 5–12 hr (free); Deep Archive = 12 hr standard / 48 hr bulk.

flashcards_qa.front: State the minimum storage durations for the S3 classes that have them.
flashcards_qa.back: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are 30 days, Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval are 90 days, and Glacier Deep Archive is 180 days.

flashcards_qa.front: Access patterns for a dataset are completely unpredictable and you want to avoid retrieval charges. Which storage class?
flashcards_qa.back: S3 Intelligent-Tiering. It charges a small monitoring and auto-tiering fee, moves objects between tiers automatically, and has no retrieval charges.

flashcards_qa.front: Is One Zone-IA less durable than S3 Standard?
