flashcards_qa.back: Its stated durability is still eleven nines, but it stores data in a single AZ, so availability is lower and the data is lost if that AZ is destroyed. The AZ resilience, not the durability figure, is the difference.

flashcards_qa.front: An archive must sometimes be read back in milliseconds. Which Glacier tier, and how do the others compare?
flashcards_qa.back: Glacier Instant Retrieval, which retrieves in milliseconds. Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, and Deep Archive takes up to about 48 hours.

flashcards_qa.front: Does Intelligent-Tiering charge you for retrievals?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It has no retrieval charges, but it does charge a small per-object monitoring and auto-tiering fee.

flashcards_qa.front: Is Standard-IA stored in a single Availability Zone?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Standard-IA replicates across at least three AZs. One Zone-IA is the single-AZ variant, cheaper but lost if that AZ is destroyed.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare the three Glacier tiers on retrieval time and minimum duration.
flashcards_qa.back: Glacier Instant Retrieval retrieves in milliseconds with a 90-day minimum. Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, also with a 90-day minimum. Deep Archive takes up to about 48 hours with a 180-day minimum.

flashcards_qa.front: A compliance archive must be retrievable within 12 hours at the lowest possible cost. Which class?
flashcards_qa.back: Glacier Flexible Retrieval, whose standard and bulk retrievals fall within hours. Deep Archive is cheaper but can take up to 48 hours, and Instant Retrieval costs more than needed.

flashcards_qa.front: If durability is identical across S3 classes, what should actually drive your choice?
flashcards_qa.back: Availability, AZ resilience, retrieval time and cost, and any minimum storage duration. Durability is eleven nines everywhere, so it is not a differentiator.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Directory bucket? (S3 Express One Zone)
flashcards_qa.back: Special single-AZ bucket type used by Express One Zone.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Express One Zone? (S3 Express One Zone)
flashcards_qa.back: High-performance single-AZ S3 storage class.

flashcards_qa.front: What kind of bucket does S3 Express One Zone use, and where does it live?
flashcards_qa.back: A directory bucket, which is created in a single Availability Zone that you choose.

flashcards_qa.front: What performance and cost profile does S3 Express One Zone offer?
flashcards_qa.back: Roughly ten times the performance of S3 Standard at around 50 percent lower cost per request, with single-digit millisecond latency.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the availability trade-off with S3 Express One Zone?
flashcards_qa.back: It stores data in one Availability Zone, so availability is lower and an AZ failure directly affects your workload.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Express One Zone: When or why would you use this?
flashcards_qa.back: Best for co-locating compute + storage; integrates with SageMaker training, Athena, EMR, Glue.

flashcards_qa.front: Why would you accept a single-AZ storage class over a multi-AZ one?
flashcards_qa.back: For the latency and cost benefits: co-locating storage with compute in one AZ gives single-digit millisecond access and avoids cross-AZ data charges. You accept that an AZ failure takes the data offline.

flashcards_qa.front: Can you use a general purpose bucket with S3 Express One Zone?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Express One Zone uses directory buckets, created in one Availability Zone you choose. General purpose buckets serve the other storage classes.

flashcards_qa.front: Both S3 Express One Zone and One Zone-IA use a single AZ. What are they each for?
flashcards_qa.back: Express One Zone is for high performance, giving roughly ten times S3 Standard throughput with single-digit millisecond latency. One Zone-IA is for cheap infrequent access, trading availability for a lower storage price.

flashcards_qa.front: You see two single-AZ S3 classes in the answer options. How do you tell which the question wants?
flashcards_qa.back: If the requirement is speed, very high request rates, or low latency for compute in the same AZ, it is Express One Zone. If the requirement is low cost for rarely accessed data, it is One Zone-IA.

flashcards_qa.front: Why does putting storage and compute in the same Availability Zone help?
flashcards_qa.back: Requests do not cross AZ boundaries, so latency drops to single-digit milliseconds and cross-AZ data transfer charges disappear. The cost is losing AZ-level redundancy.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Transition action? (S3 Lifecycle Rules)
flashcards_qa.back: Lifecycle action moving an object to another storage class.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Expiration action? (S3 Lifecycle Rules)
flashcards_qa.back: Lifecycle action deleting objects/versions after a period.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Non-current version? (S3 Lifecycle Rules)
flashcards_qa.back: A prior object version (not the latest) in a versioned bucket.

flashcards_qa.front: What is S3 Analytics? (S3 Lifecycle Rules)
flashcards_qa.back: Feature recommending Standard↔Standard-IA transition timing.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the two kinds of action an S3 lifecycle rule can take?
flashcards_qa.back: Transition, which moves objects to a different storage class, and expiration, which deletes them.

flashcards_qa.front: How can you limit a lifecycle rule to only some objects in a bucket?
flashcards_qa.back: Scope the rule by key prefix, by object tags, or by both.

flashcards_qa.front: Besides expiring current objects, what else can lifecycle rules clean up?
flashcards_qa.back: They can delete non-current, older versions of objects, and they can abort and remove incomplete multipart uploads.

flashcards_qa.front: What does S3 Analytics recommend, and what are its limits?
flashcards_qa.back: It recommends transitions between S3 Standard and Standard-IA only, not One Zone-IA or Glacier. It produces a daily CSV report and takes about 24 to 48 hours to start populating.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a lifecycle transition action delete objects?
flashcards_qa.back: No. A transition moves objects to a different storage class. Deleting them is an expiration action.

flashcards_qa.front: Can S3 Analytics tell you which objects to move to Glacier?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Its recommendations cover Standard to Standard-IA transitions only, and it does not cover One Zone-IA or Glacier.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a lifecycle transition copy objects into another bucket?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It changes the storage class of objects in place, or expires them. Copying into another bucket is replication.

flashcards_qa.front: In a versioned bucket, what is the difference between expiring current objects and expiring non-current versions?
flashcards_qa.back: Expiring current objects adds a delete marker so the object appears deleted. Expiring non-current versions permanently removes the older versions, which is how you actually reclaim storage.

flashcards_qa.front: A bucket holds large source images and small generated thumbnails with different retention needs. How do you build the lifecycle rules?
flashcards_qa.back: Write separate rules scoped by prefix or by object tag, for example one rule transitioning the source-image prefix to Glacier after 90 days and another expiring thumbnails after 30 days, since thumbnails can be regenerated.

flashcards_qa.front: A requirement says deleted objects must be recoverable for 90 days at minimal cost. How do you satisfy it?
flashcards_qa.back: Enable versioning so deletes only create delete markers, then use a lifecycle rule to transition non-current versions to Standard-IA or Glacier and to expire them permanently after 90 days.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Event notification? (S3 Event Notifications)
flashcards_qa.back: A message emitted on an S3 event to a target.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Resource access policy? (S3 Event Notifications)
flashcards_qa.back: A policy on SNS/SQS/Lambda allowing S3 to publish/invoke.

flashcards_qa.front: What is EventBridge? (S3 Event Notifications)
flashcards_qa.back: Event bus receiving all S3 events for advanced routing.

flashcards_qa.front: Which targets can receive S3 event notifications?
flashcards_qa.back: SNS, SQS, and Lambda as direct targets, plus Amazon EventBridge, which receives all S3 events.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 event notifications fail to reach an SQS queue. Where do you look?
flashcards_qa.back: At the resource-access policy on the target, in this case the SQS queue policy allowing S3 to send messages. S3 notifications rely on resource policies on the target rather than on an IAM role attached to S3.

flashcards_qa.front: What does routing S3 events through EventBridge add?
flashcards_qa.back: Advanced filtering on metadata such as object size and name, delivery to many targets at once, event archive and replay, and more reliable delivery.

flashcards_qa.front: How quickly do S3 event notifications normally arrive?
flashcards_qa.back: Usually within seconds, though delivery can occasionally take a minute or more.

flashcards_qa.front: Which permission mechanism do S3 event notifications use?
flashcards_qa.back: Resource-access policies on the destination, meaning the SNS topic policy, SQS queue policy, or Lambda resource policy. They do not use an IAM role attached to S3.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to filter S3 events by object size and send them to several targets with replay. Direct notifications or EventBridge?
flashcards_qa.back: EventBridge, which supports advanced filtering on metadata, multiple targets, and archive and replay. Direct SNS, SQS, and Lambda notifications offer only basic prefix and suffix filtering.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare SNS, SQS, and Lambda as S3 notification targets.
flashcards_qa.back: SNS fans one event out to many subscribers. SQS buffers events in a queue for a consumer to poll at its own pace. Lambda invokes a function directly to process the event.

flashcards_qa.front: What do direct S3 notifications lack that EventBridge provides?
flashcards_qa.back: Advanced filtering on metadata such as size and name, fan-out to many targets from a single rule, and archive and replay of events for debugging.

flashcards_qa.front: Where must permissions be granted for S3 to publish an event to a Lambda function?
flashcards_qa.back: On the Lambda function's resource policy, allowing the S3 service to invoke it. S3 event notifications depend on the target's resource-access policy, not on a role attached to S3.

flashcards_qa.front: When should you send S3 events to EventBridge rather than direct to SNS, SQS, or Lambda?
flashcards_qa.back: When you need filtering beyond simple prefix and suffix, multiple targets from one event, event archive and replay, or stronger delivery guarantees.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Prefix? (S3 Performance)
flashcards_qa.back: Key path segment; performance limits apply per prefix.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Multipart upload? (S3 Performance)
flashcards_qa.back: Parallel upload of a file in parts.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Transfer Acceleration? (S3 Performance)
flashcards_qa.back: Edge-location routing to speed transfers.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Byte-Range Fetch? (S3 Performance)
flashcards_qa.back: Requesting specific byte ranges to parallelize/partial-read.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the per-prefix request rate limits for S3?
flashcards_qa.back: Three thousand five hundred PUT, COPY, POST, and DELETE requests per second, and 5,500 GET and HEAD requests per second.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Performance: Recall a key exam fact.
flashcards_qa.back: No limit on number of prefixes; spread load across prefixes to scale.

flashcards_qa.front: What first-byte latency should you expect from S3?
flashcards_qa.back: Around 100 to 200 milliseconds.

flashcards_qa.front: At what object sizes is multipart upload recommended and required?
flashcards_qa.back: Recommended above 100 MB, and required above 5 GB.

flashcards_qa.front: Uploads from a distant office are slow. Which S3 feature helps, and is it compatible with multipart upload?
flashcards_qa.back: S3 Transfer Acceleration, which routes uploads via a nearby edge location and then over the AWS private network. It is compatible with multipart upload, so the two can be combined.

flashcards_qa.front: You only need the first megabyte of each large object, and you want parallel downloads. Which feature?
flashcards_qa.back: Byte-Range Fetches, which let you request specific ranges of an object, both for partial reads and to download different ranges in parallel.

flashcards_qa.front: You are hitting S3 request rate limits on one bucket. What is the fix?
flashcards_qa.back: Spread the objects across more key prefixes, because the limits apply per prefix rather than per bucket, so more prefixes multiply the available throughput.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each S3 optimization to its problem: uploads from far away, uploading one very large file, and downloading large files quickly.
flashcards_qa.back: Transfer Acceleration for distance. Multipart upload for one very large file, parallelizing the upload. Byte-Range Fetches for parallel or partial downloads.

flashcards_qa.front: Which S3 feature parallelizes uploads and which parallelizes downloads?
flashcards_qa.back: Multipart upload parallelizes uploads by splitting the object into parts. Byte-Range Fetches parallelize downloads by requesting different ranges concurrently.

flashcards_qa.front: Does S3 Transfer Acceleration help because it splits the file into parts?
flashcards_qa.back: No, that is multipart upload. Transfer Acceleration addresses geographic distance by routing through a nearby edge location onto the AWS backbone. The two can be combined.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you reason about scaling S3 throughput beyond 3,500 writes per second?
flashcards_qa.back: The limits are per prefix, so distributing keys across N prefixes gives roughly N times the throughput. Designing key names so traffic spreads over many prefixes is how you scale.

flashcards_qa.front: For each of a 20 GB upload, a slow transatlantic upload, and a large file you only need part of, which S3 optimization applies?
flashcards_qa.back: Multipart upload for the 20 GB file, since it is required above 5 GB anyway. Transfer Acceleration for the transatlantic upload. A Byte-Range Fetch for reading only part of the file.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SSE-S3? (S3 Encryption)
flashcards_qa.back: Server-side encryption with AWS-managed keys (AES-256).

flashcards_qa.front: What is SSE-KMS? (S3 Encryption)
flashcards_qa.back: Server-side encryption with KMS-managed keys (auditable).

flashcards_qa.front: What is SSE-C? (S3 Encryption)
flashcards_qa.back: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Client-side encryption? (S3 Encryption)
flashcards_qa.back: Encrypting data before upload; client manages keys.

flashcards_qa.front: What is aws:SecureTransport? (S3 Encryption)
flashcards_qa.back: Condition key; false when not using HTTPS.

flashcards_qa.front: What is DSSE-KMS? (S3 Encryption)
flashcards_qa.back: Dual-layer server-side encryption with KMS.

flashcards_qa.front: What encryption applies to a new S3 object if you specify nothing?
flashcards_qa.back: SSE-S3, which is the default: AES-256 encryption with keys managed entirely by AWS.

flashcards_qa.front: What does SSE-KMS give you, and what is the operational risk on a busy bucket?
flashcards_qa.back: It gives auditability, since every key use is logged in CloudTrail, plus control over the key. The risk is that it consumes your KMS API quota, so a high-throughput bucket can be throttled.

flashcards_qa.front: How does SSE-C work, and does S3 keep the key?
flashcards_qa.back: You send your own encryption key in the request header on every single call, and the request must use HTTPS. S3 uses the key to encrypt or decrypt and then discards it, so it never stores the key.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you force all requests to a bucket to use HTTPS?
flashcards_qa.back: With a bucket policy that denies requests when the condition aws:SecureTransport is false.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Encryption: What is DSSE-KMS?
flashcards_qa.back: DSSE-KMS = dual-layer KMS encryption.

flashcards_qa.front: A bucket has default encryption set to SSE-S3 but a bucket policy requiring SSE-KMS headers. Which wins?
flashcards_qa.back: The bucket policy, because policies are evaluated before default encryption is applied. An upload without the required header is rejected rather than falling back to the default.

flashcards_qa.front: A high-volume bucket using SSE-KMS starts returning throttling errors. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: Because every object operation calls KMS, and the bucket's request rate is exceeding the KMS API request quota for the account and Region.

flashcards_qa.front: Which S3 encryption option requires HTTPS, and why?
flashcards_qa.back: SSE-C, because you transmit your encryption key in the request header on every call, so the connection must be encrypted.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the four S3 encryption options and who holds the keys in each.
flashcards_qa.back: SSE-S3 uses keys AWS fully manages. SSE-KMS uses KMS keys you control. SSE-C uses keys you supply on every request and S3 does not store. Client-side encryption means you encrypt before upload and AWS never sees the plaintext or the key.

flashcards_qa.front: Does SSE-S3 consume your KMS API quota?
flashcards_qa.back: No. SSE-S3 uses keys AWS fully manages with no KMS calls. SSE-KMS calls KMS on every operation, which gives auditability but can be throttled on busy buckets.

flashcards_qa.front: With SSE-C, does S3 ever handle your plaintext data?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. You send the key with each request and S3 performs the encryption, so it briefly handles plaintext. Client-side encryption is where you encrypt first and S3 only sees ciphertext.

flashcards_qa.front: A bucket doing tens of thousands of requests per second with SSE-KMS is being throttled. What is happening and what are the options?
flashcards_qa.back: Each request makes a KMS API call, so the account's KMS request quota is the bottleneck. Options are requesting a KMS quota increase, using S3 Bucket Keys to reduce KMS calls, or switching to SSE-S3 where auditability is not required.

flashcards_qa.front: Which S3 encryption method would you pick for regulatory key control, for simplicity, and for keeping AWS from ever seeing plaintext?
flashcards_qa.back: SSE-KMS for regulatory key control, since it gives key policies and CloudTrail audit. SSE-S3 for simplicity, as it is the default and needs no configuration. Client-side encryption when AWS must never see plaintext, with SSE-C as the middle ground that still requires HTTPS.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Access point? (S3 Access Points)
flashcards_qa.back: A named entry point to a bucket with its own DNS and policy.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Access point policy? (S3 Access Points)
flashcards_qa.back: Policy (like a bucket policy) attached to an access point.

flashcards_qa.front: What is VPC origin? (S3 Access Points)
flashcards_qa.back: Configuring an access point for private VPC-only traffic.

flashcards_qa.front: What is VPC endpoint? (S3 Access Points)
flashcards_qa.back: Private network path to reach the access point.

flashcards_qa.front: What does each S3 Access Point have of its own?
flashcards_qa.back: Its own DNS name and its own access point policy.

flashcards_qa.front: You have one bucket serving fifteen applications and the bucket policy has become unmanageable. What is the fix?
flashcards_qa.back: Create an S3 Access Point per application, each with its own DNS name and policy. That distributes access control across small policies instead of one enormous bucket policy.

flashcards_qa.front: What origin types can an S3 Access Point have?
flashcards_qa.back: Internet origin, reachable publicly, or VPC origin, which restricts access to a specific VPC.

flashcards_qa.front: What does a VPC-origin access point require in order to work?
flashcards_qa.back: A VPC endpoint for S3, whose endpoint policy must allow both the underlying bucket and the access point itself.

flashcards_qa.front: Do S3 Access Points remove the need to think about the bucket policy's size and complexity?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes, largely. Each access point carries its own small policy with its own DNS name, so permissions scale by adding access points rather than growing one monolithic bucket policy.

flashcards_qa.front: An application in a VPC cannot reach a VPC-origin access point. What is the usual cause?
flashcards_qa.back: A missing or incorrect VPC endpoint policy. VPC-origin access points require a VPC endpoint whose policy permits both the bucket and the access point.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the architectural advantage of access points over a single bucket policy?
flashcards_qa.back: Each use case gets its own access point with a dedicated DNS name and a narrow policy, so permissions scale by adding access points instead of growing one monolithic bucket policy that is hard to review and easy to get wrong.

flashcards_qa.front: How do S3 Access Points change where access control lives?
flashcards_qa.back: They move it out of the bucket policy. Each access point carries its own policy for one use case, so access management scales horizontally rather than concentrating in a single, ever-growing bucket policy.

flashcards_qa.front: Trace the full path and permissions needed for a private VPC-origin access point.
flashcards_qa.back: The client in the VPC resolves the access point's DNS name, traffic goes through the S3 VPC endpoint, and the endpoint policy must allow both the bucket and the access point. The access point policy and the bucket policy must then permit the operation.

flashcards_qa.front: What is S3 Tables? (S3 Tables & Apache Iceberg)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed tabular storage in Iceberg format within table buckets.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Table bucket? (S3 Tables & Apache Iceberg)
flashcards_qa.back: Specialized S3 bucket for tabular (Iceberg) data.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Apache Iceberg? (S3 Tables & Apache Iceberg)
flashcards_qa.back: Open table format with ACID, schema/partition evolution, time travel.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Time travel? (S3 Tables & Apache Iceberg)
flashcards_qa.back: Querying historical versions of table data.

flashcards_qa.front: What format do S3 Tables use, and what kind of bucket holds them?
flashcards_qa.back: Apache Iceberg format, stored inside table buckets, which are a purpose-built bucket type for tabular data.

flashcards_qa.front: Which capabilities does Apache Iceberg bring, and where did it originate?
flashcards_qa.back: ACID transactions, row-level updates and deletes, schema evolution, partition evolution, and time travel with rollback. It originated at Netflix.

flashcards_qa.front: Is Iceberg tied to a single query engine?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It is engine-agnostic, supported by Spark, Flink, Trino, Presto, and Hive, and it also exposes an Iceberg REST endpoint.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Tables & Apache Iceberg: What's the answer/service for — Integration is via the Glue Data Catalog?
flashcards_qa.back: Integration is via the Glue Data Catalog → Athena, Redshift, EMR, SageMaker, Glue ETL, Firehose, QuickSight.

flashcards_qa.front: How is access to S3 Tables controlled and how is the data encrypted?
flashcards_qa.back: Through IAM policies, resource policies, SCPs, SQL grants, and Lake Formation. Encryption uses either S3-managed keys or your own KMS keys.

flashcards_qa.front: Can an S3 table bucket be made publicly accessible?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Public access is not allowed for table buckets, and HTTPS is required for access.

flashcards_qa.front: Are S3 table buckets just general purpose buckets with a naming convention?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Table buckets hold managed Apache Iceberg tables with automatic maintenance such as compaction, and are queried as tables. General purpose buckets store raw objects with no table semantics.

flashcards_qa.front: Which Iceberg capability is unusual for a data lake, and why does it matter?
flashcards_qa.back: ACID transactions with row-level updates and deletes. Traditional lakes only append immutable files, so being able to update or delete individual rows transactionally, and satisfy requests such as GDPR erasure, is a significant change.

flashcards_qa.front: Is Apache Iceberg a file format that replaces Parquet?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Iceberg is a table format managing metadata, snapshots, schema, and ACID semantics over a set of files, which are usually Parquet. They work together.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare S3 Tables with a plain S3 data lake.
flashcards_qa.back: S3 Tables provide managed, transactional Iceberg tables with automatic optimization and table-level semantics. A plain S3 data lake holds raw objects, and you supply any table format, catalog, and maintenance yourself.

flashcards_qa.front: How does Iceberg give a data lake warehouse-like behavior?
flashcards_qa.back: By layering a table format over the files: it tracks metadata and snapshots so it can offer ACID transactions, row-level updates and deletes, schema and partition evolution, and time travel to a previous state, all while data stays as objects in S3.

flashcards_qa.front: How do S3 Tables become queryable across the AWS ecosystem?
flashcards_qa.back: Through integration with the Glue Data Catalog, which registers the tables so Athena, Redshift, EMR, and third-party Iceberg-compatible engines can discover and query them.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Storage Lens? (S3 Storage Lens)
flashcards_qa.back: Org-wide S3 analytics for usage, cost, and protection.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Default dashboard? (S3 Storage Lens)
flashcards_qa.back: Preconfigured multi-account/region Storage Lens dashboard.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Advanced metrics? (S3 Storage Lens)
flashcards_qa.back: Paid metrics with longer retention and CloudWatch publishing.

flashcards_qa.front: What scope does S3 Storage Lens cover, and what history does it give you?
flashcards_qa.back: It analyzes storage across an entire AWS Organization, with 30 days of usage and activity metrics in its free tier.

flashcards_qa.front: At what levels can Storage Lens aggregate its metrics?
flashcards_qa.back: Organization, account, Region, bucket, and prefix.

flashcards_qa.front: Can the default S3 Storage Lens dashboard be removed?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The default dashboard, which spans multiple accounts and Regions, can be disabled but not deleted.

flashcards_qa.front: In what formats can Storage Lens export its reports, and where?
flashcards_qa.back: To S3, in either CSV or Parquet.

flashcards_qa.front: S3 Storage Lens: What is Free?
flashcards_qa.back: Free = ~28 usage metrics, 14-day retention; Advanced (paid) = extra metrics, CloudWatch publishing, prefix-level, 15-month retention.

flashcards_qa.front: Do the free S3 Storage Lens metrics include activity metrics and 15 months of history?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The free tier gives basic usage metrics with 14 days of retention. Activity metrics, prefix-level detail, and 15-month retention require the paid advanced tier.

flashcards_qa.front: What is unusual about the default Storage Lens dashboard's lifecycle?
flashcards_qa.back: It can be disabled if you do not want it, but it cannot be deleted.

flashcards_qa.front: Can S3 Analytics recommend transitions to Glacier?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Its recommendations cover Standard to Standard-IA only, and it is per-bucket. Organization-wide storage analytics is S3 Storage Lens.

flashcards_qa.front: What do you get by paying for Storage Lens advanced metrics?
flashcards_qa.back: Activity metrics, detailed status-code metrics, and prefix-level aggregation, with retention extended from 14 days to 15 months.

flashcards_qa.front: A question asks how to see storage usage trends across every account in the organization. Which service, and which is the wrong answer?
flashcards_qa.back: S3 Storage Lens, which is organization-wide. S3 Analytics would be wrong, since it is per-bucket and only advises on Standard to Standard-IA transitions.

flashcards_qa.front: What is EBS volume? (Amazon EBS)
flashcards_qa.back: Network block storage attachable to an EC2 instance.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Snapshot? (Amazon EBS)
flashcards_qa.back: Point-in-time backup of an EBS volume (stored in S3).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Delete-on-termination? (Amazon EBS)
flashcards_qa.back: Attribute controlling volume deletion when the instance terminates.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Elastic Volumes? (Amazon EBS)
flashcards_qa.back: Live modification of volume size/type/performance.

flashcards_qa.front: What are EBS's three defining characteristics?
flashcards_qa.back: It is network-attached rather than local, it persists beyond termination of the instance, and it is locked to a single Availability Zone.

flashcards_qa.front: Can one EBS volume be attached to several EC2 instances at once?
flashcards_qa.back: Normally no, only one instance at a time. The exception is io1 and io2 volumes with Multi-Attach enabled.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon EBS: What's the answer/service for — Move across AZs via snapshot?
flashcards_qa.back: Move across AZs via snapshot → restore in target AZ.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the delete-on-termination default for a root volume versus an additional volume?
flashcards_qa.back: On for the root volume, so it is deleted with the instance. Off for additional volumes by default, so they survive termination.

flashcards_qa.front: What can Elastic Volumes change on a live EBS volume, and what is the restriction?
flashcards_qa.back: Size, volume type, and performance settings can all be changed while the volume is in use. The restriction is that size can only be increased, never decreased.

flashcards_qa.front: Which EBS volume types tie IOPS to size, and which let you set IOPS independently?
flashcards_qa.back: gp2 IOPS scale with the volume size. gp3, io1, and io2 let you provision IOPS independently of capacity.

flashcards_qa.front: You need an EBS volume's data available in another Availability Zone. How?
flashcards_qa.back: Take a snapshot, which is stored in S3 and therefore Region-scoped, then create a new volume from it in the target AZ. EBS volumes themselves cannot cross AZs.

flashcards_qa.front: You terminate an instance and lose the root disk but keep the data disk. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: Because delete-on-termination defaults to on for the root volume and off for additional volumes.

flashcards_qa.front: You over-provisioned a 1 TB EBS volume and want it to be 500 GB. Can Elastic Volumes do that?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Elastic Volumes can only increase size. To shrink, create a smaller volume and copy the data across.

flashcards_qa.front: Can an EBS volume be mounted by instances in two Availability Zones?
flashcards_qa.back: No. EBS is AZ-locked and attaches to one instance at a time, apart from io1 and io2 Multi-Attach within an AZ. Multi-AZ shared access is what EFS provides.

flashcards_qa.front: You need 16,000 IOPS on a small 100 GB volume. Which EBS types work?
flashcards_qa.back: gp3, io1, or io2, because they let you provision IOPS independently of size. gp2 would not, since its IOPS scale with capacity, requiring a much larger volume.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you make sure data on an attached volume survives instance termination?
flashcards_qa.back: Check the delete-on-termination flag. It defaults to on for the root volume and off for additional volumes, so set it to off on any volume whose data must persist.

flashcards_qa.front: How do snapshots let you work around EBS being AZ-locked?
flashcards_qa.back: A snapshot is stored durably at the Region level, so you can create a new volume from it in any AZ in that Region, or copy the snapshot to another Region and restore it there.

flashcards_qa.front: What is EFS? (Amazon EFS)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed NFS file system shared across instances/AZs.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Performance mode? (Amazon EFS)
flashcards_qa.back: General Purpose vs Max I/O.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Throughput mode? (Amazon EFS)
flashcards_qa.back: Bursting, Provisioned, or Elastic.

flashcards_qa.front: What is EFS-IA? (Amazon EFS)
flashcards_qa.back: Infrequent Access tier with retrieval cost.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon EFS: What is EFS?
flashcards_qa.back: EFS = managed NFS, mountable by many instances across AZs; Linux-only (POSIX).

flashcards_qa.front: How is EFS priced compared with EBS?
flashcards_qa.back: It is pay-per-use with no capacity to provision, but it costs roughly three times as much per GB as gp2 EBS.

flashcards_qa.front: How is access to EFS controlled, and how is it encrypted at rest?
flashcards_qa.back: Network access is controlled with security groups on the mount targets. Encryption at rest uses AWS KMS.

flashcards_qa.front: Name EFS's performance modes and throughput modes.
flashcards_qa.back: Performance modes are General Purpose, which is the default, and Max I/O. Throughput modes are Bursting, Provisioned, and Elastic.

flashcards_qa.front: Which storage tiers does EFS offer, and how do files move between them?
flashcards_qa.back: Standard, EFS-IA, and Archive, plus One Zone variants. Lifecycle policies move files between tiers based on access, saving up to around 90 percent.

flashcards_qa.front: Can Windows EC2 instances mount an EFS file system?
flashcards_qa.back: No. EFS is Linux-only, exposing a POSIX NFS file system. For Windows shares you would use FSx for Windows File Server.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare the EFS throughput modes.
flashcards_qa.back: Bursting throughput scales with the size of the file system and accumulates burst credits. Provisioned throughput is set independently of size, for small file systems needing high throughput. Elastic scales automatically with demand and is the simplest for unpredictable workloads.

flashcards_qa.front: Is EFS One Zone appropriate for production data that cannot be regenerated?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It stores data in a single AZ, so it is lost if that AZ fails, which suits development or reproducible data. Standard replicates across multiple AZs for production.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each requirement to EFS or EBS: many Linux instances sharing files across AZs, and a single database instance needing low-latency block storage.
flashcards_qa.back: EFS for the shared multi-AZ Linux file access. EBS for the single-instance block storage, since it attaches to one instance and stays within its AZ.

flashcards_qa.front: Does Max I/O mode give lower latency than General Purpose mode in EFS?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Max I/O scales to much higher aggregate throughput but with higher latency per operation. General Purpose is the default and gives the lowest per-operation latency.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you select EFS performance and throughput modes for a workload?
flashcards_qa.back: Use General Purpose for latency-sensitive workloads, and Max I/O only when thousands of clients need extreme aggregate throughput and can tolerate higher latency. For throughput, use Elastic for unpredictable demand, Provisioned when a small file system needs high throughput, and Bursting when throughput needs scale naturally with size.

flashcards_qa.front: State the two EFS facts that most often distinguish it from EBS.
flashcards_qa.back: It is Linux-only, exposing a POSIX NFS file system, and it can be mounted by many instances across multiple Availability Zones at once, unlike an AZ-locked single-attach EBS volume.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Mount target? (EFS vs EBS)
flashcards_qa.back: Per-AZ access point for mounting EFS.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Multi-Attach? (EFS vs EBS)
flashcards_qa.back: io1/io2 feature allowing a volume on multiple instances.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Instance store? (EFS vs EBS)
flashcards_qa.back: Ephemeral disk physically attached to the host.

flashcards_qa.front: Summarize the EBS attachment and AZ constraints and how you move a volume.
flashcards_qa.back: An EBS volume attaches to one instance at a time, with io1 and io2 Multi-Attach as the exception, and it is locked to a single Availability Zone. To move it, take a snapshot and restore into the target AZ.

flashcards_qa.front: Which EBS types decouple IOPS from capacity?
flashcards_qa.back: gp3, io1, and io2 let you set IOPS independently. gp2's IOPS scale with the volume's size.

flashcards_qa.front: When should you avoid taking EBS snapshots, and why?
flashcards_qa.back: During peak load, because snapshot operations consume volume I/O and can degrade application performance.

flashcards_qa.front: Summarize EFS's sharing model, OS support, and cost profile.
flashcards_qa.back: It is shared across many instances and Availability Zones through mount targets, is Linux-only using POSIX, and is more expensive per GB than EBS, though lifecycle tiering to IA and Archive reduces that.

flashcards_qa.front: What happens to data on an EC2 instance store when the instance stops or fails?
flashcards_qa.back: It is lost. Instance store is ephemeral local disk, unlike EBS and EFS which persist independently of the instance.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each to EBS or EFS: one instance, one AZ, block device; many instances, several AZs, file system.
flashcards_qa.back: One instance in one AZ with a block device is EBS. Many instances across several AZs sharing a file system is EFS.

flashcards_qa.front: Which AWS storage option is not persistent, and what is it good for?
flashcards_qa.back: EC2 instance store, which is lost when the instance stops or fails. It is good for scratch space, caches, and temporary buffers where very high local IOPS matter and durability does not.

flashcards_qa.front: Does data on an EC2 instance store survive the instance being stopped?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Instance store is ephemeral and lost with the instance. EBS and EFS both persist independently of it.

flashcards_qa.front: How does each of EBS and EFS handle multi-AZ access?
flashcards_qa.back: EBS does not: you snapshot the volume and restore it into another AZ. EFS does natively, by creating a mount target in each AZ so instances anywhere in the VPC can mount the same file system.

flashcards_qa.front: A workload needs shared access from twenty Linux instances in three AZs; another needs the fastest possible local scratch space; a third needs durable block storage for one database. Which storage for each?
flashcards_qa.back: EFS for the shared multi-AZ access. Instance store for the fastest local scratch, accepting that it is ephemeral. EBS for the database's durable block storage.

flashcards_qa.front: Which storage option is ephemeral, and which is Linux-only and multi-AZ?
flashcards_qa.back: Instance store is ephemeral and lost with the instance. EFS is the Linux-only, POSIX file system that can be shared across multiple Availability Zones.

flashcards_qa.front: What is AWS Backup? (AWS Backup)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed service to centralize/automate backups.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Backup plan? (AWS Backup)
flashcards_qa.back: Definition of frequency, window, transitions, and retention.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Vault Lock? (AWS Backup)
flashcards_qa.back: WORM policy protecting backups from deletion/retention changes.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Point-in-time recovery? (AWS Backup)
flashcards_qa.back: Restore to a specific past moment (supported services).

flashcards_qa.front: Which service centralizes backups, and which resources can it cover?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Backup, covering EC2, EBS, S3, RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, Storage Gateway, and more, from a single place.

flashcards_qa.front: What resilience and recovery features does AWS Backup support?
flashcards_qa.back: Cross-Region and cross-account backups, and point-in-time recovery for supported services such as Aurora.

flashcards_qa.front: What does an AWS Backup plan define, and how do you choose what it protects?
flashcards_qa.back: Backup frequency, the backup window, transitions to cold storage, and retention. Resources are selected by tags, so tagging drives what gets backed up.

flashcards_qa.front: AWS Backup: What is Vault Lock?
flashcards_qa.back: Vault Lock = WORM: backups can't be deleted or retention shortened, even by root.

flashcards_qa.front: A compliance requirement says backups must be impossible to delete, even by an administrator. Which feature?
flashcards_qa.back: AWS Backup Vault Lock, which enforces write-once-read-many immutability so backups cannot be deleted even by the root user until the retention period elapses.

flashcards_qa.front: Can AWS Backup protect resources in other accounts and copy backups to other Regions?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. It supports both cross-account and cross-Region backup, which is the point of centralizing backup management.

flashcards_qa.front: Why use AWS Backup rather than each service's own backup mechanism?
flashcards_qa.back: Because it gives one place to define plans, retention, and cold-storage transitions across many services, with tag-based selection plus cross-account and cross-Region copies. Per-service mechanisms such as bare EBS snapshots leave you coordinating each one separately.

flashcards_qa.front: Can an administrator shorten the retention on a locked AWS Backup vault?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Vault Lock enforces write-once-read-many immutability, so backups cannot be deleted or altered before retention expires, even by root. An ordinary retention setting can be changed.

flashcards_qa.front: What exactly does Vault Lock guarantee, and why does that matter for compliance?
flashcards_qa.back: It enforces WORM immutability so no principal, including root, can delete or alter the backups within the retention period. That satisfies regulatory requirements for tamper-proof retention and protects against a malicious administrator or ransomware.

flashcards_qa.front: When do AWS Backup's centralized plans clearly beat per-service backups?
flashcards_qa.back: When you must prove consistent policy across many services and accounts, need cross-Region and cross-account copies for DR, want tag-based selection so new resources are protected automatically, or need Vault Lock immutability for compliance.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Item? (DynamoDB Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: A row in a DynamoDB table (up to 400 KB).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Attribute? (DynamoDB Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: A field of an item (can be nested, added over time, nullable).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Partition key (hash)? (DynamoDB Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: Primary key attribute used to distribute data.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Sort key (range)? (DynamoDB Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: Second key attribute; combined with partition key for uniqueness.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Cardinality? (DynamoDB Fundamentals)
flashcards_qa.back: Number of distinct values (high cardinality = better distribution).

flashcards_qa.front: How would you characterize DynamoDB in one sentence?
flashcards_qa.back: A serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database that is replicated across multiple Availability Zones by default.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Fundamentals: Recall a key exam fact.
flashcards_qa.back: No joins or aggregations (assume for exam); all data for a query should be in one item.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Fundamentals: What is Max item size?
flashcards_qa.back: Max item size = 400 KB.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Fundamentals: What is Primary key?
flashcards_qa.back: Primary key = partition key (hash) OR partition key + sort key (hash + range).

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Fundamentals: When or why would you use this?
flashcards_qa.back: Choose a HIGH-CARDINALITY partition key to maximize data distribution (avoid skew).

flashcards_qa.front: Which DynamoDB table classes exist, and when would you use the second one?
flashcards_qa.back: Standard and Standard-Infrequent Access. Standard-IA lowers storage cost for tables whose data is rarely read, at a higher per-request price.

flashcards_qa.front: You need multi-table joins and complex transactions. DynamoDB or RDS?
flashcards_qa.back: RDS, because it is relational and supports joins and rich transactions. DynamoDB is NoSQL, scales horizontally, and has no joins.

flashcards_qa.front: When must a DynamoDB partition key value be unique, and when does uniqueness apply to a pair of values?
flashcards_qa.back: With a partition key only, each item's partition key must be unique. With a composite primary key, it is the combination of partition key and sort key that must be unique.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the two forms a DynamoDB primary key can take?
flashcards_qa.back: A simple primary key, which is just the partition key, or a composite primary key made of a partition key plus a sort key.

flashcards_qa.front: You are choosing a partition key and one candidate has only five distinct values. What is the problem?
flashcards_qa.back: Low cardinality causes hot partitions and skew, because requests concentrate on a few partitions. Choose the highest-cardinality attribute so traffic distributes evenly.

flashcards_qa.front: Can DynamoDB join two tables the way SQL does?
flashcards_qa.back: No. DynamoDB is NoSQL with no joins, scaling horizontally across partitions. Joins and rich relational queries are what RDS provides, scaling mainly vertically.

flashcards_qa.front: What property should you look for when picking a DynamoDB partition key, and why?
flashcards_qa.back: The highest cardinality available, so that item and request distribution is even. Low-cardinality keys concentrate traffic on a few partitions, producing hot partitions and throttling.

flashcards_qa.front: Give two situations where DynamoDB is the wrong tool, and what you should use instead.
flashcards_qa.back: Workloads needing joins or complex multi-table transactions belong in RDS. Large binary objects belong in S3, with only their metadata and key stored in DynamoDB, since items are capped at 400 KB.

flashcards_qa.front: What is WCU? (DynamoDB Throughput (RCU & WCU))
flashcards_qa.back: Write Capacity Unit — 1 write/sec up to 1 KB.

flashcards_qa.front: What is RCU? (DynamoDB Throughput (RCU & WCU))
flashcards_qa.back: Read Capacity Unit — 1 strong or 2 eventual reads/sec up to 4 KB.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Eventually consistent read? (DynamoDB Throughput (RCU & WCU))
flashcards_qa.back: Default read that may return stale data briefly after a write.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Strongly consistent read? (DynamoDB Throughput (RCU & WCU))
flashcards_qa.back: Read returning the latest data; costs 2x RCU.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Hot partition? (DynamoDB Throughput (RCU & WCU))
flashcards_qa.back: A partition receiving disproportionate traffic, causing throttling.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Throughput (RCU & WCU): What is 1 WCU?
flashcards_qa.back: 1 WCU = 1 write/sec up to 1 KB (round item size up to next KB).

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Throughput (RCU & WCU): What is 1 RCU?
flashcards_qa.back: 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read/sec OR 2 eventually consistent reads/sec up to 4 KB (round up to next 4 KB).

flashcards_qa.front: What does asking for a strongly consistent read cost you in DynamoDB?
flashcards_qa.back: Twice the read capacity of an eventually consistent read, plus slightly higher latency. Eventually consistent is the default.

flashcards_qa.front: How does on-demand capacity compare with provisioned on cost, and how often can you switch modes?
flashcards_qa.back: On-demand costs roughly 2.5 times as much as provisioned for the same throughput. You can switch between modes once every 24 hours.

flashcards_qa.front: Total provisioned capacity looks sufficient but you keep getting ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: Because capacity is spread evenly across partitions, so a hot key or oversized items can exhaust one partition's share while the table's total capacity appears fine.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the three main remedies for DynamoDB throttling?
flashcards_qa.back: Retry with exponential backoff, redesign the key so traffic distributes more evenly across partitions, and put DAX in front to absorb hot-key reads.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the rounding units for an RCU and a WCU?
flashcards_qa.back: Reads round up to 4 KB per unit, and writes round up to 1 KB per unit.

flashcards_qa.front: How many eventually consistent reads and strongly consistent reads does one RCU buy?
flashcards_qa.back: One RCU gives two eventually consistent reads of up to 4 KB, so each costs 0.5 RCU, or one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB, costing a full RCU.

flashcards_qa.front: Why can DynamoDB throttle even when CloudWatch shows consumed capacity well below what is provisioned?
flashcards_qa.back: Because throttling is evaluated per partition. A single hot key can saturate its own partition's share of capacity while the table-wide totals still look healthy.

flashcards_qa.front: State the size units used for read versus write capacity in DynamoDB.
flashcards_qa.back: Read capacity is measured in 4 KB units and write capacity in 1 KB units, both rounded up.

flashcards_qa.front: Which read type costs one full RCU and which costs half?
flashcards_qa.back: A strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB costs one RCU. An eventually consistent read of the same size costs 0.5 RCU.

flashcards_qa.front: Traffic is steady and predictable on one table and wildly spiky on another. Which capacity mode for each?
flashcards_qa.back: Provisioned capacity for the predictable table, since it is substantially cheaper and can use auto scaling. On-demand for the spiky table, accepting roughly 2.5 times the cost for automatic scaling with no planning.

flashcards_qa.front: An item is 10 KB. How many RCUs does one eventually consistent read cost, and one strongly consistent read?
flashcards_qa.back: Ten KB rounds up to three 4 KB units. A strongly consistent read therefore costs 3 RCUs, and an eventually consistent read costs 1.5 RCUs.

flashcards_qa.front: A table with plenty of spare capacity is throttling a single popular item. How do you diagnose and fix it?
flashcards_qa.back: Recognize it as per-partition throttling from a hot key rather than a table-wide shortage. Fix it by putting DAX in front of the reads, redesigning the key to spread traffic, for example with a write-sharding suffix, and retrying with exponential backoff.

flashcards_qa.front: What is PutItem? (DynamoDB Basic APIs)
flashcards_qa.back: Create or fully replace an item.

flashcards_qa.front: What is UpdateItem? (DynamoDB Basic APIs)
flashcards_qa.back: Edit specific attributes (or create); supports atomic counters.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Query? (DynamoDB Basic APIs)
flashcards_qa.back: Retrieve by Key Condition Expression (partition + optional sort key).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Scan? (DynamoDB Basic APIs)
flashcards_qa.back: Read the entire table (expensive).

flashcards_qa.front: What is ProjectionExpression? (DynamoDB Basic APIs)
flashcards_qa.back: Return only selected attributes.

flashcards_qa.front: What is FilterExpression? (DynamoDB Basic APIs)
flashcards_qa.back: Filter non-key attributes after a query/scan.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to change one attribute on an existing item without touching the others. Which API?
flashcards_qa.back: UpdateItem, which edits specific attributes and can also create the item if it does not exist. PutItem would replace the entire item.

flashcards_qa.front: How does a DynamoDB Query select items, and what role does FilterExpression play?
flashcards_qa.back: A Key Condition Expression selects items, requiring an equality condition on the partition key and optionally a range condition on the sort key. FilterExpression then removes items based on non-key attributes, but only after they have been read.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the maximum data a single Query or Scan call returns, and how do you get more?
flashcards_qa.back: One MB per call. Beyond that you paginate, using the LastEvaluatedKey to request the next page.

flashcards_qa.front: Why is Scan expensive, and how can you make it faster?
flashcards_qa.back: Because it reads every item in the table, consuming capacity for all of them. Parallel Scan splits the table into segments processed by multiple workers, which is faster but consumes capacity even more aggressively.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the correct way to empty a large DynamoDB table?
flashcards_qa.back: Delete the table and recreate it. Scanning and deleting item by item consumes enormous read and write capacity and takes far longer.

flashcards_qa.front: State the limits on BatchWriteItem and BatchGetItem, and how partial failures are reported.
flashcards_qa.back: BatchWriteItem handles up to 25 items or 16 MB and supports only Put and Delete, not Update. BatchGetItem handles up to 100 items or 16 MB. Anything that fails comes back as UnprocessedItems or UnprocessedKeys for you to retry.

flashcards_qa.front: Does PutItem leave attributes you did not specify untouched?
flashcards_qa.back: No. PutItem replaces the whole item, so unlisted attributes are lost. UpdateItem is what modifies only the attributes you name.

flashcards_qa.front: Does adding a FilterExpression to a Query reduce the capacity it consumes?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The filter is applied after the items have been read, so you still pay the full read cost, and it cannot reference key attributes.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a DynamoDB Scan read only the items matching your filter?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Scan reads the entire table and filters afterwards, so you pay for all of it. Query reads only the items under the partition key you specify.

flashcards_qa.front: You must retrieve all orders for one customer from a large table. Query or Scan, and why?
flashcards_qa.back: Query, using the customer ID as the partition key, so DynamoDB reads only that customer's items. A Scan would read the whole table and filter, costing vastly more.

flashcards_qa.front: Does a ProjectionExpression reduce the number of items returned?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It reduces which attributes come back. Reducing which items are returned is FilterExpression, and that runs after the read so it does not save capacity.

flashcards_qa.front: Why is FilterExpression a poor way to reduce DynamoDB costs?
flashcards_qa.back: Because it runs after the query or scan has already read the items, so the read capacity is consumed regardless. To reduce cost you must narrow what is read, using better keys or an index.

flashcards_qa.front: You must fetch a specific customer's items and separately empty a table. What is the right approach for each?
flashcards_qa.back: Use a Query on the customer's partition key for the fetch, rather than a Scan. To empty the table, delete and recreate it rather than scanning and deleting each item.

flashcards_qa.front: What is LSI? (DynamoDB Indexes (LSI & GSI))
flashcards_qa.back: Local Secondary Index — alternative sort key, same partition key.

flashcards_qa.front: What is GSI? (DynamoDB Indexes (LSI & GSI))
flashcards_qa.back: Global Secondary Index — alternative primary key with its own capacity.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Projection? (DynamoDB Indexes (LSI & GSI))
flashcards_qa.back: The set of attributes copied into an index.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Indexes (LSI & GSI): What is LSI?
flashcards_qa.back: LSI = same partition key + alternative sort key; must be created at table creation; up to 5; uses base table RCU/WCU.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Indexes (LSI & GSI): What is GSI?
flashcards_qa.back: GSI = different partition key (and optional sort key); can be added/modified anytime; has its own provisioned RCU/WCU.

flashcards_qa.front: Writes to a GSI are being throttled. What happens to the base table?
flashcards_qa.back: It is throttled too. GSI write throttling propagates back to the base table, which is a frequently tested caveat.

flashcards_qa.front: What do LSIs and GSIs have in common?
flashcards_qa.back: Both index scalar attributes and both support attribute projection, so you choose which attributes are copied into the index.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a Local Secondary Index be added to an existing DynamoDB table?
flashcards_qa.back: No. LSIs must be created with the table. GSIs can be added at any time, define a new partition key, and have their own capacity.

flashcards_qa.front: Which index type's throttling can bring down writes to the base table?
flashcards_qa.back: A GSI. If its writes are throttled, writes to the base table are throttled as well.

flashcards_qa.front: Does throttling on an LSI affect the base table the way GSI throttling does?
flashcards_qa.back: No. GSI write throttling propagates to the base table, whereas an LSI shares the table's capacity directly and does not create that separate cascade.

flashcards_qa.front: How do LSIs and GSIs differ across the three attributes that matter most?
flashcards_qa.back: Key structure: an LSI changes only the sort key, while a GSI changes the partition key too. Creation timing: an LSI must exist at table creation, a GSI can be added later. Capacity: an LSI draws on the table's capacity, a GSI has its own.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to query by a different sort order on the same partition key, and elsewhere by a completely different attribute. Which index for each?
flashcards_qa.back: An LSI for the alternative sort key on the same partition key, though it must have existed since table creation. A GSI for querying by a completely different attribute, since it defines a new partition key and can be added at any time.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the operational risk of a GSI with insufficient write capacity?
flashcards_qa.back: Its write throttling cascades to the base table, so an under-provisioned index can throttle your primary write path.

flashcards_qa.front: What is PartiQL? (DynamoDB PartiQL)
flashcards_qa.back: A SQL-compatible query language for DynamoDB (no joins).

flashcards_qa.front: Which statements does PartiQL support against DynamoDB?
flashcards_qa.back: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. It does not support joins.

flashcards_qa.front: Does PartiQL give DynamoDB capabilities it did not have before?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It adds SQL-like syntax over the existing operations but no new functional capability beyond the native APIs.

flashcards_qa.front: Where can you run PartiQL statements against DynamoDB?
flashcards_qa.back: From the console, NoSQL Workbench, the APIs, the CLI, and the SDKs, and it supports batch operations.

flashcards_qa.front: You want to join two DynamoDB tables using PartiQL. Is that possible?
flashcards_qa.back: No. PartiQL provides SQL-like syntax but still has no join support, because DynamoDB itself does not join.

flashcards_qa.front: Can PartiQL join two DynamoDB tables?
flashcards_qa.back: No. PartiQL provides SQL-like syntax for select, insert, update, and delete, but no joins, because DynamoDB itself does not join.

flashcards_qa.front: What does PartiQL give you, and what does it not?
flashcards_qa.back: It gives SQL-like syntax over DynamoDB, which makes ad-hoc access more familiar. It does not give joins or any capability the native DynamoDB APIs lack.

flashcards_qa.front: What is DAX? (DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX))
flashcards_qa.back: DynamoDB Accelerator — in-memory cache for DynamoDB.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Hot key? (DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX))
flashcards_qa.back: A heavily accessed key causing throttling, mitigated by DAX.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ElastiCache? (DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX))
flashcards_qa.back: In-memory cache for arbitrary/computed data.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX): What is DAX?
flashcards_qa.back: DAX = seamless in-memory cache for DynamoDB, microsecond read latency, no app changes.

flashcards_qa.front: Which problem does DAX solve, and what is its default cache TTL?
flashcards_qa.back: It solves hot-key read throttling and high read latency, serving cached reads in microseconds. The default item cache TTL is five minutes.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX): Recall a key exam fact.
flashcards_qa.back: Up to 10 nodes; multi-AZ with 3+ nodes recommended in production.

flashcards_qa.front: What does DAX cache, and what does ElastiCache cache?
flashcards_qa.back: DAX caches DynamoDB objects, query results, and scan results. ElastiCache stores results of computation your application performs, such as aggregations.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to cache the result of an expensive application-side aggregation, not raw DynamoDB reads. Which service?
flashcards_qa.back: ElastiCache, which caches whatever your application computes. DAX is specifically a read-through cache for DynamoDB items, queries, and scans.

flashcards_qa.front: Will DAX help with write throttling on a hot key?
flashcards_qa.back: No. DAX addresses hot-key read throttling and read latency. Write throttling needs a key redesign, write sharding, or more capacity.

flashcards_qa.front: Would you use DAX to cache the result of an aggregation your application computed?
flashcards_qa.back: No. DAX is a read-through cache for DynamoDB items, queries, and scans. Caching application-computed results is what ElastiCache is for.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you choose between DAX and ElastiCache?
flashcards_qa.back: If you are caching DynamoDB reads, queries, or scans, use DAX, since it requires almost no code change. If you are caching results your application computed, such as aggregations across sources, use ElastiCache.

flashcards_qa.front: What performance does DAX deliver, and for which problem?
flashcards_qa.back: Microsecond read latency, and it is specifically aimed at hot-key read throttling and repeated reads of the same items.

flashcards_qa.front: What is DynamoDB Stream? (DynamoDB Streams)
flashcards_qa.back: Ordered log of item-level table changes.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Event source mapping? (DynamoDB Streams)
flashcards_qa.back: Lambda mechanism to poll a stream and invoke the function.

flashcards_qa.front: What is View type? (DynamoDB Streams)
flashcards_qa.back: What the stream record contains (keys/new/old/both).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Global table? (DynamoDB Streams)
flashcards_qa.back: Multi-region, multi-active replicated table (requires Streams).

flashcards_qa.front: What do DynamoDB Streams capture?
flashcards_qa.back: Item-level create, update, and delete changes, delivered in the order they occurred.

flashcards_qa.front: What can consume a DynamoDB Stream?
flashcards_qa.back: Lambda through an event source mapping, which polls synchronous batches, Kinesis Data Streams, or a KCL application.

flashcards_qa.front: How long do DynamoDB Streams retain data, and do you manage the shards?
flashcards_qa.back: Retention is up to 24 hours, and shards are managed automatically, so there is no provisioning to do.

flashcards_qa.front: What view types can a DynamoDB Stream be configured with?
flashcards_qa.back: KEYS_ONLY, NEW_IMAGE, OLD_IMAGE, and NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES.

flashcards_qa.front: What prerequisite must be met before enabling DynamoDB global tables?
flashcards_qa.back: DynamoDB Streams must be enabled on the table, since streams are the mechanism behind cross-Region replication.

flashcards_qa.front: You enable a stream on an existing busy table. Do you see the changes from last week?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Enabling a stream does not backfill history. Only changes that occur after it is enabled appear.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a DynamoDB Stream be used to reconstruct changes made before it was enabled?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Streams do not retroactively populate historical changes, so only post-enablement activity is captured.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to keep DynamoDB change history for a year. How?
flashcards_qa.back: Consume the stream and persist it, for example through Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose into S3, since the stream itself retains only 24 hours.

flashcards_qa.front: You want DynamoDB global tables but streams are disabled. What must happen first?
flashcards_qa.back: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table, because global tables depend on them for cross-Region replication.

flashcards_qa.front: Do you provision shards for a DynamoDB Stream?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Its shards are managed automatically and retention is fixed at up to 24 hours. Provisioning shards and choosing retention up to 365 days describes Kinesis Data Streams.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare the DynamoDB Stream view types NEW_IMAGE, OLD_IMAGE, and NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES.
flashcards_qa.back: NEW_IMAGE gives the item as it is after the change. OLD_IMAGE gives it as it was before. NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES gives both, which is what you need to compute what actually changed.

flashcards_qa.front: State the two limitations of DynamoDB Streams that catch people out.
flashcards_qa.back: Enabling a stream does not backfill past changes, and retention is only 24 hours, so anything you need long term must be persisted elsewhere.

flashcards_qa.front: Sketch a pipeline that lands DynamoDB changes in Redshift and OpenSearch.
flashcards_qa.back: Enable DynamoDB Streams, consume with Lambda or forward to Kinesis Data Streams, feed Kinesis Data Firehose, and let Firehose deliver into S3, Redshift, and OpenSearch.

flashcards_qa.front: What is TTL? (DynamoDB TTL)
flashcards_qa.back: Time To Live — auto-expiration of items by timestamp.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Unix epoch time? (DynamoDB TTL)
flashcards_qa.back: Seconds since 1970, the required TTL timestamp format.

flashcards_qa.front: How does DynamoDB TTL decide what to delete, and what does it cost in capacity?
flashcards_qa.back: It deletes items once the Unix epoch timestamp in a designated numeric attribute has passed. The deletions consume no write capacity.

flashcards_qa.front: Do TTL deletions show up anywhere besides the table?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. They also remove the items from LSIs and GSIs, and they appear as delete records in DynamoDB Streams.

flashcards_qa.front: How quickly does DynamoDB delete an expired item?
flashcards_qa.back: Not immediately. A background process removes it within roughly 48 hours of expiration.

flashcards_qa.front: An item's TTL timestamp passed an hour ago. Can a Query still return it?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. Expired items remain readable until the background deletion happens, so applications must filter them out client-side.

flashcards_qa.front: Why can you not rely on TTL for precise, immediate expiry?
flashcards_qa.back: Because deletion is a background process that can take up to about 48 hours, and until it runs the expired items are still returned by reads, queries, and scans.

flashcards_qa.front: You set the TTL attribute to an ISO-8601 date string and nothing expires. Why?
flashcards_qa.back: Because the TTL attribute must be a Number holding a Unix epoch timestamp in seconds. A string value is ignored.

flashcards_qa.front: Does DynamoDB TTL consume write capacity when it deletes items?
flashcards_qa.back: No. TTL deletions are a background process consuming no WCU, but they can take up to about 48 hours. An explicit DeleteItem is immediate and does consume WCU.

flashcards_qa.front: What must an application account for when relying on DynamoDB TTL?
flashcards_qa.back: That expired items are still returned until the background delete runs, up to about 48 hours later, so queries need client-side filtering on the expiry attribute.

flashcards_qa.front: What side effects do TTL deletions have?
flashcards_qa.back: They remove the item from any LSIs and GSIs, and they generate delete records in DynamoDB Streams, so downstream consumers see them.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Large-object pattern? (DynamoDB Patterns with S3)
flashcards_qa.back: Blob in S3, metadata/pointer in DynamoDB.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Metadata-index pattern? (DynamoDB Patterns with S3)
flashcards_qa.back: DynamoDB indexes S3 object metadata for querying.

flashcards_qa.front: Users upload 50 MB documents that must be searchable by metadata. How do you split storage?
flashcards_qa.back: Store the documents themselves in S3 and keep the metadata plus the S3 key or URL in DynamoDB. That respects DynamoDB's 400 KB item limit while keeping metadata queryable.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Patterns with S3: What's the answer/service for — Use S3 event notifications?
flashcards_qa.back: Use S3 event notifications → Lambda → DynamoDB to index object metadata.

flashcards_qa.front: In the S3-plus-DynamoDB pattern, what does DynamoDB actually serve?
flashcards_qa.back: Metadata queries, such as finding objects in a date range, totalling storage per customer, or filtering by attribute, using the stored pointer to fetch the object from S3.

flashcards_qa.front: Can you store a 5 MB binary object directly in a DynamoDB item?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Items are limited to 400 KB. Put the object in S3 and store a pointer to it in DynamoDB.

flashcards_qa.front: Why not just keep everything in S3 and query the metadata there?
flashcards_qa.back: Because S3 is object storage, not a query engine, so it cannot efficiently answer questions like all objects for this customer in this date range. Indexing that metadata in DynamoDB gives you those queries.

flashcards_qa.front: Split the responsibilities in the S3-plus-DynamoDB pattern.
flashcards_qa.back: S3 stores the object bytes, cheaply and without size constraints. DynamoDB stores and indexes the metadata, including the S3 key, and answers the queries.

flashcards_qa.front: What signals in a scenario tell you to split storage between S3 and DynamoDB?
flashcards_qa.back: Objects larger than DynamoDB's 400 KB item limit, combined with a need to query attributes about those objects. S3 holds the payload and DynamoDB indexes the metadata with a pointer.

flashcards_qa.front: What is VPC endpoint? (DynamoDB Security & Features)
flashcards_qa.back: Private path to DynamoDB without the public internet.

flashcards_qa.front: What is PITR? (DynamoDB Security & Features)
flashcards_qa.back: Point-in-time recovery with no performance impact.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Global table? (DynamoDB Security & Features)
flashcards_qa.back: Multi-region, multi-active replicated table (needs Streams).

flashcards_qa.front: What is LeadingKeys? (DynamoDB Security & Features)
flashcards_qa.back: IAM condition key limiting access to a user's own partition-key rows.

flashcards_qa.front: What is DynamoDB Local? (DynamoDB Security & Features)
flashcards_qa.back: Local downloadable version for development/testing.

flashcards_qa.front: How is DynamoDB secured for access, encryption, and private connectivity?
flashcards_qa.back: Access is fully controlled through IAM, data is encrypted at rest with KMS and in transit with SSL/TLS, and VPC endpoints allow private access without traversing the internet.

flashcards_qa.front: What backup options does DynamoDB provide?
flashcards_qa.back: Point-in-time recovery, which is continuous, and on-demand backup and restore, which produces a snapshot.

flashcards_qa.front: DynamoDB Security & Features: What is Global tables?
flashcards_qa.back: Global tables = multi-region, multi-active; require DynamoDB Streams.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you develop against DynamoDB offline, and how do you migrate an existing database into it?
flashcards_qa.back: DynamoDB Local for offline development and testing, and AWS DMS for migrating data in from another database.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you restrict a mobile client to only its own rows and only some attributes?
flashcards_qa.back: Use a federated identity to obtain temporary credentials for a restricted IAM role. Within that role, the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition limits access to rows whose partition key matches the user, and attribute conditions limit which attributes they can see.

flashcards_qa.front: Which fine-grained access mechanism is row-level and which is column-level?
flashcards_qa.back: dynamodb:LeadingKeys gives row-level restriction, tying access to the partition key value. Attribute-based conditions give column-level restriction.

flashcards_qa.front: What must be enabled before a table can join a global table configuration?
flashcards_qa.back: DynamoDB Streams, which underpin the cross-Region replication.

flashcards_qa.front: Should each mobile app user get their own IAM user for DynamoDB access?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Use a federated identity provider to issue temporary credentials against a restricted role, which scales and avoids managing per-user IAM identities.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe the two fine-grained access controls available in DynamoDB.
flashcards_qa.back: dynamodb:LeadingKeys restricts a principal to items whose partition key matches a value tied to their identity, giving row-level isolation. Attribute conditions restrict which attributes may be read or written, giving column-level control.

flashcards_qa.front: Can DynamoDB point-in-time recovery restore to any second in its window?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. PITR records changes continuously, so you can restore to any point within the retention window. On-demand backup instead captures a discrete snapshot.

flashcards_qa.front: Design multi-tenant row-level isolation for a DynamoDB table accessed from client devices.
flashcards_qa.back: Have users authenticate to a federated identity provider, exchange that for temporary credentials on a restricted IAM role, and put a dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition in the role's policy so each user can only touch items whose partition key is their own identifier.

flashcards_qa.front: State the global tables prerequisite and the difference between the two DynamoDB backup types.
flashcards_qa.back: Global tables require DynamoDB Streams to be enabled. For backups, PITR is continuous and lets you restore to any point in the window, while on-demand backup is a discrete snapshot.

flashcards_qa.front: What is RDS? (Amazon RDS)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed relational database service.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ACID? (Amazon RDS)
flashcards_qa.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Read replica? (Amazon RDS)
flashcards_qa.back: A read-only copy used to scale read traffic.

flashcards_qa.front: Which engines does Amazon RDS support?
flashcards_qa.back: Aurora, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, and SQL Server.

flashcards_qa.front: What workload profile does RDS suit, and how does the exam usually frame it?
flashcards_qa.back: OLTP and relatively small datasets. On the exam RDS is generally not the big-data answer, appearing instead as a transactional store or as a source feeding Redshift.

flashcards_qa.front: Are all RDS engines ACID compliant?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. Every RDS engine is fully ACID compliant.

flashcards_qa.front: How does RDS scale, and what can it not scale?
flashcards_qa.back: It scales vertically by resizing the instance, and it scales reads horizontally with read replicas. It cannot scale writes horizontally.

flashcards_qa.front: How is RDS secured?
flashcards_qa.back: Network isolation in a VPC, encryption at rest with KMS, and SSL/TLS for connections in transit.

flashcards_qa.front: A workload runs thousands of small transactional updates per second; another scans billions of rows for analytics. RDS or Redshift for each?
flashcards_qa.back: RDS for the transactional updates, since it is built for OLTP. Redshift for the analytical scans, since it is a columnar OLAP warehouse.

flashcards_qa.front: Write throughput on an RDS instance is saturated. Will adding read replicas help?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Read replicas scale reads only. To handle more writes you must scale the instance vertically, since RDS cannot scale writes horizontally.

flashcards_qa.front: Is DynamoDB fully ACID compliant with support for complex joins?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It offers transactions but no joins, and scales horizontally. Full relational ACID behavior with joins is what RDS provides.

flashcards_qa.front: Is Redshift a good fit for thousands of small transactional writes per second?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Redshift is a columnar OLAP warehouse built for large scans and aggregations. High-volume small transactional writes belong in RDS or DynamoDB.

flashcards_qa.front: State the ACID properties, and give two cases where RDS is the wrong answer.
flashcards_qa.back: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. RDS is wrong for large-scale analytics, where Redshift belongs, and for very high-volume key-value workloads needing horizontal scale, where DynamoDB belongs.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the practical limit of RDS's scaling model?
flashcards_qa.back: Reads scale out with replicas, but writes only scale up, by moving to a larger instance. There is no horizontal write scaling, so the write ceiling is the largest instance available.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Shared lock? (RDS Locks (Shared & Exclusive))
flashcards_qa.back: FOR SHARE — allows reads, prevents writes; multiple holders.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Exclusive lock? (RDS Locks (Shared & Exclusive))
flashcards_qa.back: FOR UPDATE — prevents reads and writes; single holder.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Deadlock? (RDS Locks (Shared & Exclusive))
flashcards_qa.back: A lock that is never released because a transaction didn't complete.

flashcards_qa.front: What does a shared lock allow and block, and how many transactions can hold it?
flashcards_qa.back: A shared lock, taken with FOR SHARE, allows other transactions to read the rows but blocks writes to them, and multiple transactions can hold it at once.

flashcards_qa.front: What does an exclusive lock allow and block, and how many transactions can hold it?
flashcards_qa.back: An exclusive lock, taken with FOR UPDATE, blocks both reads and writes by other transactions, and only one transaction can hold it.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you lock at table level, and does Redshift have an equivalent?
flashcards_qa.back: With LOCK TABLES and UNLOCK TABLES. Redshift has its own LOCK command for table-level locking.

flashcards_qa.front: RDS Locks (Shared & Exclusive): Recall a key exam fact.
flashcards_qa.back: An interrupted/incomplete locking transaction can cause a deadlock.

flashcards_qa.front: Under a FOR SHARE lock, can other transactions still read the rows?
flashcards_qa.back: Yes. A shared lock allows reads while blocking writes, and several transactions can hold it. FOR UPDATE is the exclusive lock that blocks reads and writes and permits one holder.

flashcards_qa.front: What causes a deadlock in a relational database?
flashcards_qa.back: Transactions holding locks that are never released while each waits on a lock the other holds, so neither can proceed. Long-running or unfinished locking transactions are the usual source.

flashcards_qa.front: State what each lock type blocks and how many holders each permits.
flashcards_qa.back: A shared lock, FOR SHARE, blocks writes but permits reads and allows multiple concurrent holders. An exclusive lock, FOR UPDATE, blocks both reads and writes and permits a single holder.

flashcards_qa.front: You must guarantee no other transaction can even read a row while you modify it. Which lock, and what is the alternative?
flashcards_qa.back: FOR UPDATE, an exclusive lock held by one transaction that blocks reads and writes. FOR SHARE would only block writes while still allowing reads.
