flashcards_qa.front: What is the most common operational problem with OpenSearch clusters?
flashcards_qa.back: Running out of disk space, which is why storage sizing, index lifecycle management, and tiering to UltraWarm or cold matter so much.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare hot, UltraWarm, and cold OpenSearch storage on speed and cost.
flashcards_qa.back: Hot is on local node storage, fastest and most expensive, and fully writable. UltraWarm is S3 with a local cache, cheaper, and suited to read-mostly data. Cold is pure S3, cheapest, and intended for rarely accessed data that you attach when needed.

flashcards_qa.front: Do OpenSearch rollups discard the original data to save space?
flashcards_qa.back: No, rollups summarize historical data into coarser buckets alongside it. Transforms are the feature that builds a different aggregated view without discarding anything either.

flashcards_qa.front: Does Remote Reindex keep two OpenSearch clusters continuously in sync?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Remote Reindex is a one-off copy of a single index. Continuous mirroring from a leader to a follower cluster is cross-cluster replication.

flashcards_qa.front: State the master node best practice and the prerequisites for the warm and cold tiers.
flashcards_qa.back: Use three dedicated master nodes to avoid split-brain, since two cannot form a reliable quorum. UltraWarm requires a dedicated master, and cold requires both a dedicated master and UltraWarm, and is not available on T2 or T3 instances.

flashcards_qa.front: OpenSearch Index Management & Stability: What's a hard concept to master in this lesson?
flashcards_qa.back: The storage/shard sizing formulas and hot/warm/cold trade-offs.

flashcards_qa.front: What is JVM memory pressure? (OpenSearch Performance & Serverless)
flashcards_qa.back: Memory strain from unbalanced/too-many shards.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Collection? (OpenSearch Performance & Serverless)
flashcards_qa.back: Serverless index grouping (search or time-series).

flashcards_qa.front: What is OCU? (OpenSearch Performance & Serverless)
flashcards_qa.back: OpenSearch Compute Unit (serverless capacity).

flashcards_qa.front: Your OpenSearch cluster reports high JVM memory pressure. What are the likely causes and fixes?
flashcards_qa.back: Unbalanced shards or simply too many shards, since each carries memory overhead. Reduce the shard count and delete unused indices.

flashcards_qa.front: What is OpenSearch Serverless, and what replaces the domain concept?
flashcards_qa.back: A 2023 offering that auto-scales capacity for you. Instead of domains you create collections, of either the search or the time-series type.

flashcards_qa.front: How is encryption and security policy handled in OpenSearch Serverless?
flashcards_qa.back: It is always encrypted, and you supply a KMS key. Security policies can be configured once and applied across many collections at the same time.

flashcards_qa.front: How is OpenSearch Serverless capacity measured and bounded?
flashcards_qa.back: In OpenSearch Compute Units, or OCUs. You set an upper limit to control cost, and the lower limit is always two indexing plus two search OCUs.

flashcards_qa.front: Is adding more shards a reliable way to improve OpenSearch performance?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Too many shards causes JVM memory pressure and can make performance worse. Often fewer, larger shards perform better, and reducing shards is the standard fix for memory pressure.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the two structural things to remember about OpenSearch Serverless?
flashcards_qa.back: It uses collections, of the search or time-series type, rather than domains, and its minimum capacity is always two indexing plus two search OCUs.

flashcards_qa.front: In OpenSearch Serverless, do you decide the shard strategy?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Serverless manages that, exposing only collections and OCU limits, with a 2 plus 2 minimum. Choosing instance types, node counts, and shard strategy belongs to managed domains.

flashcards_qa.front: An index was created with far too many shards and the cluster is unstable. What do you do?
flashcards_qa.back: Reduce the shard count, by reindexing into an index with fewer, larger shards and deleting unused indices, since excess shards drive JVM memory pressure.

flashcards_qa.front: Explain the less-is-more principle for OpenSearch shards.
flashcards_qa.back: Each shard is a separate Lucene index with its own memory and management overhead, so a large number of small shards consumes heap without improving throughput. Consolidating into fewer, larger shards and deleting unused indices relieves JVM memory pressure.

flashcards_qa.front: Summarize the OpenSearch Serverless model.
flashcards_qa.back: Capacity is auto-scaled and measured in OCUs, with a minimum of two indexing plus two search and a maximum you set for cost control. Data is organized into collections, of either search or time-series type, rather than into domains, and everything is encrypted with a KMS key you provide.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SPICE? (Amazon QuickSight)
flashcards_qa.back: In-memory calculation engine accelerating queries.

flashcards_qa.front: What is RLS/CLS? (Amazon QuickSight)
flashcards_qa.back: Row-/column-level security (CLS is Enterprise).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Direct Query? (Amazon QuickSight)
flashcards_qa.back: Hitting the source (e.g., Athena) directly, not SPICE.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Amazon QuickSight, and which sources can it read?
flashcards_qa.back: A serverless business intelligence and visualization service for end users. It reads from Redshift, Aurora and RDS, Athena, OpenSearch, and uploaded files, among others.

flashcards_qa.front: Can QuickSight replace an ETL pipeline?
flashcards_qa.back: No. It offers only limited data preparation. Heavy transformation belongs in Glue or Spark before the data reaches QuickSight.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon QuickSight: What is SPICE?
flashcards_qa.back: SPICE = in-memory columnar acceleration; 10 GB/user default; >30-min Athena import still times out.

flashcards_qa.front: What security features does QuickSight offer?
flashcards_qa.back: MFA, VPC connectivity, row-level security, column-level security in the Enterprise edition only, and private VPC access through an ENI, which can extend over Direct Connect.

flashcards_qa.front: QuickSight cannot reach a Redshift cluster in another Region. What is the fix, and what does cross-account need?
flashcards_qa.back: Add an inbound security group rule on the Redshift cluster allowing the QuickSight server IP addresses for that Region. Cross-Region or cross-account access more generally needs Enterprise edition with a private subnet and ENI, plus VPC peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, or VPC sharing.

flashcards_qa.front: How can QuickSight users be provisioned?
flashcards_qa.back: Through IAM, by email signup, or with the Active Directory Connector, which is Enterprise edition only and supports AWS-managed keys only.

flashcards_qa.front: A team wants to join and heavily reshape several large datasets. Should they do it in QuickSight?
flashcards_qa.back: No. QuickSight's data preparation is limited, so heavy ETL should happen in Glue or Spark first, with QuickSight used to visualize the prepared data.

flashcards_qa.front: Which QuickSight features require the Enterprise edition?
flashcards_qa.back: Column-level security and the Active Directory Connector, along with encryption at rest and the cross-account and cross-Region private connectivity options.

flashcards_qa.front: What specific network change lets QuickSight query a Redshift cluster in a different Region?
flashcards_qa.back: An inbound security group rule on the Redshift cluster permitting the QuickSight service IP ranges for the QuickSight Region.

flashcards_qa.front: Split the roles of QuickSight and Glue or Spark.
flashcards_qa.back: QuickSight visualizes prepared data as dashboards and analyses for business users. Glue and Spark do the extraction, cleansing, joining, and heavy transformation beforehand.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare SPICE with direct query in QuickSight.
flashcards_qa.back: SPICE loads data into QuickSight's in-memory engine, giving fast dashboards and isolating the source from query load, but the data is a snapshot needing refresh. Direct query hits the source live, so results are always current but every interaction loads the source.

flashcards_qa.front: Which QuickSight security feature is available in all editions, and which is Enterprise only?
flashcards_qa.back: Row-level security is available in any edition. Column-level security requires Enterprise.

flashcards_qa.front: You must connect QuickSight to a Redshift cluster in another Region and another account. What is needed?
flashcards_qa.back: For the cross-Region part, an inbound security group rule allowing the QuickSight server IPs. For cross-account, Enterprise edition with a private subnet and ENI, plus connectivity through VPC peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, or VPC sharing.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe SPICE's purpose and limits, and the difference between RLS and CLS.
flashcards_qa.back: SPICE is QuickSight's in-memory engine, giving fast dashboard performance from a cached snapshot that must be refreshed, with extra capacity billed per GB. Row-level security filters which rows a user sees and works in any edition, while column-level security hides columns and needs Enterprise.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Dashboard? (QuickSight Pricing, Dashboards & ML Insights)
flashcards_qa.back: Read-only shareable snapshot of analysis.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Embedded dashboard? (QuickSight Pricing, Dashboards & ML Insights)
flashcards_qa.back: Dashboard placed in your app via JS SDK/API.

flashcards_qa.front: What is ML Insights? (QuickSight Pricing, Dashboards & ML Insights)
flashcards_qa.back: Anomaly detection, forecasting, auto-narratives.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Random Cut Forest? (QuickSight Pricing, Dashboards & ML Insights)
flashcards_qa.back: Algorithm for anomaly detection/forecasting.

flashcards_qa.front: How is QuickSight priced per user, and what else is billable?
flashcards_qa.back: On annual commitment, Standard is about $9, Enterprise about $18, and Q with natural language about $28 per user per month. Month-to-month costs more, and additional SPICE capacity is billed per GB.

flashcards_qa.front: Which two capabilities does QuickSight Enterprise add?
flashcards_qa.back: Encryption at rest and Active Directory integration.

flashcards_qa.front: What is a QuickSight dashboard, and what does embedding require?
flashcards_qa.back: A read-only, shareable snapshot of an analysis, whose viewers must themselves be QuickSight users. Embedding uses the JavaScript SDK or API, requires authentication to be handled, and requires the hosting domain to be whitelisted.

flashcards_qa.front: What does QuickSight ML Insights provide?
flashcards_qa.back: Anomaly detection and forecasting, both powered by Random Cut Forest, and auto-narratives that describe the data in plain English.

flashcards_qa.front: What does the QuickSight Insights tab offer?
flashcards_qa.back: Suggested insights for the dataset, which QuickSight generates automatically based on the data and visuals.

flashcards_qa.front: Which algorithm underpins QuickSight's anomaly detection, and what else does it power?
flashcards_qa.back: Random Cut Forest, which powers both anomaly detection and forecasting in QuickSight.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the constraints when embedding QuickSight dashboards?
flashcards_qa.back: The hosting domain must be whitelisted, and you cannot use Active Directory, Cognito, or SSO directly as the embedding authentication mechanism, so authentication has to be handled and passed through the SDK or API.

flashcards_qa.front: What do you get by upgrading QuickSight to Enterprise?
flashcards_qa.back: Encryption at rest, Active Directory integration, column-level security, and the private cross-account and cross-Region connectivity options, at roughly double the per-user price.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare the QuickSight Standard, Enterprise, and Q editions on price and capability.
flashcards_qa.back: On annual pricing, Standard is about $9 per user per month for core BI, Enterprise about $18 adding encryption at rest, Active Directory, and column-level security, and Q about $28 adding natural-language querying.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish QuickSight anomaly detection from forecasting.
flashcards_qa.back: Anomaly detection flags data points that deviate from the learned pattern. Forecasting projects future values from historical trend and seasonality. Both are implemented with Random Cut Forest.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the QuickSight ML Insights capabilities and the algorithm behind them.
flashcards_qa.back: Anomaly detection and forecasting, both using Random Cut Forest, plus auto-narratives that summarize the data in plain English.

flashcards_qa.front: What must be in place to embed a QuickSight dashboard in your own application?
flashcards_qa.back: The JavaScript SDK or embedding API, an authentication flow you implement and pass through rather than AD, Cognito, or SSO directly, and the hosting domain added to the whitelist.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Calculated field? (QuickSight Calculated Fields & LAC)
flashcards_qa.back: A new field derived from existing fields.

flashcards_qa.front: What is LAC-A? (QuickSight Calculated Fields & LAC)
flashcards_qa.back: Level-aware aggregate at a specified level.

flashcards_qa.front: What is LAC-W? (QuickSight Calculated Fields & LAC)
flashcards_qa.back: Level-aware window aggregation.

flashcards_qa.front: What is FIXED vs FLOAT? (QuickSight Calculated Fields & LAC)
flashcards_qa.back: 4-decimal fixed type vs 16-significant-digit float type.

flashcards_qa.front: What can a QuickSight calculated field do?
flashcards_qa.back: Create a new field from existing ones using arithmetic, logical, and conditional expressions, plus date, numeric, string, table, and aggregation functions.

flashcards_qa.front: What does LAC-W do in QuickSight, and what are its two evaluation options?
flashcards_qa.back: LAC-W aggregates over a window or partition using window functions such as sumOver, maxOver, and denseRank. It can be evaluated as PRE_AGG, before display-level aggregations, or PRE_FILTER, before display filters are applied.

flashcards_qa.front: What does LAC-A do in QuickSight, and what is notable about the level field?
flashcards_qa.back: LAC-A computes an aggregate at a level you specify, before the display level, as in sum(sales, [country]). The level field does not have to appear in the visual.

flashcards_qa.front: QuickSight Calculated Fields & LAC: What is FIXED decimal type?
flashcards_qa.back: FIXED decimal type = 4 decimal places (division/rounding/overflow issues); use FLOAT (16 significant digits) for precision.

flashcards_qa.front: Your QuickSight calculation loses precision. Which data type is likely the cause?
flashcards_qa.back: FIXED, which keeps only four decimal places. Use FLOAT instead, which holds about 16 significant digits.

flashcards_qa.front: Must the grouping field in a LAC-A expression appear in the visual?
flashcards_qa.back: No. LAC-A computes at the specified level before the display level, so you can aggregate by country even when country is not on the visual.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish PRE_AGG from PRE_FILTER in a LAC-W expression.
flashcards_qa.back: PRE_AGG evaluates the window calculation before the visual's own aggregations are applied. PRE_FILTER evaluates it even earlier, before the display filters, so filtered-out rows still contribute.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare LAC-A with LAC-W in QuickSight.
flashcards_qa.back: LAC-A computes an aggregate at a specified grouping level, independent of what is on the visual. LAC-W computes a window or partition aggregation using window functions such as sumOver and denseRank.

flashcards_qa.front: At which points in the QuickSight calculation order do PRE_AGG and PRE_FILTER apply?
flashcards_qa.back: PRE_FILTER applies before display filters, so all rows are included regardless of filtering. PRE_AGG applies after filters but before the visual's aggregation.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare the FIXED and FLOAT data types in QuickSight.
flashcards_qa.back: FIXED stores only four decimal places, so it can introduce rounding errors in calculations. FLOAT stores about 16 significant digits and is the safer choice where precision matters.

flashcards_qa.front: Explain the difference between LAC-A and LAC-W, and the two LAC-W evaluation points.
flashcards_qa.back: LAC-A aggregates at a level you name, before the display level, and that level need not appear in the visual. LAC-W aggregates over a window or partition using window functions, and it can be evaluated as PRE_FILTER, before display filters, or PRE_AGG, before the visual's aggregations.

flashcards_qa.front: What is the precision trade-off between FIXED and FLOAT in QuickSight?
flashcards_qa.back: FIXED is limited to four decimal places, which is fine for currency-style values but loses precision in chained calculations. FLOAT carries about 16 significant digits, so it preserves precision at the cost of possible floating-point representation quirks.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Visibility timeout? (Amazon SQS)
flashcards_qa.back: Time a polled message is hidden while processed.

flashcards_qa.front: What is FIFO queue? (Amazon SQS)
flashcards_qa.back: Ordered, exactly-once queue (name ends .fifo).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Dead Letter Queue? (Amazon SQS)
flashcards_qa.back: Queue for repeatedly failing messages.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Redrive to source? (Amazon SQS)
flashcards_qa.back: Return DLQ messages to the source queue.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon SQS: What is SQS?
flashcards_qa.back: SQS = managed queue; standard = at-least-once (duplicates), best-effort ordering, auto-scaling; FIFO = exact order, exactly-once, 5-min dedup, lower throughput.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe how an SQS consumer processes a message, and how many consumers can receive a given message.
flashcards_qa.back: A consumer polls for messages, up to 10 at a time, processes them within the visibility timeout, and then explicitly deletes them. Each message is handled by one consumer only, so SQS does not fan out.

flashcards_qa.front: What are SQS retention limits, and how do you handle messages larger than the size limit?
flashcards_qa.back: Retention ranges from 1 minute to 14 days, defaulting to 4 days. For large payloads use the SQS Extended Client, which stores the body in S3 and passes a reference through the queue.

flashcards_qa.front: How does an SQS dead-letter queue work, and what are the rules around it?
flashcards_qa.back: Messages move to the DLQ once MaximumReceives is exceeded. The DLQ type must match the source, so FIFO with FIFO and standard with standard. Give the DLQ a long retention period, and use redrive-to-source to send fixed messages back for reprocessing.

flashcards_qa.front: How is data in SQS secured in flight and at rest, and what controls access?
flashcards_qa.back: In flight it uses HTTPS, and at rest KMS encrypts the message body but not the metadata. Access is controlled through IAM policies plus SQS queue access policies.

flashcards_qa.front: Two applications must both process every incoming order event. Is a single SQS queue enough?
flashcards_qa.back: No. In SQS each message is consumed and deleted by one consumer, so there is no fan-out. Use SNS fan-out to multiple queues, or Kinesis, which supports multiple consumers and replay.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare SQS standard and FIFO queues on ordering, delivery guarantees, and throughput.
flashcards_qa.back: Standard gives best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery with very high throughput. FIFO preserves order within a message group and gives exactly-once processing, but with lower throughput.

flashcards_qa.front: Does KMS encryption in SQS cover the message attributes and metadata?
flashcards_qa.back: No. KMS encrypts the message body only, not the metadata or attributes.

flashcards_qa.front: When would you choose Kinesis Data Streams over SQS?
flashcards_qa.back: When you need multiple independent consumers of the same data, the ability to replay history, or ordered streaming analytics. SQS is a queue where a message is consumed once and deleted, with no replay.

flashcards_qa.front: A FIFO SQS queue can deliver the same throughput as a standard queue. True?
flashcards_qa.back: No. FIFO trades throughput for ordering within a message group and exactly-once processing, whereas standard queues offer near-unlimited throughput with only best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery.

flashcards_qa.front: You attach a standard queue as the dead-letter queue for a FIFO queue. Will that work?
flashcards_qa.back: No. The DLQ must be the same type as its source queue, so a FIFO queue needs a FIFO DLQ and a standard queue needs a standard DLQ.

flashcards_qa.front: Contrast the SQS consumption model with the Kinesis consumption model.
flashcards_qa.back: SQS is consume-then-delete: one consumer takes a message, processes it, and deletes it, so it is gone. Kinesis keeps records for the retention period, so many consumers can read the same data independently and replay it.

flashcards_qa.front: Walk through configuring a dead-letter queue for an SQS queue and recovering the messages later.
flashcards_qa.back: Set a redrive policy on the source queue naming the DLQ and a MaximumReceives threshold, make the DLQ the same type as the source, and give it long retention. Once the bug is fixed, use redrive-to-source to move the messages back for reprocessing.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Pub/sub? (Kinesis Data Streams vs SQS)
flashcards_qa.back: Multiple independent consumers of the same stream (Kinesis).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Decoupling? (Kinesis Data Streams vs SQS)
flashcards_qa.back: Separating producers/consumers via a queue (SQS).

flashcards_qa.front: What capabilities does Kinesis Data Streams offer that make it a stream rather than a queue?
flashcards_qa.back: Data can be consumed many times by different consumers, replayed within the retention window, and is ordered per shard, supporting a pub/sub model. Consumers track position through checkpointing, which the KCL stores in DynamoDB.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SQS designed for, and what happens to a message after it is consumed?
flashcards_qa.back: It is designed for decoupling components, with effectively one reader per queue. A message is deleted after successful consumption, and failures can be routed to a dead-letter queue.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare Kinesis Data Streams and SQS FIFO on how ordering is achieved and what delivery guarantee you get.
flashcards_qa.back: Kinesis orders records within a shard, chosen by partition key, with at-least-once delivery. SQS FIFO orders within a message group ID and provides exactly-once processing.

flashcards_qa.front: Which of Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose, and SQS support replay, and what is each one's retention?
flashcards_qa.back: Only Kinesis Data Streams supports replay. Retention is up to 365 days for Kinesis Data Streams, none for Firehose since it does not store data, and up to 14 days for SQS.

flashcards_qa.front: Kinesis Data Streams vs SQS: When or why would you use this?
flashcards_qa.back: Use SQS for decoupling/queues; Kinesis for streaming/analytics/multiple consumers.

flashcards_qa.front: An exam question mentions multiple consumers needing to reprocess historical events. Which service, and which one would be wrong?
flashcards_qa.back: Kinesis Data Streams, because it supports multiple consumers and replay. SQS would be wrong, since it is for decoupling with a single consumer per message and no replay.

flashcards_qa.front: Can you reprocess messages already consumed from an SQS queue?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Consumed messages are deleted, so there is no replay. Only Kinesis Data Streams supports replaying data within its retention window.

flashcards_qa.front: Summarize Kinesis Data Streams versus SQS in one line each.
flashcards_qa.back: Kinesis Data Streams is a streaming service with ordered shards, many consumers, and replay. SQS is a queue for decoupling, with one consumer per message and no replay.

flashcards_qa.front: You must choose between Kinesis Data Streams and SQS. Which requirements point to each?
flashcards_qa.back: Multiple consumers, replay of history, ordering per key, or streaming analytics point to Kinesis Data Streams. Simple decoupling of producers from a single consumer, with per-message delete and a DLQ for failures, points to SQS.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SNS topic? (Amazon SNS & Fan-Out)
flashcards_qa.back: Pub/sub channel that subscribers listen to.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Fan-out? (Amazon SNS & Fan-Out)
flashcards_qa.back: Publish once to SNS, deliver to many subscribers.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Message filtering? (Amazon SNS & Fan-Out)
flashcards_qa.back: JSON policy limiting messages per subscription.

flashcards_qa.front: What is SNS FIFO topic? (Amazon SNS & Fan-Out)
flashcards_qa.back: Ordered/deduped topic (SQS FIFO subscribers).

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon SNS & Fan-Out: What is SNS?
flashcards_qa.back: SNS = pub/sub: every subscriber gets all messages (unless a filter policy applies).

flashcards_qa.front: One event must be delivered to several independent processing pipelines, each with its own queue and no data loss. What pattern do you use, and what must you configure?
flashcards_qa.back: The SNS fan-out pattern: publish once to an SNS topic and subscribe multiple SQS queues to it. Each queue needs an access policy allowing the SNS topic to write to it.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon SNS & Fan-Out: What's the answer/service for — Fan-out solves S3's one-event-rule-per-event-type+prefix limit (S3?
flashcards_qa.back: Fan-out solves S3's one-event-rule-per-event-type+prefix limit (S3→SNS→many queues).

flashcards_qa.front: You need SNS fan-out that preserves order and deduplicates. What must both the topic and the subscribers be?
flashcards_qa.back: The topic must be an SNS FIFO topic, and its subscribers must be SQS FIFO queues.

flashcards_qa.front: Different subscribers should receive only some of the messages published to a topic. How do you achieve that, and what happens if you do nothing?
flashcards_qa.back: Attach a JSON filter policy to each subscription so it receives only matching messages. A subscription with no filter policy receives all messages.

flashcards_qa.front: How is SNS secured, and what do you need for S3 to publish to a topic in another account?
flashcards_qa.back: HTTPS in flight and KMS at rest. Access is controlled by IAM plus SNS access policies, and cross-account or service publishing, such as allowing S3 to publish, is granted through the topic's access policy.

flashcards_qa.front: You set up SNS fan-out to three SQS queues but no messages arrive in them. What is the most likely cause?
flashcards_qa.back: The SQS queue access policies do not allow the SNS topic to send messages to them, which is a required step in the fan-out pattern.

flashcards_qa.front: Can a standard SQS queue subscribe to an SNS FIFO topic?
flashcards_qa.back: No. Subscribers to an SNS FIFO topic must be SQS FIFO queues.

flashcards_qa.front: A subscription has no filter policy attached. Which messages does it receive?
flashcards_qa.back: All messages published to the topic. Filtering is opt-in, so no filter policy means no filtering.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare SNS with SQS on delivery model.
flashcards_qa.back: SNS is publish/subscribe: a published message goes to all subscribers of the topic. SQS is a queue: each message is consumed by one consumer and then deleted.

flashcards_qa.front: Why use SNS fan-out instead of having the producer publish directly to several SQS queues?
flashcards_qa.back: Fan-out keeps the producer decoupled and avoids partial-failure data loss, since one publish to the topic reliably delivers to every subscribed queue. Publishing to each queue in turn means a failure part way through loses messages for some queues.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern and its one mandatory permission step.
flashcards_qa.back: The producer publishes once to an SNS topic, and multiple SQS queues subscribe so each gets its own copy for independent processing. Each subscribed queue must have an access policy permitting the SNS topic to write to it.

flashcards_qa.front: Different message types published to one topic must reach different subscribers. How do you implement that?
flashcards_qa.back: With SNS message filtering: attach a JSON filter policy to each subscription so it receives only the message types matching it, while a subscription without a policy receives everything.

flashcards_qa.front: What is State machine? (AWS Step Functions)
flashcards_qa.back: The overall workflow definition.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Task state? (AWS Step Functions)
flashcards_qa.back: A state that performs real work (e.g., Lambda).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Map state? (AWS Step Functions)
flashcards_qa.back: Runs steps for each dataset item in parallel.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Parallel state? (AWS Step Functions)
flashcards_qa.back: Runs separate branches concurrently.

flashcards_qa.front: What does Step Functions give you that hand-rolled orchestration in code does not?
flashcards_qa.back: A visual workflow representation, error handling and retries defined outside the application code, audit history of executions, built-in wait states, and support for executions lasting up to one year.

flashcards_qa.front: In what language are Step Functions workflows defined, and do you need to write it by hand for the exam?
flashcards_qa.back: In Amazon States Language, a JSON-based definition. You do not need to write ASL by hand for the exam.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the Step Functions state types.
flashcards_qa.back: Task, Choice, Wait, Parallel, Map, Pass, Succeed, and Fail.

flashcards_qa.front: You must run the same processing step on every item in a dataset concurrently. Which state type, and how does it differ from the other parallel option?
flashcards_qa.back: The Map state, which runs the steps for each item in the dataset in parallel and is data-oriented. The Parallel state instead runs a fixed set of different branches at the same time.

flashcards_qa.front: Give typical use cases for AWS Step Functions.
flashcards_qa.back: Orchestrating machine learning pipelines, coordinating batch jobs, and sequencing multi-service workflows across AWS.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to fan out the same task over 10,000 records, and elsewhere to run three different branches at once. Which state for each?
flashcards_qa.back: Map for the 10,000 records, since it runs per item over a dataset. Parallel for the three different branches, since it runs distinct branches concurrently.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe the difference between Map and Parallel in terms of what is being parallelized.
flashcards_qa.back: Map is data-parallel: the same steps run for each item in a collection. Parallel is branch-parallel: several different sets of steps run at the same time.

flashcards_qa.front: In a Step Functions workflow, which state performs the actual work, and which adds conditional branching?
flashcards_qa.back: The Task state performs the real work by invoking a service such as Lambda or Glue. The Choice state evaluates conditions to decide the next state.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare Step Functions with Glue Workflows for orchestration.
flashcards_qa.back: Step Functions orchestrates across many AWS services, with retries, error handling, and long-running executions. Glue Workflows only orchestrates Glue jobs, crawlers, and triggers within Glue.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish the Map state from the Parallel state in Step Functions.
flashcards_qa.back: Map iterates a dataset and runs the same steps for each item in parallel. Parallel runs several separate, differently defined branches at the same time and waits for all of them.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the Step Functions state types and say what scope of orchestration the service covers.
flashcards_qa.back: Task, Choice, Wait, Parallel, Map, Pass, Succeed, and Fail. Step Functions orchestrates across AWS services generally, in contrast to Glue Workflows, which is limited to Glue resources.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Amazon AppFlow? (Amazon AppFlow)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed SaaS-to-AWS integration service.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Flow? (Amazon AppFlow)
flashcards_qa.back: A configured AppFlow data transfer.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to pull data out of a SaaS application into AWS without writing integration code. Which service?
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon AppFlow, which transfers data between SaaS applications and AWS with no custom integration code.

flashcards_qa.front: Which sources and destinations does Amazon AppFlow support?
flashcards_qa.back: Sources include Salesforce, which is the usual exam cue, plus SAP, Zendesk, Slack, and ServiceNow. Destinations include S3, Redshift, Snowflake, and Salesforce.

flashcards_qa.front: When can an AppFlow flow run, and what transformation can it do in passing?
flashcards_qa.back: On a schedule, in response to events, or on demand. It offers built-in filtering and validation transforms as the data passes through.

flashcards_qa.front: How is AppFlow data protected in transit, and can it avoid the public internet?
flashcards_qa.back: It is encrypted over the internet, and it can run privately over AWS PrivateLink instead of traversing the public internet.

flashcards_qa.front: An exam question describes moving Salesforce data into S3 on a schedule. Which service is the expected answer?
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon AppFlow. A SaaS source such as Salesforce feeding into AWS is the standard AppFlow cue.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each to a service: SaaS application integration, database migration, and Spark-based ETL.
flashcards_qa.back: AppFlow for SaaS integration, DMS for database migration, and Glue for Spark-based ETL.

flashcards_qa.front: Distinguish AppFlow, Glue, and DMS by the kind of source they handle.
flashcards_qa.back: AppFlow handles SaaS applications such as Salesforce and ServiceNow. Glue handles ETL over data already in AWS with the Data Catalog. DMS handles database-to-database migration and replication.

flashcards_qa.front: What tells you a scenario calls for AppFlow rather than another integration tool?
flashcards_qa.back: The source is a SaaS application, for example Salesforce feeding S3 or Redshift, and the requirement is to avoid writing custom integration code. Glue and DMS point instead to AWS-internal ETL and database migration.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Event bus? (Amazon EventBridge)
flashcards_qa.back: Channel receiving events (default/partner/custom).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Rule? (Amazon EventBridge)
flashcards_qa.back: Matches events and routes them to targets.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Schema registry? (Amazon EventBridge)
flashcards_qa.back: Infers event schema and generates code.

flashcards_qa.front: What is Archive/replay? (Amazon EventBridge)
flashcards_qa.back: Store and re-emit events for debugging.

flashcards_qa.front: Which service both schedules cron-style jobs and reacts to event patterns, and what was it previously called?
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon EventBridge, formerly CloudWatch Events.

flashcards_qa.front: You need to trigger an action whenever any API call of a certain type happens in your account. How?
flashcards_qa.back: Combine EventBridge with CloudTrail. Because CloudTrail records API activity, EventBridge rules can react to essentially any API call in the account.

flashcards_qa.front: Which targets can an EventBridge rule route JSON events to?
flashcards_qa.back: Lambda, AWS Batch, ECS, SQS, SNS, Kinesis, Step Functions, CodePipeline, Systems Manager, and EC2 actions, among others.

flashcards_qa.front: What are the three kinds of EventBridge event bus, and how do you centralize events from many accounts?
flashcards_qa.back: The default bus for AWS service events, partner buses for SaaS events, and custom buses for your own applications. Cross-account centralization onto a single bus is granted with resource-based policies.

flashcards_qa.front: Which EventBridge features help with debugging and with understanding event structure?
flashcards_qa.back: Archive and replay of events lets you re-run past events for troubleshooting. The schema registry infers event schemas and generates versioned code bindings.

flashcards_qa.front: You find documentation referring to CloudWatch Events. Which service is that now?
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon EventBridge. CloudWatch Events was renamed EventBridge, so they are the same service.

flashcards_qa.front: Match each event source to the right EventBridge bus: AWS service events, a SaaS provider's events, and your own application's events.
flashcards_qa.back: The default bus carries AWS service events, a partner event bus carries the SaaS provider's events, and a custom bus carries your own application's events.

flashcards_qa.front: What is EventBridge archive and replay used for?
flashcards_qa.back: Debugging and troubleshooting, by storing events and replaying them later so you can reproduce and diagnose how consumers behaved.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare EventBridge with SNS.
flashcards_qa.back: EventBridge routes structured JSON events from many sources, including AWS services, SaaS partners, and your own applications, to many target types with content-based rules. SNS is pub/sub messaging that pushes notifications to its subscribers.

flashcards_qa.front: Name the three EventBridge bus types and what each is for.
flashcards_qa.back: Default for AWS service events, partner for SaaS provider events, and custom for your own application events.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon EventBridge: What's a hard concept to master in this lesson?
flashcards_qa.back: The three bus types (default/partner/custom) and cross-account resource-based policies.

flashcards_qa.front: Name two EventBridge features beyond simple routing, and how you make it react to any API call.
flashcards_qa.back: Archive and replay of events for troubleshooting, and the schema registry which infers schemas and generates versioned code bindings. Pairing EventBridge with CloudTrail lets rules react to essentially any API call in the account.

flashcards_qa.front: What is MWAA? (Amazon MWAA)
flashcards_qa.back: Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow.

flashcards_qa.front: What is DAG? (Amazon MWAA)
flashcards_qa.back: Directed Acyclic Graph workflow (Python).

flashcards_qa.front: What is Airflow web server? (Amazon MWAA)
flashcards_qa.back: UI for visualizing/scheduling DAGs.

flashcards_qa.front: Amazon MWAA: What is MWAA?
flashcards_qa.back: MWAA = managed Apache Airflow; batch-oriented workflows defined as Python DAGs.

flashcards_qa.front: How do you get an Airflow workflow into Amazon MWAA?
flashcards_qa.back: Write the DAG in Python, optionally zipped with its plugins, and upload it to an S3 bucket. MWAA then picks it up, schedules it, and orchestrates the runs.

flashcards_qa.front: Where does MWAA run, and how is access to the Airflow web UI controlled?
flashcards_qa.back: It runs inside a VPC and should be deployed across at least two Availability Zones. The Airflow UI is reached through a public or private endpoint, with access governed by IAM.

flashcards_qa.front: How does MWAA scale, and what runs the schedulers and workers?
flashcards_qa.back: It auto-scales the number of Airflow workers up to configured limits, and the schedulers and workers run in Fargate containers.

flashcards_qa.front: Which AWS services does MWAA commonly orchestrate?
flashcards_qa.back: Athena, AWS Batch, EMR, Glue, Redshift, Kinesis, Lambda, SageMaker, and S3, among others.

flashcards_qa.front: How are workflows expressed in MWAA compared with Glue Workflows or Step Functions?
flashcards_qa.back: MWAA uses Python DAGs, so workflows are code. Glue Workflows are configured within Glue, and Step Functions are defined in Amazon States Language rather than in general-purpose code.

flashcards_qa.front: You need complex, code-based coordination that your team already writes in Airflow. Which service, and what are the alternatives?
flashcards_qa.back: Amazon MWAA, which runs Python Airflow DAGs. The alternatives are Step Functions, defined in ASL for cross-service orchestration, and Glue Workflows, which only orchestrate Glue resources.

flashcards_qa.front: Where do MWAA DAGs live, and what does the deployment footprint look like?
flashcards_qa.back: DAGs are uploaded to an S3 bucket. The environment itself runs inside a VPC and should span at least two Availability Zones.

flashcards_qa.front: Engineers outside the VPC need to reach the Airflow web UI. What endpoint configuration is required?
flashcards_qa.back: A public endpoint, with access still controlled through IAM. A private endpoint would restrict the UI to callers inside the VPC.

flashcards_qa.front: Compare public and private endpoints for the MWAA Airflow UI.
flashcards_qa.back: A public endpoint makes the UI reachable from the internet, still gated by IAM, which suits users outside the VPC. A private endpoint keeps the UI reachable only from inside the VPC or connected networks.

flashcards_qa.front: What drives the choice between MWAA, Step Functions, and Glue Workflows?
flashcards_qa.back: MWAA if the team wants complex, code-based Airflow DAGs in Python, or already has them. Step Functions for cross-service orchestration defined declaratively in ASL. Glue Workflows when orchestration is confined to Glue jobs, crawlers, and triggers.

flashcards_qa.front: Describe the MWAA architecture.
flashcards_qa.back: Python DAGs are uploaded to S3, the environment runs in a VPC across at least two Availability Zones, schedulers and workers run in Fargate containers and auto-scale, and the Airflow UI is exposed through a public or private endpoint governed by IAM.

mc.question: A workload only needs to read .csv files from one S3 prefix. Following least privilege, what IAM policy should you grant?

options.B: GetObject only on that bucket/prefix for .csv files (and ListBucket on that prefix)

mc.explanation: Least privilege grants only the needed actions on the specific resources — read .csv from that prefix, nothing more.

mc.question: Which tool auto-generates least-privilege policies from observed activity?
mc.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer generates least-privilege policies based on actual access activity.

mc.question: When is it acceptable to start with broader permissions?

options.B: During development, then lock down once requirements are known

mc.explanation: You can start broad while developing (unknown needs), then restrict once the required operations are clear.

mc.question: What is the principle of least privilege?

options.B: Grant only the permissions required for a task

mc.explanation: Least privilege grants only the minimum permissions needed to perform a task.

mc.question: Why avoid extraneous permissions?
mc.explanation: Unneeded permissions can be abused or exploited, increasing risk.

short.question: Define least privilege.
short.answer: Answer: Granting only the permissions required to perform a given task — nothing more.

short.question: What tool helps generate least-privilege policies?
short.answer: Answer: IAM Access Analyzer, based on observed access activity.

short.question: When can you start broad?
short.answer: Answer: During development, then lock down once you know the required services/operations.

short.question: Give an example of a least-privilege policy.
short.answer: Answer: Allow ListBucket only on a specific prefix and GetObject only on .csv files under that prefix.

short.question: Why does least privilege matter?
short.answer: Answer: Excess permissions create opportunities for abuse or exploitation.

quizzes.title: Quiz — Data Masking, Anonymization, and Key Salting

mc.question: Two users choose the same weak password. What technique ensures their stored hashes differ and defeats rainbow-table attacks?

options.B: Salting with a unique per-user salt before hashing

mc.explanation: Adding a unique random salt before hashing makes identical passwords produce different hashes and defeats rainbow tables.

mc.question: You must display only the last 4 digits of credit-card numbers. Which technique and where is it built in?

options.B: Masking; built into Glue DataBrew and Redshift

mc.explanation: Masking obfuscates part of a value and is built into Glue DataBrew and Redshift (CREATE MASKING POLICY).

mc.question: Which salt practice is correct?

options.A: Reuse one salt for all users
options.B: Use a unique, strong random salt per user and rotate periodically

mc.explanation: Salts should be strong, cryptographically secure, unique per user, and rotated periodically.

mc.question: Which anonymization approach makes data untraceable by replacing it with unrelated values?
mc.explanation: Substitution (random values) and shuffling replace data so it's not traceable to the original.

mc.question: What is the safest way to handle PII you don't need?

options.B: Delete it or don't import it in the first place

mc.explanation: Not collecting/deleting unneeded PII is the safest approach.

short.question: What is masking and where is it built in?
short.answer: Answer: Obfuscating part of a value (e.g., last 4 digits); built into Glue DataBrew and Redshift (CREATE MASKING POLICY).

short.question: List anonymization techniques.
short.answer: Answer: Substitution, shuffling, encryption (deterministic/probabilistic), hashing, or delete/don't import.

short.question: What is salting and what does it defeat?
short.answer: Answer: Adding a random salt before hashing; it defeats rainbow-table attacks and makes identical inputs hash differently.

short.question: Give salt best practices.
short.answer: Answer: Use strong random salts, rotate periodically, and use a unique salt per user (never reuse).

short.question: Deterministic vs probabilistic encryption?
short.answer: Answer: Deterministic yields the same ciphertext for the same input; probabilistic can yield different ciphertext each time.

quizzes.title: Quiz — Preventing Backups/Replication to Disallowed AWS Regions

mc.question: You must ensure RDS backups never occur outside us-east-1 and us-west-1 for compliance. What's the most direct enforcement?

options.B: An IAM/bucket policy (or SCP) restricting CreateDBSnapshot/CopyDBSnapshot to those regions

mc.explanation: Region-condition policies (IAM/S3 or an Organizations SCP) restrict backup actions to allowed regions.

mc.question: Which provides ORG-WIDE guardrails to prevent disallowed-region actions?
mc.explanation: SCPs enforce guardrails across all accounts in an organization.

mc.question: What's a common accidental cause of data ending up in a disallowed region?
mc.explanation: Well-intentioned cross-region backups/replication can accidentally place data where it's not allowed.

mc.question: How do you quickly catch accidental cross-region data movement?

options.B: Monitor with CloudTrail and CloudWatch alarms

mc.explanation: CloudTrail + CloudWatch monitoring/alarming surfaces mistakes quickly.

mc.question: When writing policies for compliance, you must consider:

options.B: Both which actions AND where (region) they're permitted

mc.explanation: Region-residency requires controlling where actions occur, not just which actions are allowed.

short.question: How do you enforce data-residency restrictions?
short.answer: Answer: Via Organizations SCPs or IAM/S3 bucket policies that condition actions on allowed regions.

short.question: What is a common accidental violation?
short.answer: Answer: Backing up or replicating data to a disallowed region for resilience.

short.question: Which services need extra care?
short.answer: Answer: Backups/replication for RDS, Aurora, Redshift, and other data stores.

short.question: How do you detect mistakes quickly?
short.answer: Answer: Monitor with CloudTrail and CloudWatch alarms.

short.question: What must policies consider beyond 'what'?
short.answer: Answer: Where (which region) actions are permitted.

quizzes.title: Quiz — IAM — Users, Groups, and Policies

mc.question: A user Charles belongs to both the Developers group and the Audit group. What policies apply to him?
mc.explanation: A user in multiple groups inherits all of those groups' policies.

mc.question: Which statement about IAM groups is TRUE?

options.D: A user must belong to a group

mc.explanation: IAM groups contain only users; they can't be nested, and a user need not belong to any group.

mc.question: Which policy element specifies which API calls are allowed or denied?
mc.explanation: Action lists the API calls; Effect is Allow/Deny; Resource is the target; Principal is who.

mc.question: What should the root account be used for?

options.B: Initial account setup only, then use IAM users

mc.explanation: Use root only for initial setup, then create and use IAM users.

mc.question: A policy attached to a single user (not a group) is called:
mc.explanation: An inline policy is attached directly to a single user.

short.question: What is IAM and is it regional?
short.answer: Answer: Identity and Access Management — a GLOBAL service for creating users, groups, and policies.

short.question: What can IAM groups contain?
short.answer: Answer: Only users (no nested groups); a user can be in multiple groups or none.

short.question: Name the IAM policy statement elements.
short.answer: Answer: Effect (Allow/Deny), Principal, Action, Resource, and optional Condition.

short.question: How does policy inheritance work?
short.answer: Answer: Group policies apply to all members; inline policies apply to one user; multi-group users inherit all their groups' policies.

short.question: What is the root account for?
short.answer: Answer: Initial account setup only — then use IAM users (never share root).

quizzes.title: Quiz — IAM — MFA and Password Policies

mc.question: Even if a user's password is stolen, what prevents account compromise?
mc.explanation: MFA requires something you own (a device) in addition to the password, so a stolen password alone isn't enough.

mc.question: Which virtual MFA app supports multiple tokens on a single device?
mc.explanation: Authy supports multiple tokens on one device; Google Authenticator handles one phone at a time.

mc.question: What does a password policy help defend against?
mc.explanation: Requiring strong, non-reused, expiring passwords defends against brute-force attacks.

mc.question: MFA combines which two factors?

options.B: Something you know (password) and something you own (device)

mc.explanation: MFA combines a known password with an owned security device.

mc.question: Which is a physical U2F MFA device?
mc.explanation: A YubiKey (Yubico) is a physical U2F security key supporting multiple users.

short.question: What two defenses protect IAM users?
short.answer: Answer: A password policy and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).

short.question: What does MFA combine?
short.answer: Answer: Something you know (password) and something you own (a security device).

short.question: Name virtual MFA options.
short.answer: Answer: Google Authenticator (one phone) and Authy (multiple tokens on one device).

short.question: Name a physical MFA option.
short.answer: Answer: A U2F key like YubiKey (also hardware key fobs like Gemalto; SurePassID for GovCloud).

short.question: What does a password policy configure?
short.answer: Answer: Minimum length, character types, expiration, and preventing password reuse.

mc.question: An EC2 instance needs to read from S3. What's the secure way to grant this?

options.A: Embed IAM user access keys on the instance
options.B: Attach an IAM role to the instance

mc.explanation: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance so it assumes the role's permissions securely (no embedded keys).

mc.question: IAM roles are intended to be used by:

options.B: AWS services (assumed to act on your behalf)

mc.explanation: Roles are assumed by AWS services to perform actions on your behalf.

mc.question: Which is a common IAM role?
mc.explanation: EC2 instance roles (and Lambda/CloudFormation roles) are common IAM roles.

mc.question: A Lambda function needs permission to write to DynamoDB. What do you attach?
mc.explanation: Attach an IAM role (execution role) to the Lambda function granting the needed permissions.

mc.question: How is a role different from a user?

options.B: Roles are assumed by services; users are for people

mc.explanation: Roles are assumed by AWS services; users represent people.

short.question: What are IAM roles for?
short.answer: Answer: Granting permissions to AWS services (assumed, not owned by people) to act on your behalf.

short.question: Give an example.
short.answer: Answer: An EC2 instance role letting the instance access S3/DynamoDB, etc.

short.question: Name common roles.
short.answer: Answer: EC2 instance roles, Lambda function roles, and CloudFormation roles.

short.question: Why use a role instead of embedding user keys?
short.answer: Answer: Roles are the secure way to grant service permissions without exposing long-lived credentials.

short.question: Who assumes a role?
short.answer: Answer: AWS services (not people).

quizzes.title: Quiz — Encryption 101 — In Flight, At Rest, Client-Side

mc.question: Which encryption protects data as it travels over the network and prevents man-in-the-middle attacks?
mc.explanation: Encryption in flight (TLS/SSL) protects data over the network so only the target can read it.

mc.question: You don't trust the storage server to ever see plaintext. Which approach?
mc.explanation: Client-side encryption encrypts/decrypts on the client so the server never sees plaintext.

mc.question: In server-side encryption at rest, who performs the encryption?

options.B: The server (after receiving the data, using a data key)

mc.explanation: The server encrypts the data at rest using a data key after receiving it.

mc.question: What does HTTPS on a website indicate?

options.B: Encryption in flight via TLS certificates

mc.explanation: HTTPS indicates encryption in flight using TLS certificates.

mc.question: Client-side encryption often uses which technique?
mc.explanation: Client-side encryption commonly leverages envelope encryption.

short.question: What is encryption in flight?
short.answer: Answer: TLS/SSL (HTTPS) encrypting data over the network so only the target can read it (prevents man-in-the-middle).

short.question: What is server-side encryption at rest?
short.answer: Answer: The server encrypts stored data with a data key after receiving it, decrypting before sending back.

short.question: What is client-side encryption?
short.answer: Answer: The client encrypts/decrypts data end-to-end; the server never sees plaintext (often envelope encryption).

short.question: What does HTTPS indicate?
short.answer: Answer: Encryption in flight via TLS certificates.

short.question: When use client-side encryption?
short.answer: Answer: When you don't trust the storage server to see plaintext.

mc.question: You must copy a KMS-encrypted EBS volume to another region. What is required (keys are per-region)?

options.B: Snapshot the volume, re-encrypt the snapshot with a different KMS key in the target region, then restore
options.C: Move the key to the other region

mc.explanation: KMS keys are region-scoped; you snapshot, re-encrypt with a different key in the target region, then restore.

mc.question: How do you audit who used a KMS key and when?

options.B: CloudTrail (every key-use API call is logged)

mc.explanation: CloudTrail logs every KMS key-use API call for auditing.

mc.question: Which KMS key type is used for encryption performed OUTSIDE AWS by users without KMS access?

options.B: Asymmetric (public key to encrypt, private to decrypt)

mc.explanation: Asymmetric keys let external users encrypt with the downloadable public key while you decrypt with the private key.

mc.question: What happens if a KMS key has NO key policy?
mc.explanation: Without a key policy, no one can access the key (unlike some other resources).

mc.question: How often are AWS managed KMS keys automatically rotated?
mc.explanation: AWS managed keys rotate automatically every year; customer managed keys can be auto (set period) or on-demand.

short.question: What is AWS KMS and how is key usage audited?
short.answer: Answer: A managed key service integrated with IAM; every key-use API call is auditable via CloudTrail.

short.question: Symmetric vs asymmetric KMS keys?
short.answer: Answer: Symmetric = one key for encrypt/decrypt (AWS services, key never exposed); asymmetric = public/private pair for encryption outside AWS or sign/verify.

short.question: Name the key ownership types.
short.answer: Answer: AWS owned (free), AWS managed (free, aws/<service>), and customer managed ($1/mo, importable).

short.question: How do you copy an encrypted volume across regions?
short.answer: Answer: KMS keys are per-region: snapshot, re-encrypt with a different key in the target region, then restore.

short.question: What does a KMS key policy do?
short.answer: Answer: Controls access to the key (like a bucket policy); without one, no access; custom policies enable cross-account access.

mc.question: Macie uses which technology to classify data?

short.question: What is Amazon Macie?

short.question: How does it notify you?

short.question: What's the exam cue for Macie?

short.question: What technology does Macie use?

mc.question: What can Secrets Manager do that SSM Parameter Store cannot?

short.question: What is AWS Secrets Manager?
short.answer: Answer: A managed service to store secrets with forced rotation (every X days) and auto-generation via Lambda.

short.question: How does it differ from SSM Parameter Store?
short.answer: Answer: Secrets Manager can force scheduled rotation and auto-generate secrets; Parameter Store cannot.

short.question: What integration is a key exam cue?
short.answer: Answer: RDS/Aurora credential storage and rotation → Secrets Manager.

short.question: How are secrets encrypted?
short.answer: Answer: With KMS.

short.question: What do multi-region secrets enable?

mc.question: You want to protect a web app from SQL injection and XSS at Layer 7. Which service, and which target is NOT supported?

options.B: WAF; supported on ALB/API Gateway/CloudFront but NOT NLB

mc.explanation: WAF protects at Layer 7 on ALB, API Gateway, CloudFront, AppSync, and Cognito — but not the NLB (Layer 4).

mc.question: You need WAF protection AND a fixed IP for your application. How?

options.B: Front the ALB with AWS Global Accelerator and attach the Web ACL to the ALB

mc.question: Which WAF rule type helps mitigate Layer-7 DDoS by limiting requests per IP?
mc.explanation: Rate-based rules count requests per IP and can block IPs exceeding a threshold (DDoS protection).

mc.question: At which layer does WAF operate?
mc.explanation: WAF operates at Layer 7 (HTTP).

mc.question: Web ACLs are scoped how?
mc.explanation: Web ACLs are regional, except for CloudFront where they're global.

short.question: What does AWS WAF protect against and at what layer?
short.answer: Answer: Common web exploits (SQLi, XSS) at Layer 7 (HTTP).

short.question: Which targets does WAF support, and which not?
short.answer: Answer: ALB, API Gateway, CloudFront, AppSync, Cognito User Pools — NOT the NLB (Layer 4).

short.question: How do you get a fixed IP with WAF?
short.answer: Answer: Front the ALB with AWS Global Accelerator and attach the Web ACL to the ALB.

short.question: Name WAF rule types.
short.answer: Answer: IP sets, header/body/URI filters (SQLi/XSS), size constraints, geo-match, and rate-based (DDoS).

short.question: How are Web ACLs scoped?
short.answer: Answer: Regional, except global for CloudFront.

mc.question: Your infrastructure is being flooded by requests from many computers worldwide to overwhelm it. Which service protects against this?

mc.question: What extra capability does Shield Advanced provide for Layer-7 attacks?

mc.question: Which resources does Shield Advanced protect?
